entries.name: Historical Romance
entries.description: The past as a pressure system, chosen for what it forbids.
entries.principle: The parent form, and the one where the promise is hardest to pay honestly, because the historical record supplies obstacles that were not resolvable and endings that were not available. A historical romance is a negotiation between two incompatible obligations: fidelity to a period whose constraints were real, and delivery of an ending the period would not have granted. The subgenres below are not settings but different settlements of that negotiation.
entries.example: Georgette Heyer's Regency novels solved it by treating period constraint as a comedy of manners rather than a tragedy; Kathleen Woodiwiss's The Flame and the Flower took the opposite settlement in 1972 and made the constraint brutal; Courtney Milan's Brothers Sinister novels solve it a third way, by choosing protagonists whose historical position made an unconventional ending genuinely reachable.
entries.application: Decide which settlement you are making before you research, because it determines which facts are load-bearing. If your ending requires the period to bend, engineer the bend into the characters' specific circumstances — money, law, distance, an unusual family — rather than into the period itself. Readers forgive an improbable individual and never forgive an anachronistic society.

entries.name: Regency
entries.description: Nine years of English history carrying the weight of an entire commercial genre.
entries.principle: The most codified setting in romance and the most misunderstood: it is not a period but a constructed idiom, invented in the 1930s and refined for ninety years, in which a narrow marriage market, an elaborate etiquette and a strict information economy produce obstacles from manners alone. Its central technical gift is that it makes proximity scarce and conversation consequential, so a conversation in a ballroom can carry the load an action sequence carries elsewhere.
entries.example: Georgette Heyer built the idiom in Regency Buck in 1935 and codified its vocabulary across thirty further novels — Austen supplies the period, Heyer supplies every convention; Loretta Chase's Lord of Scoundrels demonstrated that the idiom could carry serious psychological damage; Julia Quinn's Bridgerton novels showed it could carry lightness at scale; Mary Balogh uses it for grief and disability with no loss of period texture.
entries.application: Learn the idiom before you break it, because the readership knows it better than you do. Use the information economy — who may speak to whom, who is watching, what cannot be said aloud — as your primary obstacle generator, and reserve invented scandal for when the real constraints have run out. If your Regency could be relocated to a modern office without structural change, you have written a costume drama.

entries.name: Georgian & Victorian
entries.description: The century either side of the Regency, with looser rules and heavier consequences.
entries.principle: Two settings usually shelved with the Regency and structurally distinct from it. The Georgian is coarser, more violent and more openly transactional, which permits a rakishness the Regency has to code; the Victorian brings industry, empire, professional work and a far more punitive sexual double standard, which makes ruin a material rather than a social catastrophe. Both give a writer something the Regency withholds: characters who work for a living.
entries.example: Heyer's These Old Shades established the Georgian register in 1926; Jo Beverley's Malloren novels and Elizabeth Hoyt's Maiden Lane series exploit its violence and its class range; Lisa Kleypas and Sherry Thomas use the Victorian's professional and industrial classes; Courtney Milan uses its legal and scientific institutions as the actual machinery of plot.
entries.application: Choose Victorian when you want your characters to have occupations and your obstacle to have a paper trail, and Georgian when you want the constraint loosened and the stakes bodily. In the Victorian especially, let ruin be economic as well as social — a woman losing her position or her custody is more legible to a modern reader than a woman losing her invitations.

entries.name: Medieval
entries.description: Marriage as treaty, and love as the thing that happens afterwards.
entries.principle: The setting where the arranged or forced marriage is not a contrivance but the historical default, which makes it the natural home of the marriage-first plot: the couple begins bound and must find their way to consent inside an arrangement neither chose. The period's low documentation is a licence and a trap — it grants freedom, and it tempts writers into a generic pseudo-past assembled from other novels.
entries.example: Kathleen Woodiwiss's The Wolf and the Dove brought the conquest-and-captivity plot into the modern genre; Roberta Gellis's Roselynde Chronicles demonstrated that dense legal and property detail makes the period more romantic rather than less; Johanna Lindsey's medievals sold the adventure register at scale.
entries.application: Anchor the marriage in a specific transaction — land, alliance, wardship, a disputed inheritance — so the bond has terms the plot can test. The consent problem is the whole subgenre: show the couple renegotiating a union they did not choose, and the ending pays. If you skip the transaction, you have a fantasy setting with mud in it.

entries.name: Highland & Scottish
entries.description: A conquered culture, written mostly by and for the conquerors' descendants.
entries.principle: Commercially one of the most durable settings in the genre and ethically the one most in need of care, because its appeal rests on a romanticised clan society whose destruction was recent, deliberate and documented. Structurally it offers what the English historical cannot: a hero outside the metropolitan social contract, a genuine culture clash, and a language barrier that makes intimacy an achievement rather than an assumption.
entries.example: Diana Gabaldon's Outlander made the setting a global phenomenon and grounds its appeal in specific Jacobite history rather than generic tartan; Julie Garwood's The Bride established the comic English-bride-in-the-Highlands template; Karen Marie Moning and Monica McCarty work the two opposite poles of the setting, the paranormal and the closely researched.
entries.application: Name the century and the political situation, because "Highland" spans an occupation, two risings and a clearance, and the difference is the difference between a courtship and an atrocity. Use the culture clash for the obstacle and give the Scottish party the interiority — the version where a Highland hero exists to be tamed by an English heroine is the failure mode this setting is most prone to.

entries.name: Western & Americana
entries.description: Isolation, labour, and a courtship conducted without an audience.
entries.principle: The American historical setting, defined by the absence of the social apparatus that drives the English line: no ballroom, no chaperone, no marriage market. Obstacles come instead from distance, weather, work and danger, and proximity is enforced by geography rather than by scandal. The mail-order-bride and marriage-of-convenience plots are native here for the same reason the treaty marriage is native to the medieval — they were ordinary.
entries.example: Linda Lael Miller and Jodi Thomas established the modern frontier register; Lorraine Heath brought damage and grief into it; Beverly Jenkins's westerns restore the Black West that the setting's popular version erased, using documented settlement, cavalry and homesteading history.
entries.application: Make the labour real and let it do the courtship work — two people getting a herd through a winter is a proximity engine no ballroom can match. Research whose West you are writing, because the monocultural frontier of the mid-century screen version is a fabrication, and the actual demographics offer better stories than the myth.

entries.name: Contemporary Romance
entries.description: The hardest setting, because nothing external stops anyone.
entries.principle: The genre's largest category and its most technically demanding, precisely because the modern world has dismantled the obstacles the historical line runs on: no ruin, no chaperone, no legal barrier to a woman leaving. Every obstacle must therefore be internal, professional or self-imposed, which is why weak contemporary romance collapses into misunderstanding — the writer needs a barrier and has not built one out of character.
entries.example: Jennifer Crusie's Bet Me generates its obstacle entirely from two people's incompatible theories about themselves; Susan Elizabeth Phillips builds hers from status and public exposure; Emily Henry's Beach Read makes grief and artistic vocation the barrier; Talia Hibbert's Chloe Brown novels locate it in chronic illness and the fear of being managed.
entries.application: Build the obstacle from something the character would defend as a virtue — loyalty, ambition, self-sufficiency, a duty of care — because a barrier the reader respects survives contact with the modern world. If your entire conflict evaporates when the two of them have one honest conversation, you have not written a conflict; you have written a delay.

entries.name: Romantic Comedy
entries.description: The promise delivered in a register that admits it knows the ending.
entries.principle: Not a lighter romance but a differently loaded one: comedy pre-agrees with the reader that the couple will end together, and spends its tension on how ridiculous the route will be. That agreement is a licence to build obstacles from pride, error and self-deception rather than from harm — and a constraint, because a comic frame cannot absorb a wound it has not earned the tone to carry.
entries.example: Helen Fielding's Bridget Jones's Diary reset the voice-driven comic register in 1996; Jennifer Crusie's novels remain the best demonstration that farce and genuine emotional stakes can share a scene; Christina Lauren and Ali Hazelwood carry the workplace-comedy form into the current market, Hazelwood's The Love Hypothesis attaching it to academic science.
entries.application: Put the comedy in the character's judgment rather than in events — a funny person making a defensible bad decision is renewable, while a funny situation is spent once. Decide how much pain your tone can hold before you write the black moment, because the commonest failure in the form is a third act that suddenly demands the reader take seriously a book that has spent 250 pages promising they need not.

entries.name: Small-Town Romance
entries.description: A community that functions as chaperone, chorus and obstacle at once.
entries.principle: The contemporary line's most successful solution to the problem card 7 states: it re-imports the social apparatus the modern setting removed. A small town restores surveillance, reputation, unavoidable proximity and a cast that has opinions — the Regency's machinery in a modern register. Its second engine is return: someone comes back, and the past is still standing there with an address.
entries.example: Debbie Macomber's Cedar Cove and Robyn Carr's Virgin River built the modern template and the interconnected-series economy around it; Susan Mallery's Fool's Gold demonstrated the model at scale; Lucy Score's Things We Never Got Over carried it into the indie market and to bestseller lists in 2022.
entries.application: Give the town a specific economic reason to exist and a specific reason people cannot easily leave, or the constraint is decorative. Cast the secondary characters as an actual chorus with a stake in the outcome — in this subgenre the community is a character with a position on the romance, and books that treat it as scenery lose the only obstacle the setting supplies.

entries.name: Billionaire & Tycoon
entries.description: A power differential large enough to be the plot.
entries.principle: The contemporary line's other answer to the missing-obstacle problem, and the one most often written badly: extreme wealth reintroduces class, dependency and coercive potential into a setting that had abolished them. The subgenre is only as good as its honesty about that coercion — the fantasy is rescue and access, the craft problem is consent under a gradient the characters cannot pretend away.
entries.example: Harlequin's Presents line has run the tycoon plot as a continuous laboratory for decades; E.L. James's Fifty Shades of Grey took it to unprecedented scale in 2011–12 and drew sustained criticism for how it handled the gradient; Sylvia Day's Bared to You worked the same territory with markedly more attention to negotiated consent.
entries.application: Name the power gradient on the page and let the less powerful party have real leverage of their own, or the reader is watching a transaction rather than a courtship. The most reliable structural fix is to make the wealthy party need something the other cannot be bought into providing, and to let refusal be genuinely available.

entries.name: Sports Romance
entries.description: A career with a clock on it, and a body that is also a livelihood.
entries.principle: Structurally excellent because it supplies a legible external stakes system for free: seasons, rankings, contracts, injury and a short professional life. It also supplies enforced proximity through teams, travel and training, and a public dimension that makes private choices consequential. The recurring craft failure is treating the sport as flavour rather than as the source of the conflict.
entries.example: Susan Elizabeth Phillips's Chicago Stars novels established the American template; Elle Kennedy's The Deal and Sarina Bowen's hockey novels drove the new-adult and college-set boom; Rachel Reid's Game Changers series works the same machinery in queer hockey romance, where the closet and the locker room are the same problem.
entries.application: Make the sport's calendar the plot's calendar, so that the relationship's crisis and the professional crisis are the same event rather than neighbours. Let at least one character face the sport's real ending — injury, decline, retirement — because the mortality of an athletic career is the emotional material the setting exists to provide.

entries.name: Military & First Responder
entries.description: Duty as the rival, and danger as the timetable.
entries.principle: A subgenre built on a single structural asymmetry: one party has an obligation that outranks the relationship and can be invoked without warning. That produces separation the couple did not choose, a reunion economy, and a fully justified secrecy that other contemporary settings have to manufacture. It also carries an obligation of accuracy, because the readership includes the people depicted.
entries.example: Suzanne Brockmann's Troubleshooters series set the standard for combining team ensemble, procedural credibility and long-arc romance; M.L. Buchman's military romances work the same procedural register; Katie Ruggle's first-responder novels transplant it to search-and-rescue and small-town emergency services.
entries.application: Research the rank structure, the deployment cycle and the rules on relationships, because the constraints are already dramatic and inventing looser ones costs you both credibility and plot. Let the duty win at least once — a book in which the obligation is always conveniently suspended has removed the very asymmetry that makes the subgenre work.

entries.name: Paranormal Romance
entries.description: Desire with a metaphysics, and a mate bond that argues with consent.
entries.principle: Defined not by monsters but by a supernatural rule system that governs attraction itself: fated mates, bonding, scent-recognition, claiming. That system solves the contemporary line's obstacle problem by making the attraction non-negotiable, and creates the subgenre's signature ethical difficulty in the same move, because a bond neither party can refuse is a bond neither party can consent to.
entries.example: Christine Feehan's Dark Prince opened the modern boom in 1999; J.R. Ward's Dark Lover and Sherrilyn Kenyon's Dark-Hunter novels built the brotherhood-series model; Nalini Singh's Slave to Sensation is the strongest demonstration that a mating bond can be treated as a problem the characters must solve rather than a shortcut past courtship; Stephenie Meyer's Twilight took the form to a mass readership outside the genre's normal channels.
entries.application: Decide what your bond can and cannot override, and write that rule down before drafting, because the entire consent question in your book descends from it. The strongest version gives the bond a cost or a refusal condition — a mate who can walk away and does not is a choice, and a choice is what the promise requires.

entries.name: Romantasy / Fantasy Romance
entries.description: Two genres' promises in one book, and they do not automatically agree.
entries.principle: The current commercial centre of gravity, and structurally the most conflicted form in the genre. A fantasy plot wants a world with consequences and an arc that can span volumes; the romance promise is a guarantee about the book in the reader's hand. The dominant convention — one couple carried across several volumes — defers the guarantee past books one, two and three, which is not a variation on the promise but an IOU against it, and the reason so many romantasy series feel structurally unsatisfying in the middle.
entries.example: Jacqueline Carey's Kushiel's Dart demonstrated in 2001 that a fantasy world could be built out of an erotic and romantic logic rather than decorated with one; Sarah J. Maas's A Court of Thorns and Roses established the modern series template and the deferral convention with it; Rebecca Yarros's Fourth Wing carried the form to a scale that reorganised publishing schedules; Naomi Novik's Uprooted shows the single-volume settlement, where the promise is paid in full on delivery.
entries.application: Decide explicitly whether each volume pays the promise or defers it, and signal that choice to the reader in the first book, because an unsignalled deferral reads as a broken contract rather than as momentum. If you defer, the non-terminal volume still owes a completed emotional movement — a resolved question, a bond confirmed at a new level — or it owes the reader nothing at all. This is treated at length in the Relationship & Emotional Craft collection.

entries.name: Science-Fiction & Alien Romance
entries.description: The Other, negotiated rather than defeated.
entries.principle: Where paranormal inherits its rules from folklore, this subgenre invents them, which makes it the genre's laboratory for biological and cultural difference as a courtship problem: incompatible bodies, incompatible customs, translation failure, and a partner whose reproductive and social biology is genuinely not the reader's. Its second engine is confinement — a ship, a colony, a hostile planet — which supplies proximity no social setting can equal.
entries.example: Anne McCaffrey's Restoree carried a romance structure into commercial science fiction in 1967; Lois McMaster Bujold's Shards of Honor built a courtship out of two officers' incompatible codes of honour; Linnea Sinclair established the modern trade template; Ruby Dixon's Ice Planet Barbarians became the indie market's defining example of the form from 2015.
entries.application: Make one difference genuinely load-bearing — a biology, a custom, a mating requirement — and follow it through the whole book rather than distributing several as texture. Confinement is your best friend and your worst crutch: use the enclosed setting for the proximity, but give the characters somewhere to go, or the middle of the book has no geography to move through.

entries.name: Time-Travel Romance
entries.description: A lover who is also an era, and a choice that cannot be split.
entries.principle: The subgenre where the obstacle is structural rather than personal: two people who love each other belong to periods that cannot both hold them, so the ending demands that someone give up a century. That makes it the purest sacrifice plot in romance, and it lives or dies on whether the surrendered life was shown to be worth something.
entries.example: Jude Deveraux's A Knight in Shining Armor made the form a commercial category in 1989; Diana Gabaldon's Outlander, published in 1991, built an entire multi-volume saga on the cost of the choice rather than the novelty of the mechanism; Audrey Niffenegger's The Time Traveler's Wife, outside the genre's channels, showed the same structure used for grief rather than adventure.
entries.application: Establish what the traveller loses in concrete terms — people, work, medicine, a mother — before the choice arrives, because a sacrifice of an unexamined life is not a sacrifice. Keep the mechanism simple and consistent; readers forgive an unexplained stone circle and never forgive rules that bend to rescue the plot.

entries.name: Monster Romance
entries.description: A partner who is not human-shaped, and a genre arguing about what that means.
entries.principle: The fastest-growing speculative form and the one most often dismissed without being read. Structurally it isolates the question the whole genre is built on — can you be loved as you actually are — by making one party unmistakably outside the human standard of desirability, so that acceptance cannot be mistaken for attraction to a socially approved surface. Its comic and its earnest registers are both legitimate and should not be blended carelessly.
entries.example: The lineage runs through the Beauty and the Beast tradition and Angela Carter's The Bloody Chamber, which reads that tradition's sexual politics without flinching; in the current market C.M. Nascosta's Morning Glory Milking Farm demonstrated the comic-domestic register and Lily Mayne's Monstrous series the earnest one.
entries.application: Commit to the non-human body as a fact with consequences — logistics, biology, how the world treats them in public — because a monster who is a handsome man with horns is a costume, not a premise. Decide your register early; the comic version's tonal contract cannot absorb the earnest version's cruelty, and the earnest version cannot survive a joke at the monster's expense.

entries.name: Romantic Suspense
entries.description: Two promises running on one clock.
entries.principle: A hybrid with a hard structural requirement: the romance and the danger plot must be the same plot, not alternating chapters. When the threat is what forces the couple together and the relationship is what makes them vulnerable to it, the form is superb; when the mystery could be resolved without the romance, the book is two thin novels stapled together. Its native trust problem — is this person who they claim to be — is also its best emotional material.
entries.example: Mary Stewart established the modern form in the 1950s with novels such as Madam, Will You Talk?, in which the heroine's curiosity is both the plot engine and the danger; Nora Roberts and Sandra Brown built the American commercial template; Linda Howard and Karen Rose work the darker procedural end of it.
entries.application: Tie the two plots at a single joint: the thing that endangers her should be the thing she cannot tell him, or the thing he is hiding should be the thing that saves her. Resolve the danger before the emotional resolution, not simultaneously — a couple who commit to each other while still being shot at have made a decision under duress, which is exactly what the promise is supposed to rule out.

entries.name: Gothic Romance
entries.description: A house, a husband, and a question about both.
entries.principle: The genre's oldest continuous form and its most structurally distinctive: the romantic interest is also the suspect, so attraction and fear are generated by the same person and the same evidence. That fusion is the whole subgenre. It runs on isolation, an over-articulated building, a suppressed family history and an information deficit maintained by everyone except the heroine.
entries.example: Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre supplies the template and its moral spine; Daphne du Maurier's Rebecca perfected the form's central manoeuvre, in which the reader's suspicion is the plot; Victoria Holt's Mistress of Mellyn opened the mid-century paperback boom in 1960 and Phyllis A. Whitney and Barbara Michaels sustained it; Simone St. James's novels demonstrate the current dual-timeline settlement.
entries.application: Keep the suspicion genuinely live — the moment the reader is certain he is innocent, the subgenre has ended and a different book is in progress. Make the house's layout knowable and its history partly documented, so investigation has somewhere to go, and give the heroine a material reason she cannot simply leave, because a modern reader will ask.

entries.name: Dark Romance
entries.description: Coercion on the page, and an ending that has to earn its way out.
entries.principle: Defined by the deliberate presence of what other subgenres exclude — captivity, violence, revenge, a partner who is genuinely dangerous to the protagonist rather than to third parties. It is the genre's hardest promise to pay, because the ending must convert a coercive situation into a chosen one without pretending the coercion did not happen. Its content-signalling apparatus is entirely informal and community-maintained, which is a market fact with craft consequences.
entries.example: Anne Stuart's Black Ice brought a genuinely lethal hero into mainstream category-adjacent publishing; C.J. Roberts's Captive in the Dark and Penelope Douglas's Corrupt defined the modern indie form; Ana Huang's Twisted series carried its softer end to mass scale in the 2020s.
entries.application: Decide what the book is arguing about the coercion, because the form has no neutral position: either the character is changed by being confronted, or the book is endorsing what it depicts. Give the captive party agency that is real and exercised, not merely asserted, and put the reckoning on the page — the version that skips from cruelty to devotion without a cost is where this subgenre fails, and it fails often.

entries.name: Mafia & Organised-Crime Romance
entries.description: A marriage plot with a body count, and a moral position the book must take.
entries.principle: Structurally a historical marriage-of-convenience plot relocated into a modern setting that still practises arranged alliances, hierarchy, honour and inheritance — which is exactly why it works, and why it is the busiest current subgenre in the dark register. Its craft problem is not the violence but the ethics of the family business, which the book must either confront or knowingly aestheticise.
entries.example: Cora Reilly's Born in Blood series established the modern template of arranged alliance and dynastic obligation; Danielle Lori's The Sweetest Oblivion and Ana Huang's crime-adjacent novels carried it to the top of the indie charts through the late 2010s and 2020s.
entries.application: Give the family a specific structure — who outranks whom, what the alliance is for, what breaking it costs — because the hierarchy is the obstacle generator and a vague criminal atmosphere generates nothing. Let the protagonist reckon with the business at least once on the page; the books that endure in this subgenre are the ones where somebody names what the money is.

entries.name: Motorcycle Club
entries.description: A found family with bylaws, and a woman's position inside them.
entries.principle: Distinguished from other crime romance by its explicit and codified gender structure: the club has ranks, rules and named roles for women, which the book must engage rather than assume. That structure supplies the subgenre's real subject — belonging bought at the price of autonomy — and its best books are about whether the price is payable.
entries.example: Kristen Ashley's Motorcycle Man and Joanna Wylde's Reaper's Property, both from the early 2010s, established the modern form; Madeline Sheehan's Undeniable pushed its brutality and its multi-decade timeline further than the template usually allows.
entries.application: Write the club's rules explicitly and let them cost the heroine something she minds losing, because a club with no enforceable rules is just a group of men with motorcycles. The strongest version gives her a route to standing within the structure that is not simply attachment to one man — otherwise the ending resolves a romance and leaves the actual conflict untouched.

entries.name: Queer Romance
entries.description: The promise, delivered to people the genre spent a century excluding.
entries.principle: Not a tonal variant but a structural one, because several of the genre's default obstacle engines behave differently: the closet supplies a secrecy problem with real stakes, family and legal recognition cannot be assumed as the ending's furniture, and the historical settings' constraints move from social to criminal. Its central craft demand is that the happy ending be specific — what these two people can actually have, in this place, at this date.
entries.example: KJ Charles's historical novels use the criminalisation of the period as structural constraint rather than as tragedy; Alexis Hall's Boyfriend Material and Casey McQuiston's Red, White & Royal Blue demonstrated the commercial reach of the comic register in 2019–20; Cat Sebastian works the historical line and Rachel Reid the contemporary sports setting.
entries.application: Define what the happy ending consists of in your specific setting before you write it — marriage, safety, a life together in private, emigration — because the genre's default HEA furniture is jurisdiction-dependent and assuming it produces a hollow last chapter. Do not make homophobia the only obstacle; a romance in which the sole conflict is external oppression has given the couple nothing to solve between them.

entries.name: Sapphic Romance
entries.description: A tradition with its own presses, its own history and its own structural problems.
entries.principle: Distinct from queer romance generally in publishing history and in craft. It developed largely outside mainstream romance in independent presses, so its conventions were set by a different market; and it removes the gender-role asymmetry that a great deal of the genre's obstacle machinery quietly depends on, which means pursuit, protection and status differentials must be rebuilt from character rather than inherited.
entries.example: Sarah Waters's Tipping the Velvet and Fingersmith brought the historical sapphic novel to a wide literary readership; Radclyffe and the independent presses sustained the category for decades before the mainstream arrived; Casey McQuiston's One Last Stop, Alexandria Bellefleur's Written in the Stars and Ashley Herring Blake's Delilah Green Doesn't Care mark its recent mainstream commercial expansion.
entries.application: Build your differential from something other than gender — money, fame, age, expertise, who wants it more — because the ready-made asymmetries the rest of the genre borrows are not available. Read the independent-press tradition before writing in the category; its conventions differ from mainstream romance's in pacing and in heat expectations, and the readership knows the difference.

entries.name: Black Romance
entries.description: A tradition that was built, erased from the record, and rebuilt.
entries.principle: A body of work with its own founding dates, imprints and editorial history, which the standard genre history routinely omits — and the omission is itself part of the subject. Its craft distinctions are real: the community as a source of support rather than only of surveillance, the professional and historical settings that the mainstream genre treated as unmarketable, and a relationship to the "ruin" plot that the genre's default assumptions do not fit.
entries.example: Rosalind Welles's Entwined Destinies, published by Dell in 1980, is the first category romance with Black protagonists by a Black author, acquired under the editor Vivian Stephens; Kensington's Arabesque line launched in July 1994 under the editor Monica Harris; Beverly Jenkins's Night Song opened a historical practice grounded in documented nineteenth-century Black American life; Brenda Jackson, Kennedy Ryan and Alyssa Cole carry the tradition into the current market, Cole's An Extraordinary Union returning to the Civil War as espionage romance.
entries.application: Research the specific historical material rather than importing the mainstream historical's assumptions, because Black settlement, military service, professional class and church life supply obstacles and communities the standard templates do not contain. Treat the erasure as a documented fact when it is relevant and not as a grievance aside — the History collection carries it in full.

entries.name: Multicultural & Diaspora Romance
entries.description: Two families, two sets of obligations, and a courtship conducted between them.
entries.principle: Structurally the modern genre's closest relative to the historical marriage plot, because it restores something the Western contemporary abandoned: families with a legitimate stake in the outcome, and obligations that a protagonist can honour without being a coward. Its recurring failure is to reduce culture to food, festival and disapproving parent, which converts a rich obstacle system into set dressing.
entries.example: Sonali Dev's novels build conflict from the specific obligations of Indian and Indian-American family structures rather than from generic disapproval; Uzma Jalaluddin's Ayesha at Last transposes a familiar plot into a Muslim community in Toronto with its own internal politics; Helen Hoang and Jasmine Guillory work the American contemporary with the family stake intact.
entries.application: Give the family a position the reader can respect and let it be partly right, because an obstacle that is simply prejudice is one the plot can only defeat, never negotiate. Locate the conflict inside the community as well as at its boundary — internal disagreement about how to belong is where this subgenre's best material lives.

entries.name: Inspirational & Christian Romance
entries.description: A courtship with a third party in it.
entries.principle: Defined not by the absence of sex but by the presence of faith as an active participant: the characters' relationship with God is a plot line, and the romance must be compatible with it. That produces a genuinely distinct structure — a conversion or restoration arc running alongside the courtship — and a distinct market, with line guidelines that specify content at sentence level.
entries.example: Janette Oke's Love Comes Softly launched the modern category in 1979 and established the frontier-and-faith template; Francine Rivers's Redeeming Love brought a much darker redemption arc into it; Karen Kingsbury built the family-saga register; Harlequin's Love Inspired line, launched in 1997, codified the requirements that most of the category now works within.
entries.application: Make the faith load-bearing — a character whose belief costs them something in the plot — or the category's readers will read it as decoration, which is the most common criticism from inside the market. Read the line guidelines if you are writing for one; they are content specifications rather than suggestions, and they are covered in Market & Category Conventions.

entries.name: Amish Romance
entries.description: A community whose rules are the entire obstacle system.
entries.principle: Usually shelved under inspirational and structurally its own thing, because the constraint is communal and enforceable rather than personal: courtship is governed by the Ordnung, and leaving carries the concrete penalty of shunning. That gives the subgenre something the wider inspirational category lacks — a genuine, specified cost for choosing love against the community — and an obligation of accuracy toward a living people who do not write these books.
entries.example: Beverly Lewis's The Shunning opened the modern category in 1997 and named its central mechanism in the title; Wanda Brunstetter and Cindy Woodsmall built the sustained commercial market that followed.
entries.application: Research the specific affiliation you are depicting, because Amish practice varies materially between communities and a generic version is both inaccurate and dramatically inert. Let the Ordnung actually bind — the subgenre's whole power is that the rules are real and the penalty is real, and a book in which the community bends at the end has spent its own premise.

entries.name: Erotic Romance
entries.description: Sex as the site of the plot, not an interruption to it.
entries.principle: Distinguished from erotica by the promise: erotica is organised around desire and need not end in commitment, while erotic romance is a romance in which the sexual relationship is the primary vehicle for the emotional one. The structural requirement is therefore strict — every scene must change the relationship state, because scenes that merely repeat are the form's characteristic failure and the reason it is dismissed.
entries.example: Black Lace in the UK from 1993 and Ellora's Cave in the US from 2000 built the market and proved the demand ahead of mainstream publishing; Robin Schone's The Lady's Tutor demonstrated the historical register; E.L. James's Fifty Shades of Grey moved the category into mass-market visibility from 2011; Tiffany Reisz's The Siren showed the form carrying literary ambition and a genuine ethical argument about power.
entries.application: Give each scene a specific job — a boundary crossed, a truth admitted, a power shift — and cut any scene that leaves the couple where it found them. Negotiate on the page; in this subgenre consent is craft rather than compliance, and the books readers return to are the ones where the conversation before is as charged as the act.

entries.name: Reverse Harem / Why-Choose
entries.description: A promise made to more than two people.
entries.principle: The form that most directly tests what the central guarantee actually requires, by refusing the assumption that the satisfying ending is monogamous. Its structural demand is severe and usually underestimated: every relationship in the group needs its own arc, and the group itself needs a fourth arc, so a four-person book carries roughly the load of three romances plus an ensemble. The market's preferred term has shifted toward "why choose," which names the promise rather than the configuration.
entries.example: Laurell K. Hamilton's Anita Blake novels carried a multiple-partner structure into mainstream commercial fiction well before the category had a name; the modern form is overwhelmingly indie and Kindle Unlimited-native, with series such as Jaymin Eve and Jane Washington's Curse of the Gods establishing its conventions from 2017.
entries.application: Build the relationships between the partners, not only between each partner and the centre, because a group that has no bond except one shared person is a queue rather than a family. Give each pairing a distinct obstacle and resolution, and make the ending's arrangement explicit — the promise here is not that everyone is present at the end but that the arrangement is stable and chosen.

entries.name: Writing Toward a Known Ending
entries.description: The destination is fixed, so the tension has to come from the route.
entries.principle: Romance surrenders the cheapest source of narrative tension — will it work out — before page one, and every other structural decision descends from that surrender. What replaces it is not suspense about the outcome but suspense about the cost: what these two will have to give up, admit or become in order to arrive somewhere the reader already knows they arrive. A romance that tries to generate doubt about the ending is fighting its own contract and will read as either grim or dishonest.
entries.example: Jennifer Crusie's Bet Me is transparent about its ending from the first chapter and generates its tension entirely from two people's incompatible theories of themselves; Loretta Chase's Lord of Scoundrels holds attention across a long middle by making the question how much damage can be undone rather than whether the couple will marry; Mary Balogh's novels frequently open with the marriage already contracted, which removes the last residual doubt on purpose.
entries.application: Ask of every scene what it costs one of them, not whether it advances the outcome. When you feel the urge to introduce doubt about the ending, introduce doubt about the price instead — the reader will accept any amount of the second and none of the first.

entries.name: Beat Sheets and Their Limits
entries.description: Useful maps, routinely mistaken for the territory.
entries.principle: The genre has two widely used structural models and both are misapplied in the same way. Pamela Regis identified eight elements that recur across four centuries of the form, and stated explicitly that they can occur in any order, be doubled or tripled, or coexist in a single scene; and a decade later wrote that she would likely relabel them "pragmatic" rather than essential — an intention she stated in print rather than a revision she published. Almost every secondary account presents them as a sequence, which converts a description of what the genre does into a prescription for what a book must do next.
entries.example: Regis's A Natural History of the Romance Novel is the source of the eight elements and of the caution about their order; Gwen Hayes's Romancing the Beat offers the opposite kind of tool, an explicitly prescriptive four-phase beat sheet designed for drafting rather than for description, and is honest about being one.
entries.application: Use a descriptive model to diagnose a finished draft and a prescriptive one to get a first draft written, and never confuse which you are holding. If a beat sheet tells you the black moment belongs at 75% and your book's obstacle resolves naturally at 60%, the book is not wrong — but you now owe the last 40% a different job, and you should know what it is before you write it.

entries.name: Placing the Meet
entries.description: Everything before the two of them are in a room together is prologue.
entries.principle: The first meeting is the load-bearing structural event of the opening, because the relationship clock does not start until it happens and readers experience pre-meet material as delay regardless of its quality. In category-length work the meet is typically inside the first chapter; in longer single-title and historical work it can be later, but every page before it must be doing work that would be impossible afterwards.
entries.example: Julia Quinn's The Duke and I places its principals in contact almost immediately and spends its length on the consequences; Daphne du Maurier's Rebecca delays the second and more important meeting — with the house — for a long stretch and earns it because the delay is the book's subject; Diana Gabaldon's Outlander spends substantial length before the meet because it is establishing the mechanism that makes the relationship impossible.
entries.application: If your leads have not met by the end of your first act, be able to say what the pre-meet pages establish that could not be established through her eyes after he arrives. Reunion and second-chance structures are the exception that proves the rule: they front-load a meet that already happened, which is why they can open slowly and still feel fast.

entries.name: The Middle Without Repetition
entries.description: The genre's characteristic failure is not a bad ending but a stalled centre.
entries.principle: A romance middle must escalate along two axes at once — intimacy increasing and the obstacle hardening — and the commonest structural fault is a middle that repeats a single beat with cosmetic variation: another almost-kiss, another interrupted conversation, another retreat. Escalation means each encounter leaves the couple somewhere they cannot return from, so that the barrier has to be reinforced rather than merely re-asserted.
entries.example: Nalini Singh's Slave to Sensation escalates by making each contact physically and psychically costlier under an established rule system; Lisa Kleypas's historicals typically escalate social exposure alongside intimacy, so the two curves cross; Susan Elizabeth Phillips's Chicago Stars novels raise public stakes each time the private ones rise.
entries.application: Chart your middle as two lines and check that both move at every encounter. If a scene could be deleted without the reader losing information about either the closeness or the barrier, it is a repetition — cut it or give it a job. A useful test: after each middle scene, name the thing they now cannot un-know.

entries.name: Every Scene Changes the Relationship State
entries.description: The genre's single most transferable scene-level rule.
entries.principle: In a form where the plot is a relationship, a scene earns its place by altering that relationship's state — what they know about each other, what they owe each other, what they have admitted, what they can no longer do. This is stricter than the general rule that a scene should change something, and it is the standard against which romance middles, sex scenes and secondary-character scenes should all be tested.
entries.example: Talia Hibbert's Get a Life, Chloe Brown structures its middle around a list, so each scene has a declared external task and a concealed relational one; Jennifer Crusie's dialogue scenes characteristically end with one party in possession of information they did not want; Nora Roberts's long output is unusually consistent in giving each encounter a specific state change rather than a mood.
entries.application: Write the state change in the margin before drafting the scene, in the form "after this, she knows X" or "after this, he owes her Y." Scenes that resist this test are usually there for atmosphere or because the writer enjoys the characters, both of which are real pleasures and neither of which is structure.

entries.name: Duration and the Insta-Love Problem
entries.description: How much time the book covers is a structural decision, not a detail.
entries.principle: Reader resistance to fast attraction is almost never about speed of feeling; it is about insufficient evidence. A book covering four days can be entirely convincing if those days contain enough proof of character under pressure, and a book covering two years can fail if the couple's time together is asserted in summary. Compressed durations demand a pressure cooker — danger, confinement, a deadline — because extremity is what makes rapid knowledge plausible.
entries.example: Ruby Dixon's Ice Planet Barbarians compresses attraction into survival conditions where the evidence accumulates fast and physically; Mary Stewart's suspense novels typically run days and use danger to license the speed; Robyn Carr's Virgin River novels take the opposite settlement, running months and using accumulated ordinary competence as the evidence.
entries.application: Count the on-page hours your couple actually spend together, not the calendar the book covers — the first number is the one the reader feels. If the compressed version is what you want, supply an external pressure that would make anyone learn anyone else quickly, and let the reader watch the learning rather than being told it happened.

entries.name: Subplot Discipline
entries.description: A romance subplot exists to put pressure on the main line or it does not exist.
entries.principle: Because the central plot is a relationship, subplots have a narrower legitimate function here than in most fiction: they must generate proximity, supply an obstacle, expose character under conditions the romance cannot create, or provide the external stakes that make the internal ones legible. A subplot that merely runs alongside is not a subplot but a second book sharing a spine, and it is the most common reason a romance feels slack.
entries.example: Suzanne Brockmann's Troubleshooters novels tie the operational plot directly to the couple's trust problem, so the mission and the relationship fail and succeed together; Courtney Milan's historicals build legal and scientific subplots that are the mechanism of the obstacle rather than its neighbour; the weaker romantic-suspense tradition, in which the investigation could be excised without touching the courtship, is the standing counter-example.
entries.application: For each subplot, complete the sentence "without this, the couple would not have to —." If you cannot finish it, the subplot is decorative. The strongest fix is usually not deletion but attachment: give the subplot a fact that one of them must conceal from the other.

entries.name: Length as Structure
entries.description: Word count is not a container the story is poured into; it is a specification of the story.
entries.principle: Romance is the genre in which length is prescribed before writing more often than not, and each band produces a different structure. A 50,000-word category novel supports one obstacle, one setting and two points of view; a 100,000-word single title supports a secondary cast, a subplot and a second reversal. Writing a single-title structure at category length produces a book that feels rushed at the end, and the reverse produces the stalled middle described at card 4.
entries.example: Harlequin's category lines have run to specified word-count bands for decades and their novels show the resulting discipline — one obstacle, worked hard; Nora Roberts's trilogies and Diana Gabaldon's Outlander sit at the far end of the same continuum, where length permits an ensemble and a multi-strand plot.
entries.application: Decide your length before your outline and cut your obstacle count to fit — roughly one substantial obstacle per 40,000 words is a workable starting ratio. The specific bands, and the lines that enforce them, are in Market & Category Conventions; the craft point is only that the number changes the book's shape rather than its size.

entries.name: Dual Point of View as the Default
entries.description: The genre's dominant convention, and a promise readers hear you making.
entries.principle: Contemporary romance overwhelmingly alternates between the two leads, and the convention is load-bearing rather than fashionable: it lets the reader hold information one party lacks, which converts misunderstanding into dramatic irony; it proves the attraction is mutual without either party having to say so; and it makes the black moment survivable because the reader can see both sides refusing. Its cost is suspense — a reader inside both heads cannot be genuinely uncertain about feeling.
entries.example: Loretta Chase's Lord of Scoundrels uses dual POV to let the reader see two people misread each other with full access to both readings; Elle Kennedy's The Deal alternates first-person chapters to the same end in a contemporary register; Nalini Singh's Psy-Changeling novels rely on it to make a non-human interiority legible alongside a human one.
entries.application: Alternate on a scene or chapter boundary and give each lead a distinct informational position, or the second POV is only a second camera. Note that some category lines specify POV contractually — Love Inspired requires hero and heroine only, no secondary characters and no first person — so in category work this is a market rule before it is a craft choice.

entries.name: Single Point of View and What It Buys
entries.description: The older settlement, and still the right one for whole subgenres.
entries.principle: Restricting the reader to one consciousness buys back the uncertainty dual POV spends. If the reader cannot see inside him, then whether he is trustworthy, whether he returns the feeling and what he is concealing all become live questions, which is precisely what the gothic and much of romantic suspense are built on. The cost is that his interiority must be inferred from behaviour, which demands harder writing at the level of the scene.
entries.example: Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre and Daphne du Maurier's Rebecca both depend absolutely on the reader being locked out of the man's head; Victoria Holt's Mistress of Mellyn inherits the technique wholesale; Emily Henry's Beach Read demonstrates the same restriction working in a modern comic register, where the withheld interiority is a grief rather than a secret.
entries.application: Choose single POV when the man's reliability is a question the book is asking, and then be ruthless — one accidental paragraph of his thinking collapses the entire structure. Compensate by giving him observable behaviour that supports two readings at once, so the reader can be wrong in an interesting way rather than merely uninformed.

entries.name: First Person, Present Tense, and the Romantasy Shift
entries.description: A convention imported from young-adult fiction that is now reshaping the genre's largest growth area.
entries.principle: The dominant romantasy voice is first person, frequently present tense, and frequently confined to the female lead — which breaks the dual-POV convention the rest of the genre treats as a promise. The trade is deliberate: immediacy and a strong marketable voice in exchange for the mutuality that dual POV supplies for free, which is why so many books in this mode append a bonus chapter in the hero's voice to give readers what the structure withheld.
entries.example: Rebecca Yarros's Fourth Wing works in first-person present throughout and demonstrates both the propulsion and the informational cost; Sarah J. Maas's A Court of Thorns and Roses established the single-lead first-person settlement for the modern romantasy series; Alexis Hall's Boyfriend Material shows first-person single POV used for comic voice rather than for immediacy, in a contemporary setting.
entries.application: If you write single first person, plan explicitly for how the reader will learn that the feeling is returned, because you have given up the mechanism the genre normally uses. A bonus chapter is a patch, not a design; the better answer is behaviour the reader can decode ahead of the narrator, which turns the restriction into dramatic irony instead of a deficit.

entries.name: Deep Point of View and the Head-Hop
entries.description: Two different techniques that the genre's style guides frequently conflate.
entries.principle: Deep POV removes the narrative filter — no "she felt," no "he realised" — so that perception arrives as unmediated experience; head-hopping switches consciousness inside a scene. Deep POV is a prose discipline and head-hopping is a structural choice, and they are independent. The modern market strongly prefers deep POV and mostly penalises mid-scene switching, but the objection to head-hopping is practical rather than moral: it disperses tension by giving the reader every party's position at the moment tension depends on incomplete information.
entries.example: Nora Roberts moves between consciousnesses more freely than current style guidance permits and holds tension by switching only at natural pressure releases; Talia Hibbert's contemporaries demonstrate deep POV maintained across an entire novel; Georgette Heyer's free indirect style sits outside both conventions and remains readable, which is a caution against treating either as a rule.
entries.application: Learn deep POV as a default and treat a mid-scene switch as a deliberate, rare instrument with a stated purpose. If you switch, switch at a beat where the reader has just been given something, not while they are waiting for something — the objection is to dissipating tension, not to the movement itself.

entries.name: The Interiority Budget
entries.description: Thinking is the genre's primary material and its primary way of stalling.
entries.principle: Romance runs on interiority — the whole point of the form is access to the experience of falling — but internal monologue does not advance state, and a book that processes every event at length stops moving. The workable ratio puts interiority immediately after a state change, where it converts event into consequence, and starves it in the approach to one, where it functions as delay.
entries.example: Mary Balogh's novels place substantial reflection after decisive scenes and very little before them; Emily Henry's first-person narrators are heavily interior and are kept moving by an external structure of tasks and deadlines; the recurring weakness of a great deal of unpublished manuscript work is a middle in which two characters think about each other in alternating chapters without meeting.
entries.application: Put the thinking after the blow, not before it. If a character is deciding whether to act for more than a page, convert the decision into a scene with someone else in it — a resolution reached alone is a summary, and a resolution reached under pressure from another person is a plot.

entries.name: Honest Withholding
entries.description: What a point-of-view character may keep from the reader without cheating.
entries.principle: A POV character may withhold what they are not currently thinking about, and may not withhold what is at the front of their mind while the narration reports the rest of it. The distinction matters because romance is full of secrets and the genre's cheapest device is a narrator who conceals their own known intention until a reveal. Done honestly, withholding produces the recognition scene; done dishonestly, it produces a reader who feels lied to and re-reads to find the seam.
entries.example: Daphne du Maurier's Rebecca withholds by restricting the narrator's knowledge rather than her honesty, which is why the reveal survives re-reading; Sarah Waters's Fingersmith builds its structure on a narrator's genuine ignorance rather than on concealed intention; the standard failure — a first-person narrator who does not mention the thing she has been planning for a hundred pages — is common enough in the category to be a recognisable reader complaint.
entries.application: Test every concealment by asking whether the character is thinking about it during the scenes where you have suppressed it. If they are, either move the reveal earlier or change the structure so they genuinely do not know. Suppression of attention is legitimate; suppression of the reader's access to a stated consciousness is not.

entries.name: The Epilogue and the Coda
entries.description: A convention the genre defends and the wider literary culture mocks.
entries.principle: The epilogue exists because the promise is about a future the main narrative cannot reach: the reader is guaranteed an emotionally satisfying optimistic ending, and a jump forward supplies evidence rather than assurance. Its craft requirement is that it answer a question the book raised — the specific doubt about durability, not a general one — and its failure mode is a catalogue of babies and weddings that answers nothing.
entries.example: Julia Quinn's Bridgerton novels use second epilogues, published separately, precisely because readers wanted the durability evidence rather than more plot; Nalini Singh's series epilogues typically confirm a rule-system consequence established earlier, which is the strongest available use; Jane Austen's closing summaries are the form's distant ancestor and are notably brief.
entries.application: Write the epilogue to close the specific fear the black moment raised — if the doubt was that he would choose the work over her, show the choice recurring and going the other way. If your epilogue would work unchanged at the end of a different book, it is decoration and the novel ends better without it.

entries.name: Voice as the Actual Product
entries.description: In a genre with known plots, the sentences are the differentiator.
entries.principle: When the ending is guaranteed and the tropes are declared in the marketing copy, what a reader chooses between is voice — the particular quality of attention, humour and phrasing a writer brings to material everyone else is also using. This is why romance readerships are unusually author-loyal and why the genre's bestsellers are rarely the ones with the most original premises.
entries.example: Georgette Heyer's readership has survived ninety years on idiom rather than on plot novelty, since her plots recur; Jennifer Crusie and Susan Elizabeth Phillips are read for a specific comic intelligence rather than for what happens; Beverly Jenkins's voice carries substantial historical exposition without slowing, which is a stylistic achievement rather than a research one.
entries.application: Write the scene everyone writes, then find the observation only you would make in it. Resist the advice to neutralise your prose for the market; a competent invisible style is the one thing that cannot distinguish you in a category where competence is the entry requirement.

entries.name: Banter That Does Work
entries.description: The difference between two people flirting and two people performing.
entries.principle: Functional banter is a negotiation conducted in the register of a joke: each exchange moves position, tests a boundary or concedes ground, and the humour is the medium rather than the content. Non-functional banter is a series of individually good lines in which nobody's position changes, and it reads as characters auditioning. The test is whether the exchange could be summarised as an event.
entries.example: Loretta Chase's exchanges in Lord of Scoundrels are simultaneously funny and materially transactional, with each speech extracting something; Jennifer Crusie's dialogue characteristically ends with one party having conceded more than they intended; Christina Lauren's contemporaries demonstrate the modern high-volume version, where the pace itself signals compatibility.
entries.application: After drafting a banter scene, write down what changed. If the answer is that they are now more charming, cut it to a third and put the missing state change in. Give one of them something to want from the conversation — banter with an objective is a scene, and banter without one is filler with good jokes.

entries.name: The Argument Scene
entries.description: Where the book's real disagreement finally gets said out loud.
entries.principle: The argument is the genre's most concentrated craft test because it must be simultaneously in character, unfair in the specific way real arguments are unfair, and informative — the reader should learn the shape of the obstacle from what each party chooses as a weapon. Its characteristic failure is the argument in which both parties articulate their positions clearly and reasonably, which is a debate, not a fight.
entries.example: Mary Balogh's confrontation scenes let characters say the cruel accurate thing and then live with having said it; Kennedy Ryan's contemporaries build arguments where both positions are defensible and incompatible, so no reconciliation is available through logic; Sonali Dev's family conflicts turn on the participants' unequal access to what may be said aloud.
entries.application: Give each party one weapon they should not use and let at least one of them use it. Have someone win the argument and lose the position, or lose it and be right — an argument that resolves on the merits has removed the reason the couple needed to change.

entries.name: The Physicality of Talk
entries.description: Dialogue in this genre is choreography as much as speech.
entries.principle: Because so much of a romance happens between people who are not yet touching, the space around the dialogue carries a large share of the meaning: distance closed and reopened, hands, where the eyes go, who moves first. Action beats replacing dialogue tags are not merely a style preference — in a form about proximity, the beat is where the plot is.
entries.example: Lisa Kleypas's scenes track physical distance with unusual precision, so that a half-step is legible as an event; Sarah Waters's Fingersmith conveys an entire developing relationship through the handling of objects and clothes; Nalini Singh uses scent and touch as literal information channels within her rule system, making the physical beat carry plot rather than mood.
entries.application: Choreograph the scene before you write the speech — mark where each is standing and what changes. Use beats rather than adverbs and let one physical detail per scene be the thing the reader remembers; if you can delete every beat and lose nothing, the conversation is happening between disembodied positions.

entries.name: Period Idiom and the Anachronism Line
entries.description: Historical dialogue is a constructed register, not a reconstruction.
entries.principle: No historical romance is written in period language and none should be; what readers respond to is a consistent invented idiom that signals pastness while remaining transparent. The genre's actual anachronism problem is rarely vocabulary — it is modern psychological and political framing put into a period mouth, which readers detect instantly even when they cannot name what is wrong.
entries.example: Georgette Heyer's Regency idiom is a literary construction assembled from period sources and is now more influential on the subgenre than the sources themselves; Sherry Thomas's Victorians maintain register while carrying modern emotional complexity; Beverly Jenkins's historicals demonstrate how documented period detail lets a character hold a modern-seeming position that was in fact historically available.
entries.application: Build a short list of banned and required words and apply it consistently rather than reaching for archaism scene by scene. Test your characters' beliefs, not just their vocabulary: a heroine may hold a radical view if the period contained radicals and the book knows which ones, and may not hold a therapeutic view of herself that nobody had yet formulated.

entries.name: Casting the Pair
entries.description: Two characters designed so that contact is unavoidable and comfort is not.
entries.principle: The pair is a designed object, and the design criterion is productive friction: each must have something the other needs and something the other cannot tolerate, so that proximity is simultaneously rewarding and destabilising. Complementarity alone produces a couple with no reason to struggle; opposition alone produces two people with no reason to stay in the room.
entries.example: Loretta Chase's Lord of Scoundrels pairs a man convinced of his own monstrousness with a woman professionally incapable of accepting a valuation she has not verified; Nalini Singh's Slave to Sensation pairs an empath with a woman trained from birth to feel nothing, which is both the attraction and the lethal risk; Talia Hibbert's Chloe Brown pairs a woman who fears being managed with a man whose instinct is to take care of people.
entries.application: State the pair as a single sentence containing both the fit and the friction before drafting. If you can only articulate why they suit each other, you have a couple and not a plot; if you can only articulate the friction, you have an argument that will run for ninety thousand words.

entries.name: Both Leads Need a Plot
entries.description: A romance with one protagonist and one prize is a shorter book than it appears.
entries.principle: Each lead needs a want that exists independently of the relationship and would still be there if the other person vanished — a career, an obligation, a debt, a person to protect. This is what makes the choice at the end a real one, because the promise is only satisfying if the couple gave something up to reach it. A lead whose entire arc is the romance has nothing to trade.
entries.example: Suzanne Brockmann's Troubleshooters novels give both parties operational objectives that survive the romance; Courtney Milan's heroines characteristically have professional or legal projects that the courtship threatens; the standard failure is the category hero with a company and a heroine with a wound, where only one of them can lose anything.
entries.application: Write each lead's want and each lead's deadline on a separate line and check that neither reads "him" or "her." Then make the two wants incompatible enough that progress for one is a cost to the other — that incompatibility is your obstacle, and it will be more durable than any secret.

entries.name: The Wound and the Lie
entries.description: Backstory is a budget, and most drafts overspend it early.
entries.principle: Romance characters typically carry a formative injury and a false belief derived from it, and the relationship's function is to make the belief untenable. The craft problem is disclosure economy: the wound is most powerful as inference and least powerful as explanation, and a book that front-loads the trauma has converted its most valuable withheld information into exposition.
entries.example: Kennedy Ryan's contemporaries reveal formative material late and in fragments, so the reader assembles it; Mary Balogh's characters frequently disclose the wound to the other lead rather than to the reader first, which makes the telling itself the scene; the common weakness is a prologue depicting the injury, which spends the whole asset in the first five pages.
entries.application: Give the reader the behaviour before the cause, and let the other lead be the one who extracts the explanation. State the false belief in a single sentence — "no one stays," "I am only useful," "wanting things is dangerous" — and make sure the plot disproves that exact sentence rather than a general version of it.

entries.name: The Secondary Cast as Pressure
entries.description: Everyone else in the book is either applying force or taking up room.
entries.principle: Secondary characters in romance have a specific job: to supply the social weather the couple must move through — expectation, surveillance, obligation, competing claims on time and loyalty. A friend who exists to be confided in is a device for converting interiority into dialogue, which is legitimate but weak; a friend who wants something incompatible with the romance is a plot.
entries.example: Julia Quinn's Bridgerton siblings function as a permanent pressure system with opinions and interests of their own; Robyn Carr's Virgin River community operates as an active constituency in each courtship; Sonali Dev's families exert pressure that is neither villainous nor negotiable, which is the hardest and most useful version.
entries.application: Give each recurring secondary a stake in the outcome and let at least one of them be reasonably opposed. Cut or merge any character whose only function is to receive information; a confidante with a competing claim on the protagonist's loyalty does the same job and generates conflict while doing it.

entries.name: The Rival and the Ex
entries.description: A third party is a legitimate instrument and a very easy cheat.
entries.principle: A rival works when they represent a genuine alternative life the protagonist could plausibly choose, and fails when they exist to be revealed as unworthy. The reason is structural: a rival who is secretly awful resolves the triangle without anyone having to decide anything, which converts a choice into a discovery and removes the cost the ending is supposed to demonstrate.
entries.example: Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre gives its heroine a second offer that is serious, moral and survivable, which is what makes her refusal mean something; Sarah Waters's novels use rivals with real claims rather than disqualifying flaws; the standard weak version — the fiancé revealed as a cheat at the two-thirds mark — is common enough across the category to function as a recognisable shortcut.
entries.application: Make the rival someone the reader can see the protagonist marrying and being reasonably content with, then require an actual decision. If your third party has to be discredited for your ending to work, the ending is being handed over rather than earned.

entries.name: Chemistry Shown, Not Asserted
entries.description: The most-claimed and least-demonstrated quality in the genre.
entries.principle: Chemistry is not a property of characters but an effect produced in the reader by specific evidence: attention paid, accuracy of perception, the willingness to be changed by the other's presence. Narration reporting that a character is drawn to another produces nothing; a character noticing something about the other that no one else has noticed produces it immediately.
entries.example: Emily Henry's narrators demonstrate attraction through the precision of what they observe about the other person; Loretta Chase builds it through characters correctly reading each other's concealment; Rachel Reid's hockey novels generate it in shared professional competence, where each recognises what the other is doing before anyone else does.
entries.application: Replace every statement of attraction with an act of attention. Give each lead one thing they perceive about the other that is true and unflattering and that they keep to themselves — accurate private knowledge reads as intimacy faster than any amount of described desire.

entries.name: The Interconnected-Standalone Contract
entries.description: What book three owes the reader who came for book one's couple.
entries.principle: The genre's dominant series model gives each volume its own couple and its own complete promise, while carrying a shared world and a returning cast. The contract is precise: every book pays its own guarantee in full, previously resolved couples remain resolved, and no volume may create doubt about an ending already delivered. A reader who watched a couple earn their ending in book one experiences a manufactured crisis for them in book four as a breach rather than as a development.
entries.example: Lisa Kleypas's Wallflowers and Julia Quinn's Bridgerton novels each deliver a complete promise per volume while advancing a family; Robyn Carr's Virgin River novels do the same in a community frame; Nalini Singh's Psy-Changeling series carries a large arc across volumes while keeping each couple's resolution untouched once made.
entries.application: Let previous couples appear as stable and useful — dispensing advice, providing resources, modelling the ending — rather than as sources of renewed tension. If a resolved couple must face a difficulty, make it external and survivable and resolve it inside the same volume; the alternative devalues every ending in the series including the one the reader is currently buying.

entries.name: The Series Bible
entries.description: A continuity instrument, written early or paid for later.
entries.principle: Multi-book romance accumulates a specific kind of debt: names, ages, timelines, sibling order, who was in the room, what a rule system permits, and — uniquely to this genre — what each resolved couple's ending consists of, since that ending is a promise the series may not contradict. The bible is not worldbuilding apparatus but a liability register, and the entries that matter most are the small ones nobody expects to need.
entries.example: Nora Roberts's long trilogies and J.D. Robb's In Death series sustain continuity across decades of publication; Nalini Singh's Psy-Changeling books maintain an escalating rule system across many volumes where a single inconsistency would undermine earlier plots; Diana Gabaldon's Outlander sequence carries a timeline complex enough that readers maintain reference material of their own.
entries.application: Record ages, dates, physical details, the state of every resolved couple, and every rule your world has asserted, the day you assert it. Track what you have promised as carefully as what you have described — a rule stated once in book two is a constraint on book seven, and readers of this genre keep better notes than writers do.

entries.name: Seeding the Next Couple
entries.description: Casting forward without stealing from the book in hand.
entries.principle: Interconnected series must introduce future leads early enough that readers arrive invested, and the technique fails when the seeding takes attention the current couple needs. The reliable method makes the future lead useful to the present plot — an obstacle, an ally, a source of pressure — so that their page time is earned by the current book rather than borrowed from it.
entries.example: Julia Quinn's siblings appear throughout as active participants in each other's plots rather than as trailers; Lisa Kleypas's Wallflowers are introduced as a functioning alliance with a shared objective, so each is established while serving the first book; Susan Elizabeth Phillips's Chicago Stars novels frequently establish a future lead through professional conflict with the current one.
entries.application: Give the future lead a job in the current book before you give them a spark with anyone. Avoid pairing them off visibly in advance — a reader who can see the next book's couple across a crowded chapter is being marketed to rather than told a story, and the tension you are protecting for later is spent now.

entries.name: The Ensemble Town or Team
entries.description: A shared container that generates couples indefinitely.
entries.principle: The strongest series engines are institutions rather than families, because a town, team, firehouse, brotherhood or regiment supplies an endlessly renewable cast, a legitimate reason for strangers to be thrown together, and a set of shared rules that new arrivals must learn. The craft demand is that the institution have a real economy and a real hierarchy, or it becomes a backdrop that cannot generate anything.
entries.example: Robyn Carr's Virgin River and Debbie Macomber's Cedar Cove build community engines with functioning local economies; Suzanne Brockmann's Troubleshooters uses a unit whose operational structure generates both pairings and obstacles; Kristen Ashley's and Joanna Wylde's motorcycle-club series use an institution with explicit bylaws, which is why the constraint bites.
entries.application: Define what the institution does, who runs it, how someone joins and what it costs to leave, before you write the first couple. Those four answers will generate obstacles for every subsequent book; a setting defined only by its atmosphere will require you to import a new external problem each time.

entries.name: The Continuing Couple
entries.description: Following one pair past their ending without unmaking it.
entries.principle: A minority model, and the most technically difficult, because it must generate tension from a relationship the reader has been promised is secure. It works only when the source of tension moves outside the couple — a case, a war, an antagonist — and the relationship becomes the stable instrument through which the external plot is faced rather than the thing under threat. Manufacturing romantic doubt in this model breaks the original promise retroactively.
entries.example: J.D.
