Robb's In Death series marries its principals early and runs decades of investigation with the marriage as the reader's fixed point; Diana Gabaldon's Outlander sequence follows one couple through separations imposed entirely by history and circumstance; Ilona Andrews's Kate Daniels novels resolve the romance well before the series ends and continue on external stakes.
entries.application: Move the threat outside the marriage and keep it there. Generate development, not doubt: a continuing couple can face new roles, children, professional change and grief, and each of those alters the relationship without questioning it — which is what readers of this model come for.

entries.name: Length, Fatigue and the Exit
entries.description: Knowing what the last book is for, ideally before writing it.
entries.principle: Romance series are commercially rewarded for continuing and structurally punished for continuing too long: the shared container's rules get exhausted, the returning cast crowds each new couple, and later volumes increasingly service continuity rather than tell a story. Fatigue is diagnosable — when the current couple's page count falls to accommodate the ensemble, the series is running on accumulated goodwill.
entries.example: Long-running category and paranormal series across the genre show the pattern, with later volumes carrying substantial cast-servicing material; Julia Quinn's decision to publish second epilogues separately is an instructive alternative, satisfying continuity demand without spending a new book on it; Nalini Singh's practice of opening new arcs with new rule systems is the other durable answer.
entries.application: Count the proportion of each book given to the current couple, and treat a decline as a structural signal rather than a reader-service success. When it falls, either start a new arc with new rules or plan an exit — a series that ends deliberately keeps its earlier promises intact, and one that trails off retroactively devalues them.

entries.name: What the First Chapter Promises
entries.description: Every opening makes commitments the book will be judged against.
entries.principle: A romance opening declares four things whether the writer intends it or not: the register, the heat level, whose story it is, and what kind of obstacle is coming. Readers of this genre calibrate fast and abandon fast, and the commonest cause of a book being put down is not weak prose but a first chapter that promised a different book — a comic opening on a grief novel, or a quiet domestic opening on a suspense plot.
entries.example: Helen Fielding's Bridget Jones's Diary establishes voice, register and scope in its first page and never varies from them; Daphne du Maurier's Rebecca opens on the wrong end of the story and commits the reader to a retrospective structure immediately; Rebecca Yarros's Fourth Wing establishes tense, voice and mortal stakes within a few pages, which is what its readership had been told to expect.
entries.application: Read your first chapter and write down the four promises it makes, then check them against the book you actually wrote. Fixing a mismatch is nearly always a matter of changing the opening rather than the novel — the opening is the cheapest thing in the manuscript to replace and the most expensive thing to get wrong.

entries.name: The Blurb as a Structural Document
entries.description: In this genre the marketing copy is written before the book, and it is a specification.
entries.principle: Romance blurbs do something blurbs in other genres do not: they declare the tropes, the heat level and the configuration, which means the reader arrives with an itemised list of what they have been promised. Writing the blurb first is standard practice in much of the market and is a genuine drafting instrument, because a book that cannot produce a clean trope-forward blurb usually has an unclear obstacle rather than a marketing problem.
entries.example: The indie and Kindle Unlimited market has made trope-declarative blurb copy the norm, with the declared tropes frequently fixed before drafting begins; Harlequin's category lines have used tip sheets to specify content in advance for decades; the practice's formalisation is visible in current BISAC subject codes, which now include Enemies to Lovers, Fake Dating, Friends to Lovers, Second Chances and Love Triangle.
entries.application: Draft the blurb before the outline and treat any trope you cannot name as a structural gap. Then hold yourself to it: a book that under-delivers a declared trope generates the specific and damaging complaint that it was mis-sold, which readers of this genre report more precisely than readers of any other. The market mechanics are in Market & Category Conventions.

entries.name: Managing Trope Expectation
entries.description: Readers choose by trope, so a trope is a contract term rather than a description.
entries.principle: Because tropes are now selection criteria and filing categories rather than critical vocabulary, delivering one is a promise about the reading experience: enemies to lovers commits to actual antagonism, only-one-bed commits to the scene it names, and a fake-relationship book commits to the arrangement lasting long enough to matter. Subverting a declared trope is legitimate and must be done in addition to delivering it, not instead.
entries.example: The most durable enemies-to-lovers novels in the genre make the antagonism substantive and specific rather than a misunderstanding retrofitted as hostility; Casey McQuiston's Red, White & Royal Blue delivers its declared premise fully before complicating it; the recurring reader complaint about "enemies" who merely dislike each other mildly is the clearest evidence that the term now functions as a specification.
entries.application: Give each declared trope its full scene, at its full strength, before you do anything clever with it. If your enemies are not doing each other real damage, either write the damage or change the declaration — the audience for a subverted trope is people who got the trope first.

entries.name: Content Signalling and the Author's Note
entries.description: An entirely informal system that the writer is nonetheless responsible for.
entries.principle: Romance has the most developed content-warning culture in commercial fiction and no formal apparatus supporting it: retailer categories are coarse, BISAC carries a single dark-romance code and nothing finer, and every meaningful signal is author-supplied and community-enforced. The practical consequence is that the front matter is a craft surface — an author's note setting out content, heat and the shape of the ending is part of the reader contract, not an apology for the book.
entries.example: The dark-romance market operates almost entirely on author-supplied warnings and reader-maintained community lists; the closed-door and open-door distinction is signalled through cover, blurb and note rather than through any formal category; inspirational lines solve the same problem in the opposite direction, by making the imprint itself the signal.
entries.application: Signal content, heat and any deferral of the promise plainly in the front matter, and treat it as information rather than defence. Be specific about the ending's shape if it is not a conventional one — a reader who knows a volume ends on a cliffhanger can choose to enjoy it, and a reader who does not will report the book as having broken the genre's central guarantee.

entries.name: The Central-Promise Audit
entries.description: For every romance, run before submission and again after any structural revision.
items: Can you state, in one sentence, what the ending guarantees these two people have?
Does the book deliver that guarantee within its own covers, or does it defer it to a later volume?
If it defers, is the deferral signalled to the reader in the front matter and the blurb? (If not, you have written a cliffhanger the genre reads as a breach.)
Did the couple give something up to reach the ending, and can you name it?
Is the ending a choice the characters make, or a circumstance that resolves in their favour?
Would the ending still hold if the external plot had gone the other way?
Does the epilogue answer the specific doubt the black moment raised, rather than a general one?
Is there any point after the resolution where the book reopens the question? (If so, cut it — the promise is not a place the reader visits twice.)

entries.name: The Obstacle Test
entries.description: For any draft where the middle feels slow, repetitive or evasive.
items: Can you state the obstacle in one sentence that does not contain the word "misunderstanding"?
Would the obstacle survive a single honest conversation between the leads? (If not, it is a delay, not a conflict.)
Is the obstacle something at least one lead would defend as a virtue?
Do both leads have a want that exists independently of the relationship?
Are those two wants incompatible enough that progress for one costs the other?
Does the obstacle harden as intimacy increases, or does it merely persist?
Can you name what the couple cannot un-know after each middle scene?
If the obstacle is a secret, does keeping it remain the more defensible choice past the halfway point?

entries.name: Conflict Versus Misunderstanding
entries.description: For any draft in which the leads separate, argue, or withhold information from each other.
items: Is the withheld information something a reasonable person would withhold, for a reason they could state aloud?
Has either lead had a clear, uninterrupted opportunity to explain and declined it? (If so, can you defend the declining?)
Does the argument turn on incompatible positions rather than on incorrect information?
Does at least one lead say the cruel and accurate thing?
Could the conflict be resolved by a third party simply telling one of them the truth?
Does anyone behave out of character in order to keep the plot from resolving early?
Are interruptions being used to prevent a conversation more than once? (Twice is a device; three times is a tell.)
After the reconciliation, is the original disagreement actually settled, or merely overtaken by feeling?

entries.name: Chemistry and Proximity
entries.description: For any draft where readers report that they do not believe in the couple.
items: Is the attraction demonstrated through acts of attention rather than stated in narration?
Does each lead perceive something true about the other that nobody else has noticed?
Is there a structural reason these two are repeatedly in the same room?
Would the proximity survive if one of them decided to avoid the other? (If not, what forces it?)
Do they have at least one shared competence or shared task the reader can watch them perform?
Count the on-page hours they spend together — is it enough to justify what they claim to know?
Does each conversation change a position, or do they simply perform compatibility?
Is there a moment where one of them is unflattering and the other stays?

entries.name: Consent on the Page
entries.description: For any draft containing sex, coercion, a power differential, or a bond that overrides choice.
items: Is there a power gradient between the leads, and does the book name it?
Does the less powerful party have leverage of their own that they actually use?
Is refusal genuinely available at every point where consent is given?
If a supernatural or fated bond drives attraction, can it be refused, and does the book establish that before it matters?
Is enthusiastic agreement shown rather than inferred from absence of objection?
If the book depicts coercion, does it take a position on it, or does it depict and move on?
Does the period or subgenre convention you are following require its own framing on the page?
Would a reader be able to tell what the book thinks about what it has just depicted?

entries.name: Heat and Intimacy Function
entries.description: For any draft with on-page sex or a declared heat level.
items: Does each sex scene change what the couple know about or owe each other?
Could any scene be cut without altering the relationship's state? (If so, cut it.)
Does the heat level match what the cover, blurb and category have promised?
If the book is closed-door, does the scene break still carry a state change?
Is the first intimate scene placed where the obstacle is at its most costly to ignore?
Do the scenes escalate in emotional stakes rather than only in explicitness?
Is the negotiation before the act as charged as the act?
Does the physical writing stay in the point-of-view character's actual perception?

entries.name: Category and Market Fit
entries.description: For any manuscript intended for a specific line, imprint, or retail category.
items: Do you know which of the three taxonomies — retailer, publisher line, reader community — you are being judged against?
Does the word count sit inside the band for the target?
Does the point-of-view structure comply with the line's requirements, where the line specifies them?
Are the declared tropes actually delivered at full strength in the manuscript?
Does the heat level match the line's ceiling and floor?
Have you checked the line's prohibitions as well as its requirements?
If you are writing to a trope-forward market, was the blurb written before the draft?
Is anything in the manuscript that the target category structurally cannot accommodate?

entries.name: Writing Across Identity
entries.description: For any draft depicting a culture, faith, sexuality, disability or community the writer is not part of. Run before drafting, not after. Any single "no" is a stop, not a note.
items: Have you read work by writers from inside the community, in this genre, recently?
Is the community's internal disagreement present, or is it depicted as holding a single position?
Does the community supply support and pleasure in the book, or only obstacles?
Is the obstacle something the community would recognise, or something imported from outside assumptions about it?
If the setting involves a living faith or a living culture, is the practice accurate to a specific community rather than assembled generically?
Does the happy ending you are writing describe what these characters could actually have, in this place, at this date?
If you are writing a historically excluded group into a period setting, have you researched the documented record rather than assumed absence?
Would a reader from inside the community finish the book better informed, or recognise themselves as material?

entries.name: Enemies to Lovers
entries.description: Antagonism that is real, specific and costly, converted into its opposite without being retconned.

examples.text: Austen makes the hostility evidentiary rather than temperamental, so the reversal requires each of them to be shown wrong about a specific matter of fact rather than merely softened.
Chase keeps the antagonism materially transactional to the end, with each encounter extracting something, so that even the reconciliation is conducted as a negotiation rather than a surrender.
McQuiston grounds the enmity in a public incident with institutional consequences, which prevents the common failure of an antagonism that exists only in the two participants' moods.

entries.name: Rivals to Lovers
entries.description: Competition for the same scarce thing, where respect arrives before affection does.

examples.text: Thorne makes the rivalry structurally real by putting a single promotion between them, so every advance in intimacy is also a strategic concession.
The professional rivalry is the courtship, conducted entirely in overlapping speech, and the film never asks either party to stop competing in order to be together.
The commercial antagonism is genuinely asymmetrical and genuinely destructive, which is what gives the private correspondence its charge and what the film is least willing to resolve honestly.

entries.name: Friends to Lovers
entries.description: The risk is not rejection but the loss of something already working.

examples.text: The screenplay makes the friendship substantial enough to be worth protecting, so the central question is not whether they are attracted but whether attraction is worth the cost of the thing they already have. Its structural achievement is that the obstacle is generated entirely by the relationship's own value, which is the hardest and most durable version of this trope and the reason the film is still the reference point.
Austen builds the recognition out of long-established intimacy, so that the revelation is not that Knightley is loveable but that Emma has been consulting him about everything for the entire novel.
Nicholls executes the friendship and the deferral superbly and then declines the genre's guarantee, which places the book outside romance and makes it a useful boundary case rather than a model.

entries.name: Grumpy and Sunshine
entries.description: Temperamental opposition, where each party's default setting is unbearable to the other and necessary for them.

examples.text: Capra sets a cynic against an enthusiast and makes each one's manner a working method rather than a mood, so the conflict is about how to get through the world rather than about disposition.
The pairing works because the grumpy party's temper has a stated cause and a real cost to others, which keeps the softening from reading as a personality adjustment.

Hibbert inverts the expected assignment by giving the prickly role to the disabled heroine and the sunshine role to the man, which defuses the trope's habit of making one party the other's emotional caretaker.

entries.name: The Meet-Cute
entries.description: A first encounter engineered so that circumstance does the introducing.

examples.text: Guillory traps two strangers in a stopped lift and uses the enforced idleness to establish voice and compatibility before either has a chance to perform.
The collision is physical, undignified and immediately establishes the status gap the rest of the film is about, which is what separates a functional meet-cute from a charming accident.
Fielding stages the first encounter as a social humiliation observed by an audience, so the meeting carries information about class and family as well as about the two principals.

entries.name: The Meet-Ugly
entries.description: A first encounter that supplies the antagonism the rest of the book will spend.

examples.text: A single overheard sentence does the work of an entire first act, and Austen makes it retrievable rather than merely rude, so the insult can be repaid at the end.
Crusie has the heroine overhear a wager about her, which gives the antagonism a documentary basis that no amount of subsequent charm can simply dissolve.
The transactional premise means the relationship is founded on a concealed insult, so the eventual reckoning is structurally required rather than optional.

entries.name: Forced Proximity
entries.description: Circumstance removes the option of leaving, and the book finds out what is left.

examples.text: Gabaldon uses a hostile century as the confinement, so proximity is enforced by the impossibility of going anywhere at all rather than by a temporary inconvenience.
Dixon compresses survival, language barrier and physical dependence into a single premise, which is the most efficient version of the device in the current market.
A boat is the ideal confinement because it moves, so the couple are trapped together and the situation still changes around them.

entries.name: Only One Bed
entries.description: A logistical accident that converts an unspoken question into an immediate practical one.

examples.text: The blanket strung between the two beds makes the negotiation visible as an object, which is why the scene has been imitated for ninety years.
Hitchcock adds handcuffs to the shared room, demonstrating that the trope's real subject is enforced physical negotiation rather than furniture.
Proulx uses the shared tent as the point where deniability becomes impossible, which is the trope working at its full weight and outside the genre's promise.

entries.name: Trapped by Weather or Disaster
entries.description: An external event suspends ordinary life and licenses behaviour that ordinary life prevents.

examples.text: The blizzard is the mechanism that makes the repetition possible, and the film uses enforced time rather than enforced space, which is the same device rotated.
The storm strands three sets of characters simultaneously, demonstrating the device's usefulness as a structural connector rather than only as a proximity engine.
The disaster premise generates extraordinary proximity and then withholds the genre's guarantee, which makes it a romantic tragedy and a clean illustration of where the boundary sits.

entries.name: The Fake Relationship
entries.description: An arrangement that requires both parties to rehearse intimacy until the rehearsal stops being one.

examples.text: The fraud carries a legal penalty and a deadline, which supplies both a clock and a reason neither party can withdraw when it becomes uncomfortable.

examples.work: To All the Boys I've Loved Before
examples.text: Han gives each party a separate and incompatible motive for the arrangement, so the deception has two independent failure points rather than one.
Hall makes the performance a reputational necessity for both men in different registers, so the fake relationship is doing real work in two lives at once.

entries.name: Marriage of Convenience
entries.description: A contract entered for stated reasons, which then has to be renegotiated on different terms.

examples.text: Kleypas has the heroine propose the arrangement and set its conditions, which redistributes the power the trope usually hands to the man by default.
Garwood makes the marriage a political instrument between two cultures, so the private negotiation is also a diplomatic one.
The immigration premise supplies an external authority that must be convinced, which gives the couple a shared adversary and a reason to rehearse a private life in public.

entries.name: Arranged Marriage
entries.description: A union arranged by others, in which consent is the thing the book must go on to earn.

examples.text: Lori grounds the arrangement in a dynastic alliance with named obligations, so the constraint is enforceable rather than atmospheric.
Jalaluddin treats the arrangement as a live and internally contested practice within a specific community rather than as an obstacle imported from outside it.
The three daughters constitute a structured argument about the practice, with each successive refusal costing the family more, which is the most rigorous treatment the device has received on screen.

entries.name: Neighbours and Roommates
entries.description: Shared domestic space, where intimacy accumulates through logistics rather than through decision.

examples.text: Danan uses a shared lease to force cohabitation between people with incompatible public reputations, so the domestic detail is continuously loaded.
Henry puts two writers in adjacent houses with a professional wager between them, which converts every ordinary sighting into information.
Hibbert makes the man the building's superintendent, so proximity is an employment relationship as well as a domestic one and carries a power question with it.

entries.name: The Road Trip
entries.description: Confinement that moves, supplying enforced conversation and a changing external world.

examples.text: The journey to Leoch functions as a compressed education in a hostile society, so the travel does character work and exposition simultaneously.
The cross-country premise strips both parties of their social context, which is the device's central benefit: neither can be who they are at home.
A single day's wandering through a city achieves the same effect as a long journey, demonstrating that the requirement is displacement rather than distance.

entries.name: The Workplace
entries.description: A shared institution that supplies daily contact, hierarchy and a reason neither party can walk away.

examples.text: The shop provides an economic dependency that makes the antagonism consequential, since one of them can cost the other a livelihood.
Hazelwood sets the relationship inside an academic power structure and lets the structure supply the obstacle, which is more durable than any personal secret.
Thorne uses the shared office as a surveillance system, so that the couple's every interaction is performed for an audience of colleagues.

entries.name: The Bodyguard and the Protector
entries.description: One party is professionally responsible for the other's body, which makes distance impossible and objectivity fraudulent.

examples.text: The professional duty is genuinely incompatible with the attachment, and the film lets the incompatibility stand rather than resolving it by fiat.
Brockmann grounds the protective relationship in operational procedure, so the intimacy develops inside a rule structure that the reader can see being broken.

The protective dynamic slides into surveillance and decision-making on the protected party's behalf without the book registering the shift, which is the trope's characteristic failure mode rather than an incidental flaw.

entries.name: Correspondence and the Wrong Number
entries.description: Intimacy established in writing, between people who do not know who they are talking to.

examples.text: Richardson founded the whole tradition of the letter as the site of interiority, and the novel's power still comes from the reader having access to a document its recipients do not.
The correspondence and the enmity run on separate channels between the same two people, so the film's tension is entirely in the asymmetry of who knows what.
Rowell puts the reader's access to the correspondence inside a third character's job, which converts an old device into a genuine ethical problem about consent to being read.

entries.name: The Matchmaker and the Setup
entries.description: A third party arranges the meeting, and their motives become part of the plot.

examples.text: Austen makes matchmaking an exercise of social power with real casualties, so the heroine's competence at it is the thing the novel dismantles.
Kwan places the matchmaking pressure inside a family with money and standing at stake, so the interference has enforcement behind it rather than only opinion.
The matchmaker is a professional with an economic function in the community, which is the historically accurate version and the one that gives the practice weight.

entries.name: The Secret
entries.description: A withheld fact that would change everything, held by someone with a reason a reader can respect.

examples.text: Brontë makes the secret a living person with a legal claim rather than an item of information, so it cannot be resolved by disclosure and must be resolved by circumstance.
Du Maurier withholds through the narrator's genuine ignorance rather than through her dishonesty, which is why the revelation survives a second reading.
Waters gives two narrators incomplete and incompatible information, so the secret is structural rather than concealed, and neither party is required to behave stupidly to sustain it.

entries.name: The Big Misunderstanding
entries.description: The obstacle readers most reliably reject, and the one condition under which it works.

examples.text: The deception is engineered by a third party with a stated motive and material means, which is the only durable version: nobody is required to be foolish, only to be lied to competently.
The misinformation comes from an interested party and is plausible on its face, and the correction costs the heroine something rather than merely arriving.

The late separation turns on a misread that one honest exchange dissolves, which is the failure the whole trope is notorious for and a clear demonstration of why: an obstacle that evaporates on contact was never an obstacle.

entries.name: Duty Versus Desire
entries.description: An obligation that outranks the relationship and cannot be dismissed as cowardice.

examples.text: Austen makes the original refusal an act of deference to legitimate authority rather than a failure of nerve, which is what allows the novel to spend eight years on its consequences.
Brockmann gives the duty an operational structure with other people's lives attached, so choosing the relationship is genuinely not available at the moments it matters.
The obligation wins and the couple part, which is the trope executed at full strength and outside the genre's guarantee; instructive precisely because a romance cannot end here.

entries.name: The Class Divide
entries.description: Money and rank as a barrier with enforcement behind it.

examples.text: Gaskell makes the divide industrial rather than merely social, so the disagreement is about how people should be paid and the courtship cannot proceed until it is settled.
Kleypas gives the heroine capital and the hero a title, which inverts the usual direction of dependency and makes the marriage a genuine transaction between unequal assets.
Kwan locates the objection in a family with the means to enforce it, so the class barrier has a mechanism rather than only an attitude.

entries.name: Ruin and Reputation
entries.description: Social exposure as a material catastrophe rather than an embarrassment.

examples.text: Quinn uses a public compromise to force a marriage, demonstrating how efficiently the period's rules convert one observed moment into a lifetime arrangement.
Chase lets the heroine weaponise her own reputation deliberately, which turns a constraint imposed on women into an instrument one of them chooses to use.
Wharton shows the enforcement operating without anyone stating it aloud, which is the most accurate account of how the mechanism actually worked.

entries.name: The Forbidden Relationship
entries.description: A prohibition backed by law, family or institution, where the cost of proceeding is real.

examples.text: Forster wrote a deliberately happy ending for two men under a legal regime that criminalised them, and stated that the happy ending was the entire point and the reason the book could not be published in his lifetime. It is the clearest demonstration in English of the genre's central proposition — that an optimistic ending is an argument rather than an evasion — and it was made half a century before the genre organised itself enough to have the argument.
The prohibition is institutional and inherited rather than personal, which is why it cannot be negotiated and why the play resolves as tragedy rather than as romance.
Proulx makes the prohibition internal as well as external, so the barrier survives every change of circumstance that would have removed a purely social one.

entries.name: Forced Seduction
entries.description: The genre's discarded convention, in which the hero's sexual coercion of the heroine begins the romance.

examples.text: Woodiwiss's novel opened the modern historical boom and established a template in which the hero rapes the heroine early and the book proceeds as a courtship, with the assault functioning as the meeting rather than as an injury requiring reckoning. It teaches the wrong lesson at the level of structure rather than of taste: it establishes that the obstacle can be manufactured by the hero's violence and then dissolved by his subsequent tenderness, which removes the requirement that either party change.

Hull's novel supplied the abduction-and-coercion template half a century earlier and attached it to an orientalist fantasy of racial difference that the plot then resolves by revealing the abductor to be European. The two failures are connected and both were inherited: the coercion is laundered by the heroine's eventual consent, and the racial anxiety is resolved by retracting the premise rather than by examining it.

Roberts brings the same material into the self-aware dark-romance register, negotiating the coercion explicitly on the page, which is a genuine advance and still leaves the structural problem that the captor is the love interest.

entries.name: The Wager
entries.description: A bet with a person as its object, and the reckoning it obliges.

examples.text: Crusie has the heroine learn of the wager immediately, which converts a delayed betrayal into a live and negotiated fact between two adults.
Laclos treats seduction as a wager conducted between two experts and lets the instrument destroy the people using it, which is the device's most rigorous treatment in any language.
The bet is revealed late, the reckoning occupies a single scene, and the film's resolution requires the wronged party to absorb the injury without the book of account ever being settled.

entries.name: Revenge Courtship
entries.description: Attachment pursued as an instrument of harm against someone else.

examples.text: Brontë follows the logic to its conclusion across two generations and never suggests the revenge is recoverable, which is what makes it a novel about the cost rather than an endorsement.
Mitchell shows a marriage entered from spite failing on exactly those terms, and declines to supply the reconciliation the structure invites.
The revenge is contractual and itemised between the conspirators, which lets the novel show the accounting rather than the feeling.

entries.name: The Captive
entries.description: Confinement by one party of the other, and what the ending must do about it.

examples.text: Carey builds an explicit ethical and religious framework in which submission is chosen and revocable, so the confinement operates inside a system of consent the reader can see.
The film registers the imprisonment as wrong, has the captor release her before the resolution, and requires the return to be voluntary, which is the minimum the structure demands.

Woodiwiss grounds the captivity in the historical fact of conquest, which is more defensible than the invented version, and still resolves the coercion through the captor's improvement rather than through any reckoning available to the captive.

entries.name: The Deadline
entries.description: An external clock that forces decisions before the characters are ready to make them.

examples.text: The immigration deadline is administered by an indifferent third party, so it cannot be negotiated, deferred or charmed away.
Guillory uses a fixed social event as the terminus of an arrangement, which gives an otherwise low-stakes premise a date on which it must resolve.
Yarros attaches mortal risk to a training calendar, so the deadline supplies both urgency and a reason the couple cannot simply leave.

entries.name: The Prior Claim
entries.description: Someone else got there first, and their claim has standing.

examples.text: The prior claim is a legal marriage and a living woman, which is why it cannot be dissolved by anyone's preference and why the novel must remove it by other means.
Du Maurier makes the claim posthumous and therefore unanswerable, so the rival cannot be outcompeted, only reassessed.
Giffin sets the claim inside a friendship and then asks the reader to want the betrayal to succeed, without ever making the wronged party's loss cost the couple anything.

entries.name: Distance and Separation
entries.description: The barrier is physical and neither party is at fault, which removes blame and leaves only cost.

examples.text: Eight years of separation are the novel's actual subject, and Austen uses the interval to make both parties into people who could not have married at the start.
Deveraux makes the separation a matter of centuries, which converts the obstacle into a genuine sacrifice question rather than a logistical one.
Niffenegger makes the separations involuntary, recurring and unschedulable, so the relationship's problem is endurance rather than reunion.

entries.name: Incompatible Ambitions
entries.description: Two people whose wants are legitimate, achievable and mutually exclusive.

examples.text: Both parties want the same career and only one of them can have the other on the terms they are offering, and the film never pretends the conflict is resolved.
Hazelwood attaches the ambitions to an academic hierarchy in which advancement for one is structurally entangled with the other's position.
Henry makes the incompatibility aesthetic as well as professional, so the disagreement is about what writing is for and cannot be settled by either party succeeding.

entries.name: The Wound That Will Not Let Them
entries.description: A formative injury that has become a working theory about the world.

examples.text: Rivers makes the wound a learned certainty about what the heroine is worth, so every act of kindness is evidence against a belief rather than a comfort.
Hoang writes an autistic heroine whose difficulty is real, specific and not cured by love, which is the standard the trope should be held to.
Hall locates the wound in public humiliation rather than private trauma, which gives it an ongoing external cause the relationship cannot simply outlast.

entries.name: Illness, Disability and Mortality
entries.description: A body that will not do what the plot wants, and the genre's poor record with it.

examples.text: Hibbert gives both leads neurodivergence and lets it shape how they solve problems rather than what they must overcome, which is the version disabled readers have consistently asked for.

Moyes ends a disabled man's love story with his assisted death, framed as a gift to the woman who loves him, and the book was widely criticised by disabled readers and campaigners on precisely that basis. It teaches the wrong lesson twice: that a disabled life is a burden love cannot make bearable, and that a romance may resolve its central promise by removing one of the two people.
Green writes the mortality honestly and declines the genre's guarantee, which places the book outside romance and makes it a boundary case rather than a model for it.

entries.name: Faith and Conscience
entries.description: A belief that is not negotiable and not a misunderstanding.

examples.text: The faith is an active participant with its own claims on the hero, so the courtship must be reconciled with it rather than merely permitted by it.
Lewis makes the community's rule enforceable and the penalty concrete, which is why the choice costs something the reader can count.
Jalaluddin gives the community internal disagreement about its own practice, so faith generates conflict between believers rather than between belief and love.

entries.name: The Fated Bond
entries.description: A supernatural rule that makes attraction non-negotiable, and therefore makes consent a problem.

examples.text: Singh treats the mating bond as a condition the characters must interrogate and can resist, so the ending is a decision rather than a mechanism completing itself.
Ward makes the bond one pressure among several competing obligations, which keeps it from doing the work the courtship should be doing.

Feehan's lifemate bond overrides the heroine's stated refusal and the novel does not register the override as a problem, which is the convention's founding difficulty and the one later writers in the subgenre spent two decades addressing.

entries.name: Mistaken Identity
entries.description: Someone is taken for someone else, and the error becomes the relationship's foundation.

examples.text: Shakespeare runs three simultaneous misidentifications and lets each character behave intelligently on the information they have, which is why the resolution feels like disclosure rather than repair.
The error is made by the family rather than by the heroine, so her fault is silence rather than deception and the reckoning stays proportionate.
Only one party knows, which converts a symmetrical device into a sustained ethical problem about what he is entitled to do with the knowledge.

entries.name: Disguise and Crossdressing
entries.description: A deliberate change of presentation that grants access to a life otherwise closed.

examples.text: The disguise is adopted for safety and produces desire in two directions at once, which is the device's full range rather than its comic surface.
Waters makes male dress a professional instrument, an erotic one and a survival strategy in turn, and refuses to resolve it back into a single explanation.
The disguise is undertaken to obtain an education rather than a person, so the romance is a consequence of the deception rather than its purpose.

entries.name: The Secret Identity
entries.description: One party is systematically not who they are believed to be, and knows it.

examples.text: Orczy makes the concealment a marriage problem before it is an adventure problem, so the spy plot is generated by the estrangement rather than the reverse.
Rostand splits authorship from presence, which isolates the question of what is actually being loved and gives the device its most exact statement.
Rowell gives one party total knowledge and the other none, then makes the disclosure a genuine risk rather than a scheduled reveal.

entries.name: Undercover
entries.description: Deception undertaken as a professional duty, which makes the betrayal institutional as well as personal.

examples.text: Cole places two agents on the same side but in ignorance of each other, so the deception is mutual and the danger is real for both in different ways.
Hitchcock has the man's employer require the woman's sexual access to a third party, which makes the state a participant in the romance and the duty genuinely unforgivable.
Stuart's operative is lethal and remains so after disclosure, so the reveal changes the heroine's information without softening the man it is about.

entries.name: Amnesia
entries.description: Memory loss as a device for asking whether the person or the history was loved.

examples.text: Hilton makes the second courtship a deliberate act by a woman who knows everything and says nothing, which converts a gimmick into a study of sustained choice.
The premise is stated and then largely resolved by persistence rather than by either party confronting what a marriage is when one side does not remember consenting to it.

A man deceives an amnesiac woman into believing she is his wife and puts her to work in his household, and the film treats the deception as courtship and the disclosure as a minor obstacle. It teaches the wrong lesson structurally: that consent obtained by manufactured ignorance can be retroactively validated by the deceived party's eventual happiness.

entries.name: The Secret Baby
entries.description: A child the other parent does not know about, and the question of who was owed the information.

examples.text: Hardy makes the concealment a direct consequence of the social penalty for disclosure, so the secret is enforced by the society rather than chosen by the woman.
The uncertainty is treated as a workable family arrangement rather than a scandal, which is the rare version where the secret does not function as an accusation.
The comic register lets the paternity question stay open long enough to be about the two men's characters rather than about the test result.

entries.name: Concealed Rank
entries.description: Status hidden or mistaken, so that affection can be tested before position is known.

examples.text: Heyer conceals birth rather than title, which makes the revelation a question of inheritance and legitimacy with legal consequences attached.
The concealment is mutual and both parties are working, which makes the eventual disclosure a professional betrayal on one side and a constitutional impossibility on the other.
The prince conceals rank specifically to obtain evidence of being wanted for himself, which states the trope's purpose more plainly than any other version.

entries.name: The Impostor
entries.description: Someone assumes another's life, and the people who loved the original have to decide what they knew.

examples.text: The film keeps the wife's knowledge genuinely uncertain, which makes the case a question about complicity rather than about detection.
Relocating the same case to the American South after the Civil War makes the impostor's improved character a political fact as well as a private one.
The impersonation is passive and never corrected, which is a comic register's way of asking the same question about who benefits from a convenient error.

entries.name: Blackmail and Leverage
entries.description: One party holds something over the other, and the relationship proceeds under that condition.

examples.text: Waters constructs a leverage system in which every party believes they are the one applying it, and lets the reader discover the actual hierarchy late.
The leverage is exercised by an institution rather than by a lover, which is why the man's failure to intervene is the film's real betrayal.
The transaction is proposed, accepted and then largely evaded, so the film raises a genuine question about what money can buy and declines to answer it.

entries.name: The Con and the Mark
entries.description: A deliberate fraud on a person, complicated by the fraudster's attachment to them.

examples.text: Sturges has the con woman fall for the mark, get caught, and then run a second and crueller con as revenge, which is the only version that gives the deceived party a reckoning worth watching.
The film makes the mark a better operator than either con artist, which removes the condescension the device usually carries.
The fraud is sustained for the benefit of the defrauded community, which is the hardest version to judge and the reason the story keeps being retold.

entries.name: Coming Out
entries.description: Disclosure of the self rather than of a fact, with the risk borne unequally.

examples.text: Forster makes the disclosure legally dangerous and socially terminal, and still insists on the happy ending, which is what makes the novel an argument rather than a lament.
McQuiston forces the disclosure by exposure rather than by choice, which shifts the question from whether to come out to who owns the timing.
Reid ties the closet to professional survival in a specific industry, so the concealment has a career cost that can be calculated rather than only feared.

entries.name: The Return of the Presumed Dead
entries.description: Someone comes back, and the life built in their absence is now the obstacle.

examples.text: Dumas has the returning man decline to reclaim the marriage, which is the honest consequence of an absence long enough to have been survived.
Heathcliff returns transformed and solvent, and Brontë refuses to let the improvement redeem the intention behind it.
Tennyson has the returning husband choose silence, which established the pattern later fiction has been rewriting for a century and a half.

entries.name: The Twin and the Double
entries.description: A physical duplicate, and the discovery that the substitution is not equivalent.

examples.text: Hope makes the substitution a matter of state, so the romance is destroyed by the same duty that created it and cannot be salvaged.
The doubling is deployed by children against parents, which turns the device toward a remarriage plot rather than a courtship one.
Hitchcock makes the double an obsession the man constructs deliberately, which exposes the fantasy of substitution as a refusal of the actual person.

entries.name: The Reveal
entries.description: The disclosure scene itself, as a craft object with its own requirements.

examples.text: The reveal arrives too late to be acted on, which demonstrates that timing rather than content is what makes disclosure devastating.
Sturges stages the reveal as a performance the deceiver controls, so the scene is an act of aggression rather than a confession.
Hilton withholds the reveal from the character who has waited longest for it, making the reader's possession of the information the source of the tension.

entries.name: The Boss
entries.description: Authority over someone's livelihood, exercised by a person who also wants them.

examples.text: Day makes the gradient explicit and has both parties negotiate terms in writing, which is the rare version where the imbalance is treated as a problem requiring machinery.
The employment relationship is generational and the heroine's father works for the family, so the power runs through class as well as position.
The gradient of money, employment access and experience is asserted repeatedly and rarely made negotiable, so the contract that the plot is organised around never functions as one.

entries.name: Teacher and Student
entries.description: Instruction as intimacy, in a relationship that is unequal by design.

examples.text: Shaw builds the tutelage plot in full, makes the professor's investment unmistakably erotic, and then refuses the romance outright, appending an essay to explain why Eliza could not marry him without forfeiting everything the play gave her. It is the sharpest available demonstration that a romantic ending is a structural claim about power rather than a reward, and it is the reason the pack cards it against its own adaptation.
The adaptation supplies the ending Shaw explicitly refused and keeps the power relation intact while doing so, which converts a critique of the trope into an instance of it.
Schone inverts the direction, making the woman the commissioning party and the instruction something she pays for, which redistributes the authority the trope usually assigns.

entries.name: The Rake and the Innocent
entries.description: Experience against inexperience, where the gap is the attraction and the danger.

examples.text: Heyer gives the experienced party a project and a conscience, so the relationship's central question is whether he can stop treating her as an instrument.
Quinn lets the innocent party act decisively and wrongly, which breaks the passivity the trope usually assigns to her and creates a genuine reckoning.
Heyer has the heroine shoot the rake, establishing early that the experience gap does not translate into control.

entries.name: Age Gap
entries.description: A difference in years that carries a difference in power, whether or not the book says so.

examples.text: The gap is compounded by employment and by the older man's certainty that he is doing her a kindness, which is what the ending has to dismantle.
Aciman writes the asymmetry from inside the younger party's perception and does not resolve it, so the reader holds the imbalance rather than being told it was fine.
A century of difference is presented as romantic seniority with none of its implications examined, and the resulting decisions are made for the younger party throughout.

entries.name: The Virgin
entries.description: Sexual inexperience treated as a state with social and economic consequences.

examples.text: Richardson is explicit that the heroine's virtue is an asset under negotiation, which is a more honest account of the period's economics than most later fiction manages.
Garwood ties inexperience to a treaty marriage, so the wedding night is a diplomatic event as well as a private one.
Inexperience functions as a licence for the other party's authority rather than as a condition either of them has to work with.

entries.name: The Alpha Hero
entries.description: Dominance as a character design, and the question of what restrains it.

examples.text: Singh gives her alpha a pack he is accountable to, so his authority has a constituency and can be lost.
Ward places the dominance inside a military hierarchy with obligations that outrank the hero, which supplies the limit the archetype usually lacks.
Ashley writes the archetype at full strength and lets the heroine name the behaviour as unacceptable on the page, which is what distinguishes depicting dominance from endorsing it.

entries.name: The Beta and the Cinnamon Roll
entries.description: A hero whose power is competence and steadiness rather than authority.

examples.text: Hoang's hero leads through patience and explicit checking-in, which supplies tension through restraint rather than through resistance.
Hibbert makes the man rigid and anxious rather than commanding, so the couple's negotiation is about accommodation instead of submission.
Danan pairs a gentle hero with a profession that trades on performance of dominance, which turns the archetype into the book's actual subject.

entries.name: The Rescue
entries.description: One party saves the other, and the debt that creates.

examples.text: The rescue is contracted and paid for, which prevents the debt from being romantic and forces both parties to acknowledge the transaction.
Dixon makes rescue mutual and continuous under survival conditions, so neither party accumulates an unrepayable obligation.
Each rescues the other in their own competence, which is the structural fix for a device that otherwise installs a permanent hierarchy.

entries.name: Ownership and Claiming Language
entries.description: The vocabulary of possession, and whether the book examines what it is saying.

examples.text: Carey builds a formal contractual and religious framework in which the language of belonging is defined, revocable and understood by both parties.
The claiming vocabulary is used at full strength while the woman's refusal is in force, and the novel does not register the contradiction.
Wylde names the club's designation for women plainly and lets the heroine accept it, which is documentary about the subculture and leaves the reader without a position the book has taken.

entries.name: The Transactional Marriage
entries.description: Marriage as a purchase, with terms both parties can state.

examples.text: The transaction is legal, small and mutually beneficial, which keeps the power roughly level and makes the affection an unintended cost.
Lori's alliance is dynastic, so the couple are both instruments and neither is the purchaser.
The film's premise is a genuine question about what money buys, and it retreats from the answer rather than paying for the transaction it staged.

entries.name: Master and Servant
entries.description: Domestic employment as intimacy, in a relationship with no exit.

examples.text: Ishiguro shows the service relation making the declaration structurally impossible, and the withholding is the novel's whole achievement.
Waters moves her narrator through several positions of dependency and makes each one materially specific about food, wages and rooms.
The series runs employment romances alongside employer ones and makes the difference in available choices visible by direct comparison.

entries.name: Royalty and the Commoner
entries.description: A gap in station that institutions exist to enforce.

examples.text: Hope makes the constitutional obstacle absolute, so the renunciation is a matter of state rather than of feeling.
The prince's power is used to escape his position rather than to overcome hers, which inverts the usual direction of the fantasy.
Goldman makes the royal claim purely coercive and gives it no legitimacy at all, which turns the station gap into a straightforward abduction plot.

entries.name: Celebrity and Civilian
entries.description: Fame as an asymmetry of exposure rather than of authority.

examples.text: The imbalance reverses across the film, demonstrating that the relationship's problem is the differential itself rather than which party holds it.
Reid makes public visibility the mechanism of the concealment, so fame and the closet are the same obstacle.
Lee compounds fame with an age gap running the opposite way to convention, and lets the public scrutiny do the damage rather than the private incompatibility.

entries.name: Who Holds the Money
entries.description: Economic dependency as the substrate under every other power question in the genre.

examples.text: Gaskell ends with the heroine as creditor to the hero's business, which resolves the courtship by inverting the financial relation rather than by ignoring it.
Wharton shows money enforcing a social outcome without anyone needing to threaten anything, which is how the mechanism actually operated.
Mitchell makes the heroine's economic independence the thing that destroys her marriages, and declines to treat that as a moral failing or to resolve it.

entries.name: The Charged Non-Touch
entries.description: Contact withheld, so that the absence of touch carries more than touch would.

examples.text: Wright ends a handing-into-a-carriage with the man flexing his hand as he walks away, which converts an ordinary courtesy into the most-cited erotic gesture in modern screen romance. It works because the film has established a society in which that contact is the maximum available, so the physical vocabulary is doing the work the period forbids dialogue from doing.
Lean keeps the couple almost entirely unphysical and puts the whole charge into proximity in public places, which is why the restraint reads as pressure rather than as coolness.
The adaptation stages long stretches of near-contact in ordinary rooms, using duration rather than staging to make the withholding legible.

entries.name: The Almost-Kiss
entries.description: An interruption that converts an intention into a fact both parties now have to carry.

examples.text: The series uses the ballroom's surveillance as the interrupting mechanism, so the interruption is structural rather than coincidental.
Shakespeare interrupts with plot rather than with accident, which is why the deferral raises the stakes instead of relieving them.
Shiina extends the device across volumes and makes each near-miss a genuine misreading of the other's position, which is the shojo tradition's characteristic refinement of it.

entries.name: The First Kiss
entries.description: The scene the whole first half has been arranging, and the state change it must deliver.

examples.text: The adaptation withholds it almost entirely and puts the charge into the second proposal, demonstrating that the kiss is optional if the acknowledgement is not.
The kiss arrives early, in anger, and creates the plot rather than resolving it, which is the underused version.
Takaya makes physical contact literally dangerous under her rule system, so the approach carries consequence before anyone has decided anything.

entries.name: Slow Burn
entries.description: Deferral sustained long enough that the waiting becomes the reader's pleasure rather than their complaint.

examples.text: Rooney makes the deferral a class and communication problem rather than a will-they-won't-they, so each separation has a specific and different cause.
Stewart runs the burn under a suspicion plot, so the delay is generated by the heroine's uncertainty about whether the man is dangerous.
The series takes two full seasons and makes the delay a function of one character's unfamiliarity with being treated well, which is a reason rather than a device.

entries.name: The Closed Door
entries.description: The scene break as a deliberate instrument, and what it costs and buys.

examples.text: Oke's closed door is a genre requirement and she uses the constraint to put the intimacy into domestic labour instead, which is where the book's actual courtship happens.
Heyer's entire erotic register is conversational, demonstrating that a closed door costs nothing when the dialogue is carrying the charge.
The film's most consequential scene happens off-screen and is reported afterwards in shame, which makes the omission the point rather than a compromise.

entries.name: The First Time
entries.description: A scene that must change what the couple know about each other, not only what they have done.

examples.text: Kennedy makes the scene the point at which a stated arrangement stops being deniable, so its function is contractual as well as erotic.
Aciman writes the aftermath as the significant part and the act as almost incidental, which is the correct weighting for a first time that matters.

examples.work: A Court of Mist and Fury
examples.text: Maas places the scene at the point where a bond is knowingly accepted rather than discovered, which is the version that treats consent as an event.

entries.name: The Morning After
entries.description: The negotiation that decides what last night was.

examples.text: Bowen and Kennedy make the morning the site of the actual risk, because the acknowledgement is what neither man can take back.
O'Leary's premise means the two rarely occupy the room at the same time, so the morning after is conducted in notes and the delay is structural.
Nicholls builds the entire novel out of a single morning after that both parties spend twenty years reinterpreting.

entries.name: Negotiated Kink
entries.description: Power exchanged deliberately, with terms, in a form where terms are the craft.

examples.text: Reisz writes negotiation as characterisation, so the terms each party asks for are the fastest available route into who they are.
Day makes limits explicit and revisited rather than established once, which is the practical difference between depicting a dynamic and depicting a relationship.
Schone puts the commissioning power with the woman and keeps the instruction contractual, so the exchange is legible as an arrangement rather than a seduction.

entries.name: Public Intimacy and the Witness
entries.description: Being seen, and the difference that makes to what was done.

examples.text: The series makes observation the enforcement mechanism of the entire society, so any public contact is simultaneously an act and a legal event.
The adaptation stages intimacy under the observation of a household and a clan, which converts privacy into a resource the couple must obtain.
Waller-Bridge makes the audience itself the witness through direct address, then has another character notice her doing it, which weaponises the device.

entries.name: Sex as Turning Point
entries.description: The act that makes the previous arrangement impossible to return to.

examples.text: Waller gives the affair a fixed duration from the outset, so the encounter's function is to establish what will have to be given up.
Hibbert uses the scene to expose the gap between what her heroine has contracted for and what she has begun to want.
Yazawa treats sex as the point at which her characters' incompatible plans for their own lives become visible to each other.

entries.name: Aftercare and the Tender Scene
entries.description: What happens afterwards, treated as the load-bearing part.

examples.text: Reisz makes the care following an intense scene the proof of the relationship's safety, which is the argument the book is constructed to make.
Hoang writes tenderness as a learned and effortful skill for a character to whom it does not come naturally, so it registers as achievement rather than default.
Ryan places gentleness against a history of violence in the heroine's previous relationship, which makes ordinary care legible as extraordinary.

entries.name: Escalation Beyond the Body
entries.description: Intimacy that deepens after the physical questions are settled.

examples.text: Henry moves the escalation into professional disclosure and family obligation, so the second half raises stakes the first half had no access to.
Simsion's escalation is entirely in the negotiation of how two people will actually live, which is where the novel's difficulty is.
Oseman escalates through disclosure to families, schools and each other's mental health rather than through physical progression, which is the series' deliberate structural choice.

entries.name: The Meddling Family
entries.description: Relatives with a stake, standing and a plan of their own.

examples.text: Austen makes the interference financial and legally enforceable, so the family's opinion has money behind it rather than only feeling.
The adaptation gives the objecting mother a coherent argument about duty that the film declines to dismiss, which is what makes the confrontation a contest.
Dev makes the family's claims legitimate and incompatible with each other, so there is no single interference to be overcome.

entries.name: The Best Friend
entries.description: The confidant, and the problem of a character who exists to be told things.

examples.text: The two best friends are given their own romance, which converts a pair of listening devices into participants with their own stake.
The friendship carries a status transaction, so advice given is never disinterested.
Blake makes the friend group the mechanism by which the relationship becomes public, so their knowledge has consequences.

entries.name: The Disapproving Parent
entries.description: Objection from someone with authority, love and a reason.

examples.text: The objection is inherited rather than argued, which is why it cannot be answered and why the play must resolve by catastrophe.
Patel gives the parental pressure a community context in which it is ordinary rather than villainous, so refusing it has social costs beyond the family.
Kamio makes the disapproving parent the wealthiest person in the story, so the objection comes with the power to enforce it materially.

entries.name: The Chaperone and the Watcher
entries.description: An institution of surveillance that generates plot by restricting access.

examples.text: Heyer constructs the guardianship so that the watcher and the suitor are the same person, which makes the supervision itself the erotic problem.
Heyer's heroine has outlived the chaperone system, and the novel's tension comes from a freedom the society has not authorised.
Chadha transposes the surveillance apparatus into a contemporary Indian family and finds it fully operational, which is the point the adaptation exists to make.

entries.name: The Gossip Economy
entries.description: Information as currency, and reputation as the thing it buys and destroys.

examples.text: Eliot shows a whole town revising its opinion on inadequate evidence and treats the process as a social mechanism rather than as malice.
Heyer's plot is driven almost entirely by what may be said, to whom, and in what order.
The series gives the gossip an on-screen narrator, which externalises the economy and lets the show comment on its own machinery.

entries.name: The Ex
entries.description: A former partner with standing, history and an unfinished account.

examples.text: The film treats the ex as the person who knows exactly why it failed, which makes their presence an argument rather than a threat.
The former husband is the one character who can name the heroine's actual fault, and the plot requires her to accept the diagnosis.
Henry makes the ex-couple perform their old relationship for a friend group, so the past is a public obligation rather than a private feeling.

entries.name: The Love Triangle
entries.description: Two claims on one person, both of which must be real.

examples.text: McCullough's competing claim is a vocation rather than a person, which removes the possibility of the rival being discredited.
Yazawa lets both claims remain legitimate for hundreds of chapters and refuses to signal a correct answer.
Ahn keeps the friendship group's claim in competition with the romantic one, which is the triangle rotated away from its usual axis.

entries.name: The Child as Stakeholder
entries.description: A third party whose interests are genuinely prior to the couple's.

examples.text: The child initiates and drives the plot, so his stake is not a complication but the mechanism.
Oke makes the marriage a child-care arrangement first and a relationship second, which is historically accurate and structurally efficient.
Carr makes an abandoned infant the reason the heroine stays, so the child creates the proximity the romance requires.

entries.name: The Villain Who Wants Her
entries.description: An unwanted claim backed by power, which makes refusal dangerous.

examples.text: Goldman gives the claimant absolute legal authority and no legitimacy whatsoever, which strips the device to its mechanics.
Hardy makes one unwanted suitor pitiable and the other charming, and lets both destroy things, which is more unsettling than a straightforward villain.
Hoffman makes the unwanted claim persist past the man's death, which literalises what coercive attachment actually feels like.

entries.name: The Found Family
entries.description: A community chosen rather than inherited, which the romance must join rather than escape.

examples.text: The town becomes the family, and the romance's progress is measured by the couple's willingness to be known by it.
Hatori builds an ensemble in which every member has a claim on the protagonist, so the eventual pairing costs the group something.
Score uses an inherited small-town network as the support system the heroine has never had, which makes staying the actual romantic decision.

entries.name: The Institution
entries.description: An organisation with rules that outrank the couple's preferences.

examples.text: The training programme's authority over the man's future is absolute, so the relationship is conducted in the margins it permits.
The household's hierarchy determines who may marry whom and on what terms, and the series treats the rules as facts rather than obstacles.
Sheehan's club has enforceable bylaws about women's status, and the novel follows the cost of them across decades rather than resolving them.

entries.name: The Public Audience
entries.description: Spectators with no personal stake, whose attention is itself a force.

examples.text: Guillory makes political press scrutiny the obstacle, so the relationship's problem is entirely one of exposure rather than of feeling.
The telenovela frame makes the audience's expectations a character, which lets the show discuss what viewers are demanding of it.
The protagonist's relationship with the audience is treated as an evasion of intimacy, and the romance is the thing that finally interrupts it.

entries.name: Second-Chance Romance
entries.description: Two people who already failed at this, attempting it with the evidence in hand.

examples.text: Ryan reunites a divorced couple and requires them to address the specific failure that ended the marriage rather than to rediscover attraction.
Henry structures the novel as alternating past and present, so the reader watches the failure and the repair simultaneously.
Silver makes the missed chance a matter of loyalty to a third party, so the delay is ethical rather than accidental.

entries.name: The Reunion After Years
entries.description: A separation long enough that both parties have become people the other has not met.

examples.text: The failure to appear is caused by an accident neither party can explain, which makes the reunion a matter of interpretation rather than of forgiveness.
The earlier version of the same story is colder about the woman's concealment, which makes the reunion an act of pride rather than of romance.
Tóibín's reunion is with a place and a former life rather than only a person, so the choice is between two complete futures.

entries.name: The Grand Gesture
entries.description: A large public act, and the question of whether it substitutes for a decision.

examples.text: The gesture is small, private and directed at someone who has already refused him, which is why it reads as persistence rather than as spectacle.
The rain-soaked proposal resolves a hesitation the film has never given a cause, so the gesture is doing the work that character development should have done.
The cue-card sequence is a declaration made to a friend's wife at her home, framed as romantic rather than as the intrusion it depicts, and the film never registers the difference.

entries.name: The Declaration
entries.description: Saying it, in a genre where saying it is the structural obligation.

examples.text: The declaration is preceded by a professional collapse that has stripped the speaker of everything he was offering, which is what makes the terms credible.
Quinn has the declaration made in writing and read by the wrong person first, so the disclosure is out of the speaker's control.
Eliot stages the declaration in a thunderstorm and gives her heroine the decisive line, at the cost of an inheritance she knowingly forfeits.

entries.name: The Public Proposal
entries.description: An offer made where refusal would be a public act.

examples.text: The wedding's audience is already assembled, which converts a private decision into a performance the heroine must improvise through.
Chadha stages the proposal inside a family celebration, so consent and community approval arrive as a single event.
The fire-escape climb restates the rescue economy the film claims to be resolving, and the transaction the plot was built on is never actually settled.

entries.name: The Wedding
entries.description: The ceremony as evidence, and the risk of it standing in for the ending.

examples.text: The film uses four ceremonies as a structural device for measuring one man's avoidance, so the weddings are diagnostic rather than celebratory.
Bellefleur builds the arrangement around a family wedding and lets the ceremony expose the fake relationship rather than confirm the real one.
Cole makes the wedding a matter of state with constitutional consequences, so the ceremony carries obligations beyond the couple.

entries.name: Marriage in Trouble
entries.description: A couple already married, and a romance that must be conducted inside the failure.

examples.text: McCarey runs the entire courtship after the divorce petition, so every scene is two people sabotaging an outcome they have both formally requested.
Ryan makes the original failure specific, diagnosable and partly nobody's fault, which is why the repair takes an entire novel.
Tolstoy runs a failing marriage and a failing affair in parallel and declines to let either resolve, which marks the outer boundary of what the genre can absorb.

entries.name: Reconciliation After Betrayal
entries.description: Repair after a real injury, and what the injuring party must actually do.

examples.text: Neither party ever fully admits fault, and the film makes the reconciliation a matter of both accepting the other's version, which is more honest than an apology.
Crusie builds a cast in which everyone is running a deception, so forgiveness is negotiated rather than granted.

McNaught's hero horsewhips the heroine and later forces himself on her under a mistaken belief about her conduct, and the novel proceeds to reconciliation without requiring him to reckon with either act. It is the clearest single demonstration of the era's structural error: the injury is treated as a misunderstanding to be corrected rather than as harm to be answered for, which means the reconciliation costs the person who caused it nothing.

entries.name: The Ending That Defers
entries.description: A volume that does not pay the guarantee, and what it owes instead.

examples.work: A Court of Mist and Fury
examples.text: Maas completes a full emotional movement inside the volume before opening the larger arc, which is what a non-terminal book has to do to earn the deferral.

The volume ends on a reversal that suspends the relationship's status, and readers who arrived through the genre's promise rather than through fantasy publishing reported it as a broken contract rather than as momentum.
A second consecutive deferral compounds the problem, because the reader now has no basis for estimating when the guarantee will be paid.

entries.name: Starting Again After Loss
entries.description: A romance that follows bereavement, where the previous love was not a mistake.

examples.text: The film ends on an arrangement rather than a union and treats it as sufficient, which is one of the earliest screen arguments for a satisfying ending that is not a marriage.
Sparks frames the whole courtship inside an ending already in progress, so the reader holds the loss throughout rather than encountering it.
Hoffman makes the previous attachment genuinely destructive and still refuses to treat surviving it as a simple gain.

entries.name: The Epilogue Baby
entries.description: The genre's most-mocked convention, and the specific question it can answer.

examples.text: Phillips makes the child the plot's origin rather than its coda, which is the version where the ending's evidence has been earned across the whole book.
Quinn's second epilogues exist because readers wanted durability evidence, and the practice is an honest response to a real structural gap.
The adaptation uses the child to raise the stakes of a later separation rather than to signal contentment, which is the convention doing plot work.

entries.name: The Ever After Revisited
entries.description: Returning to a resolved couple without unmaking their resolution.

examples.text: Macomber returns to earlier couples as stable community fixtures who dispense resources and advice, which is the interconnected-series contract observed exactly.
Balogh closes a family series by resolving the sibling who has been present throughout, so the revisiting is structural rather than nostalgic.
The game continues past marriage into an ongoing domestic state with its own small events, which is a medium-native answer to the question of what happens after the guarantee is paid.

entries.name: The Guarantee, Stated
entries.description: The genre's defining obligation: an emotionally satisfying, optimistic resolution of the central relationship, delivered inside the book.

examples.work: A Natural History of the Romance Novel
examples.text: Regis defines the form by its ending rather than by its content, which is what allows four centuries of otherwise unrelated books to be discussed as one tradition.
Dunmore's heroine is a suffragist whose politics make the conventional ending unavailable, so the book must invent terms on which the guarantee can be paid without her surrendering the campaign.
The film is frequently described as the great romance and resolves by separating the couple permanently, which is precisely the outcome the guarantee exists to exclude.

entries.name: What the Promise Is Not
entries.description: Not marriage, not permanence, not monogamy, and not the absence of future difficulty.

examples.text: The closing arrangement is neither marriage nor exclusivity, and the film argues that it is enough, which is the earliest mainstream statement of the position the genre later formalised.
Maxwell's ending is a political marriage the couple choose to continue on renegotiated terms, so the satisfaction comes from the terms rather than from the institution.
Ishiguro withholds every component of the promise deliberately and the novel is greater for it, which demonstrates that the guarantee is a genre commitment rather than a measure of quality.

entries.name: HEA and HFN, and the Difference That Matters
entries.description: Happy ever after asserts permanence; happy for now asserts sufficiency. Both satisfy the promise; they are not interchangeable.

examples.text: Linklater ends on a moment of chosen sufficiency that promises nothing beyond the room, and it is more emotionally complete than most declarations of permanence because both parties know exactly what they are choosing and what it costs. It is the clearest demonstration available that a happy-for-now ending is a full settlement rather than a hedge, and that the guarantee is about certainty of feeling rather than duration.
The earlier film ends on a deferred arrangement that the sequel reveals as unpaid, which is the risk a happy-for-now takes and the reason it must be chosen rather than defaulted into.
