entries.application: Be honest about which parts of your process are compressible. If revision is where your books become good, a rapid-release schedule is buying visibility with the thing that makes your work worth finding.

entries.name: The Blurb as Specification
entries.description: In this genre the description is written first and functions as a design document.
entries.principle: A romance description does work that descriptions in other genres do not: it declares the tropes, signals the heat, identifies the configuration and implies the ending's shape. Because readers select on those declarations, the description is effectively a specification the book must satisfy, and writing it before drafting is a legitimate structural instrument rather than a marketing shortcut.
entries.example: The practice has a direct precedent in the category system's tip sheets, where the specification also preceded the manuscript; the indie market rebuilt the same mechanism from the reader's side rather than the publisher's.
entries.application: Draft the description first and treat every promise in it as a scene you owe. If a promise in the copy has no corresponding scene at the end of the draft, either write the scene or remove the promise before publication.

entries.name: Keywords, Categories and Adjacency
entries.description: Discovery metadata determines which readers ever see the book.
entries.principle: Storefront placement is driven by category selection, search terms and adjacency to similar titles, which means a book's discoverability is largely set by decisions made at upload rather than by the writing. The consequence for craft is indirect but real: a book positioned into a category it half-fits will be found by readers primed for something else, and their disappointment is registered as a quality judgement.
entries.example: The reader-community vocabulary supplies most of the effective search language, and it frequently diverges from the formal subject codes, so the two must be handled as separate systems that both need to be satisfied.
entries.application: Choose categories where your book is a strong fit rather than where competition is lowest. Visibility to the wrong readership is worse than obscurity, because it converts into reviews that follow the book permanently.

entries.name: Title Conventions
entries.description: Titles in romance are search terms, category signals and occasionally legal problems.
entries.principle: Romance title conventions cluster tightly by subgenre — historicals signal rank and scandal, contemporaries signal register and often the trope, dark romance signals its content in a word or two. Because titles are also search terms, they are commercially load-bearing, and the genre has learned the hard way that attempting to enclose common title language legally is both ineffective and reputationally costly.
entries.example: The 2018 dispute over a trademark asserted on a common single-word title term drew widespread objection across the field and prompted intervention from author advocacy organisations, and it remains the standard cautionary case for attempts to privatise generic title vocabulary.
entries.application: Search your title before committing, both for existing books and for genre-signal accuracy. Pick a title your reader would plausibly type, and do not attempt to enclose words the genre uses in common.

entries.name: Women's Fiction: The Boundary
entries.description: The most consequential adjacent category, and the line is precise rather than tonal.
entries.principle: Romance requires a central love story and an emotionally satisfying, optimistic ending. Women's fiction centres a woman's journey, in which a relationship may be significant but is not the structural spine and need not resolve optimistically. The distinction is not about literary ambition or heat level; it is about which arc the book is organised around and whether the guarantee is made. Books are routinely mis-shelved across this line, and the resulting complaints are among the genre's most predictable.
entries.example: Novels marketed inside romance that resolve the protagonist's arc while declining to resolve the couple's are the standard failure case, and readers report them as broken promises rather than as different books — which is accurate, because the promise was signalled and not paid.
entries.application: Ask which arc your ending resolves. If the book's final movement settles the protagonist's life rather than the relationship, you have written women's fiction and should position it there, where it will be read on its own terms rather than against a guarantee it never made.

entries.name: Young Adult and New Adult
entries.description: Age brackets rather than genres, and one of them failed for reasons that had nothing to do with content.
entries.principle: Young adult and new adult describe intended readership rather than form, and any genre may contain them. Young adult romance carries real craft shifts — stakes scaled to the protagonist's world, institutional power differentials, voice constraints and a common expectation of hope or agency at the end. New adult was launched as a bracket for the college-age readership and did not survive as a category, and the reasons were structural: no professional body, no awards apparatus, bookseller resistance, and a name that already meant something different in stores.
entries.example: The college-set romance that new adult was created to hold continued to sell strongly after the category label collapsed, migrating to the indie market and to contemporary romance, which demonstrates that the failure was one of infrastructure rather than of demand.
entries.application: Treat the bracket as a positioning decision and the craft shifts as real. Do not read the collapse of new adult as evidence about its content, and do not attempt to revive a category label the trade has abandoned when the books themselves sell perfectly well under existing ones.

entries.name: Line-Native Categories
entries.description: Medical, holiday and their relatives are publisher lines that readers experience as subgenres.
entries.principle: Some familiar romance categories exist because a line existed, not because the form differs. Medical romance is a Harlequin line with setting-driven constraints — professional ethics, shift patterns, life-and-death stakes arriving on someone else's schedule — rather than a distinct narrative structure. Holiday romance is a seasonal publishing slot with a fixed retail window that shapes length, tone and delivery date. Both are real constraints and neither is a form.
entries.example: The medical setting supplies enforced proximity, a professional prohibition on the relationship and an external stakes system, which is why the line has persisted; the constraints are the setting's, not a subgenre's.
entries.application: If you are writing to one of these, write to the line's actual specification and the setting's real conditions. If you are not, take the setting and ignore the label, because outside the line it carries no expectations you are obliged to meet.

entries.name: Cosy and Low-Angst
entries.description: A reader-side category defined by emotional register and the absence of specific content.
entries.principle: The cosy or low-angst designation promises a reading experience rather than a subject: limited external threat, no betrayal, no third-act rupture, and a guarantee that the discomfort will stay within bounds. It is one of the clearest cases of the reader taxonomy operating independently, since neither the retailer nor the publisher systems have a field for it, and it makes a promise about the middle of the book rather than its ending.
entries.example: The vocabulary is entirely community-generated and enforced through recommendation networks and shelf tags, with terms describing the intensity ceiling rather than the content, which the formal codes have no capacity to express.
entries.application: If you claim the register, honour it in the middle rather than only in the ending, because the promise is about how the book feels to read. A cosy romance with a conventional betrayal at the two-thirds mark has broken its specific contract while keeping the genre's general one.

entries.name: The Terms That Died
entries.description: Category labels have short lives, and reading old advice as current is a standing hazard.
entries.principle: The romance market retires terminology regularly — bodice ripper, chick lit and new adult among the most consequential — and each retirement leaves behind a body of writing advice that no longer describes anything. Some terms died because they were pejorative, some because their infrastructure collapsed, and some because the market renamed the same books. A writer relying on older guidance needs to know which of the three occurred.
entries.example: Reverse harem's shift toward why-choose is a live instance of a community renaming in progress, and the two terms currently coexist with the newer one gaining ground because it names the promise rather than the configuration.
entries.application: Date every piece of market advice you rely on, including advice in this collection. Where a term has been retired, find out whether the books went with it — usually they did not, and they are being sold under a different name.

entries.name: What the Market Cannot Yet Categorise
entries.description: The gaps in the systems, which are where the next categories come from.
entries.principle: All three taxonomies lag the writing. Books arrive that no code describes, no line would acquire and no established reader vocabulary names, and they are discoverable only through community recommendation until the systems catch up. This is a normal condition rather than a defect, and it is worth knowing because the gap is simultaneously a discoverability problem and the place where new categories originate.
entries.example: Trans romance has a formal subject code and, as of this pack's research, effectively no established craft or market literature — a category that exists in the classification system and not yet in the apparatus around it. Monster romance spent years being sold entirely through community channels before the formal systems registered it at all.
entries.application: If your book falls in a gap, expect to build the readership through community channels rather than through storefront placement, and describe the book in the nearest available reader vocabulary while stating plainly what it actually is. The formal systems will follow if the readership arrives; they do not lead.

entries.name: The Sentimental Novel and the Letter
entries.description: The form's oldest machinery: interiority delivered as private correspondence the reader is permitted to read.
entries.principle: The eighteenth-century sentimental novel established the technical foundation the genre still runs on — sustained access to a woman's inner life, the courtship as the object of narrative attention, and virtue under negotiation as a plot. The epistolary method was not decorative: a letter is a document with a writer, a recipient and a purpose, which gives interiority a reason to exist on the page and lets the reader hold information its characters do not.
entries.example: Richardson's *Pamela* (1740) is explicit that the heroine's virtue is an asset under negotiation, and its whole force comes from the reader's access to documents its other characters cannot see; the tradition runs directly to the modern epistolary and correspondence romance.
entries.application: Read the eighteenth-century material when you want to understand why interiority is the genre's primary resource rather than a stylistic preference. The letter's structural gift — a stated reader, a stated purpose, and information asymmetry — is available to any book willing to give its interiority a recipient.

entries.name: Austen and the Marriage Plot
entries.description: The period supplies the constraints; Austen supplies the technique for making constraint generate plot.
entries.principle: Austen's contribution to the genre is not romance but method: free indirect style, a marriage market with legible economics, and obstacles constructed entirely from manners, money and information. Her novels demonstrate that a society's rules about who may speak to whom can carry the load that action carries elsewhere, which is the technical foundation of the entire historical line.
entries.example: *Pride and Prejudice* (1813) makes hostility evidentiary rather than temperamental, so the reversal requires each party to be shown wrong about a matter of fact; *Persuasion* (1817) makes a refusal an act of deference to legitimate authority and spends eight years on its consequences.
entries.application: Study Austen for the information economy rather than for the courtship. What a character may say, to whom, in whose hearing, is the most reliable obstacle generator the historical setting offers, and it is transferable to any setting with enforceable social rules.

entries.name: The Brontës and the Sensation Novel
entries.description: The nineteenth century supplies the genre's darker inheritance: the dangerous man, the secret, and the house.
entries.principle: Where Austen gives the genre its social machinery, the Brontës and the sensation novelists give it the gothic apparatus — a romantic interest who is also the suspect, a suppressed family history, and a heroine whose investigation is the plot. This is the lineage of romantic suspense, gothic romance and a large part of dark romance, and its distinguishing feature is that attraction and fear are generated by the same person.
entries.example: *Jane Eyre* (1847) supplies the template and its moral spine, with a prior claim that is a living woman rather than an item of information; *Wuthering Heights* (1847) follows the revenge logic across two generations and never suggests it is recoverable.
entries.application: When you want a hero whose danger is real rather than performed, work from this tradition rather than from the modern alpha. The nineteenth-century version is more useful because the threat is specific and the book takes a position on it.

entries.name: Heyer Invents the Regency
entries.description: The most codified setting in romance was constructed in the 1930s and is not a period but an idiom.
entries.principle: Georgette Heyer built the Regency romance as a working literary system — vocabulary, social calendar, class markers, a comic register and a set of reusable plot shapes — and the subgenre's conventions derive from her rather than from the period. This is the single most consequential correction in the genre's popular history: Austen supplies the era, Heyer supplies every convention, and a writer studying "the Regency" is mostly studying Heyer.
entries.example: *Regency Buck* (1935) established the idiom; *These Old Shades* (1926) had already done comparable work for the Georgian; and the thirty further novels codified a vocabulary the subgenre still uses.
entries.application: Read Heyer before reading about the Regency, and know which of your period details are historical and which are Heyer's. The distinction matters when you break a convention, because breaking a historical fact and breaking a genre convention have different consequences with readers.

entries.name: Mills & Boon Before Romance
entries.description: The firm that became synonymous with the genre spent its first quarter-century publishing something else.
entries.principle: Mills & Boon was founded in 1908 as a general publisher — its early list included educational books, Shakespeare and political material — and turned toward romance in the 1930s as a commercial specialisation. The company's significance is not that it invented romance but that it industrialised it: a reliable monthly supply of books to a specification, sold through subscription and lending libraries to a readership that bought the imprint.
entries.example: The firm's early catalogue bears no resemblance to its later identity, and the shift to romance was a business decision about a reliable market rather than an editorial vocation.
entries.application: Treat the category system as a distribution innovation rather than a literary one. Its conventions exist because they made a supply chain work, which is why they are specifications rather than aesthetics.

entries.name: Harlequin Before Romance
entries.description: The other half of the eventual monopoly also began somewhere else.
entries.principle: Harlequin was founded in Canada in 1949 publishing westerns, mysteries and general reprints, and moved to romance exclusively from 1964 after finding that the Mills & Boon titles it was reprinting outsold everything else on its list. The company's method was distribution: mass-market paperbacks sold through drugstores, supermarkets and newsstands rather than bookshops, reaching readers the trade did not serve.
entries.example: The reprint relationship preceded the ownership one — Harlequin distributed Mills & Boon titles in North America before acquiring the firm in 1971.
entries.application: Note that the genre's dominant institution discovered romance by measuring sales rather than by choosing it. That empirical posture explains the whole category system's later behaviour, including its repeated adjustments to heat level.

entries.name: The Merger and the North American System
entries.description: 1971 produced the structure most writers now think of as the category system.
entries.principle: Harlequin's acquisition of Mills & Boon in 1971 combined a British editorial operation with a North American mass-market distribution machine, and the result was the numbered, monthly, specification-driven line system at continental scale. It made romance the most reliably published genre in the English-speaking world and simultaneously created the archival problem the genre still has, because libraries did not accession numbered category titles.
entries.example: The line-and-number identifier remains the most stable bibliographic fact about many category titles of the period, and is frequently the only way a book from the era can now be identified with confidence.
entries.application: When researching this period, work from line and number rather than from title and author. Where a category title cannot be verified, record the gap rather than filling it — the documentation problem is a fact about the genre, not a failure of research.

entries.name: Vivian Stephens and the Editorial Invention of the Modern Category
entries.description: One editor's decisions shaped more of the contemporary genre than the standard history credits.
entries.principle: Vivian Stephens edited at Dell and then at Harlequin, where she launched and shaped lines that moved category romance toward American settings, working heroines and contemporary sexual frankness. She also acquired the first category romance with Black protagonists by a Black author, and she was a founder of the professional body that later marginalised her. The standard account of the genre's modernisation frequently omits her entirely, which is itself part of this section's subject.
entries.example: Her editorial work included the Dell Candlelight Ecstasy line and Harlequin American Romance, and she acquired *Entwined Destinies* (1980) — a record that makes her one of the most consequential editors in the genre's history.
entries.application: When you read a history of the modern category romance that names no editors, treat it as incomplete. The line specifications that shaped what could be written were editorial decisions with names attached.

entries.name: RWA 1980 and the Contractual Achievement
entries.description: The professional body's first significant act was about copyright and pen names, not about craft.
entries.principle: The Romance Writers of America was founded in 1980, and its earliest and most durable achievement was contractual: negotiating arrangements under which authors could register copyright in their own names and retain their pen names rather than leaving them as publisher property. That single change is why the modern romance author has a portable brand, and it underlies the whole subsequent economy of author-led series and self-publishing.
entries.example: Publisher-owned pen names were standard practice before this; the V.C. Andrews estate case later established in US tax law that an author's name is itself a taxable estate asset, which is the same principle arriving from the other direction.
entries.application: Understand that the ability to take your readership with you between publishers was won rather than given. It is the precondition for almost every career strategy the genre now takes for granted.

entries.name: Silhouette and the Imprint Wars
entries.description: A competitor emerged, was bought, and the consolidation set the terms for a decade.
entries.principle: Silhouette was launched by Simon & Schuster in 1980 to compete directly with Harlequin in North America, and was acquired by Harlequin in 1984. The episode is routinely misreported as Silhouette having been a Harlequin line from the start. The consolidation left one company with a dominant share of category romance and the ability to set specifications across most of the market.
entries.example: The competitive period between 1980 and 1984 produced a rapid expansion of lines and specifications, and the acquisition ended it — after which the number of distinct specifications available to writers contracted.
entries.application: Read the period's expansion of heat levels and settings as a product of competition rather than of editorial liberalisation. When the competition ended, so did much of the experimentation.

entries.category: The Boom and the Bodice Ripper
entries.name: 1972 and the Forced-Seduction Era
entries.description: A single Avon paperback opened the modern historical boom and established a convention the genre spent thirty years correcting.
entries.principle: Kathleen Woodiwiss's *The Flame and the Flower* (1972) established the long, explicit, single-title historical as a mass-market category and with it a template in which the hero's sexual coercion of the heroine functions as the beginning of the romance rather than as an injury requiring reckoning. The convention dominated the historical market for over a decade. It must be described accurately rather than euphemised, and it must be placed in its legal context without that context being used as a defence: marital rape was not criminalised in all fifty US states until 1993.
entries.example: The template has an earlier ancestor in E. M. Hull's *The Sheik* (1919), which combined abduction and coercion with an orientalist premise the plot resolves by revealing the abductor to be European — retracting the premise rather than examining it.
entries.application: Read the era to understand what the genre corrected and how long it took. The structural lesson is precise: a coercion that the hero's later tenderness dissolves removes the requirement that either party change, which is why books built on it have no second act.

entries.category: The Boom and the Bodice Ripper
entries.name: The American Contemporary
entries.description: Category romance relocated to the United States, and the genre's largest market began writing for itself.
entries.principle: Through the 1970s the category system's settings shifted from a largely British and European frame to American ones, with American heroines, workplaces and social textures. The change enlarged the readership substantially and made contemporary category romance a native form rather than an import. The popular account of this shift is unreliable in its particulars and worth stating carefully.
entries.example: Janet Dailey was the first American woman published by Mills & Boon, in 1974, and her significant innovation was the American-set category romance. She is frequently but incorrectly described as Harlequin's first American author; Harlequin had published Americans well before then.
entries.application: When citing this period, check whether a claimed first is a first for the company, the line, the country or the format. The genre's popular history is full of firsts that dissolve on inspection.

entries.category: The Boom and the Bodice Ripper
entries.name: The Oversupply Collapse
entries.description: The mid-1980s correction was a distribution failure, and it is routinely misread as a failure of demand.
entries.principle: The category system expanded rapidly into the early 1980s, with many competing lines pushing a large monthly volume into a fixed amount of retail space. Returns rose to unsustainable levels and lines were cancelled. The lesson usually drawn — that readers turned away from category romance — is not supported: the channel filled, and the correction was structural.
entries.example: By the mid-1980s the market carried well over a dozen competing lines and dozens of titles a month, with return rates at levels no publishing category can absorb; the consolidation that followed reduced the number of specifications rather than the number of readers.
entries.application: Distinguish channel failure from demand failure whenever you read that a romance category declined. The distinction has direct consequences for writers, because a subgenre whose line closed may have a larger readership than one whose line survived.

entries.category: The Boom and the Bodice Ripper
entries.name: The 1990s Single-Title Boom
entries.description: Romance moved into longer books sold on the author's name, and the genre's major careers were built.
entries.principle: Through the 1990s the commercial centre of romance shifted from the category line to the single title: longer books, secondary casts, subplots, author-branded series and bookstore placement. The shift changed what the genre could do structurally, and it created the author-as-brand economy that the 1980 copyright and pen-name settlement had made possible.
entries.example: The decade's historical romance in particular moved to greater length and psychological complexity, and the authors who defined it worked at a scale the category band could not accommodate.
entries.application: Read the transition when you are moving from short to long forms yourself. The extra length demands a second structural element rather than a longer version of the first, and the 1990s single titles are where that problem was solved at scale.

entries.name: Entwined Destinies and the First Black Romance from a Major Publisher
entries.description: A specific book, a specific line, a specific editor, and a record that is repeatedly stated incorrectly.
entries.principle: *Entwined Destinies* was published by Dell in 1980 as Candlelight number 575, written by Elsie B. Washington under the name Rosalind Welles and acquired by the editor Vivian Stephens. It is the first category romance with Black protagonists by a Black author to be published in the United States. The broader claim commonly made for it — first romance by a Black author from any major American publisher — is not supported by the sources and should not be repeated. The title is frequently misremembered, and the book is sometimes attributed to the wrong publisher; both errors are common enough that any source repeating them should be treated as unreliable on the surrounding material too.
entries.example: The book's identification depends on its line and number, which is the same archival problem described at card 7 — the category system's own record-keeping is now the most reliable evidence about it.
entries.application: Cite this book by title, author, pen name, publisher, line, number and year, because partial citations are how the errors propagate. Where you cannot verify a claim about the early Black romance market, mark it unverified rather than reconciling conflicting secondary sources.

entries.name: Odyssey Books, Arabesque, and Where This History Actually Starts
entries.description: The institutional history of Black romance publishing begins in 1990, not 1994, and the four-year difference is the whole point.
entries.principle: The standard account starts with Kensington's Arabesque line, launched July 1994 under the editor Monica Harris, as the first romance line from a major publisher dedicated to Black romance. That claim is true as stated and it is not where the history begins. **Odyssey Books, a Black-owned independent press founded in 1990 by Leticia Peoples — a federal employee with no publishing background who was told there was no market and put her own retirement savings in — published Black romance four years earlier.** It issued eleven titles and ceased operating in 1996 — and the usual word for that is contested, since Peoples described the decision as retiring rather than scaling up to compete with the majors.
entries.example: Odyssey published Donna Hill's debut *Rooms of the Heart* as a 1990 launch title, Rochelle Alers in 1991, and Francis Ray's debut *Fallen Angel* in 1992; both authors on Arabesque's July 1994 launch covers — Ray and Sandra Kitt — were already Odyssey authors. Any history that begins at Arabesque erases the press that started it and the woman who funded it.
entries.application: Research this material from specialist sources — university special collections and dedicated documentation projects — rather than from general genre references, which reproduce each other's errors here at a high rate. And when you are told an institutional history begins at the point a major corporation entered it, check what was already running four years earlier on somebody's savings.

entries.name: The Dismissal Problem
entries.description: The best-selling fiction genre is the least critically respected, and the reasons are documented rather than mysterious.
entries.principle: Romance's critical standing is not explained by quality distribution, which is comparable to other popular genres. It is explained by a set of documented factors: the readership and authorship are overwhelmingly women, the subject is emotional life, the format was mass-market and disposable, and reviewing institutions systematically did not cover it. Academic study only institutionalised in 2009 with the founding of a scholarly association and journal — roughly two centuries after the form's commercial establishment.
entries.example: The critical literature that does exist arrived late and had to argue for the field's existence first: Radway's *Reading the Romance* (1984) and Modleski's *Loving with a Vengeance* (1982) approached the genre as a sociological phenomenon, and Regis's *A Natural History of the Romance Novel* (2003) was the first sustained structural defence.
entries.application: State the dismissal as a documented fact with causes rather than as a grievance. A writer who understands why the genre was ignored can also see which of those causes still operate on their own book's reception.

entries.name: The Archive Problem
entries.description: Much of the genre's own history is materially difficult to read, and the gaps are not random.
entries.principle: Libraries did not accession numbered category romance, mass-market paper degrades, and small and specialist imprints left thin bibliographic records. The result is a genre whose commercial centre for three decades is now among its least accessible material. The gaps fall hardest on exactly the parts of the record already least documented — category titles, small-press queer romance, and the Black romance lines of the 1980s and 1990s.
entries.example: Specialist collections and documentation projects now hold much of what survives of the early Black romance market, and are the primary rather than supplementary source for it.
entries.application: When the record is thin, say so on the page. A confident claim about an under-documented title is a fabrication with an assured tone, and in this genre the temptation is constant.

entries.name: Electronic Publishing and the Erotic Romance Market
entries.description: Digital publishing arrived in romance a decade before the wider trade noticed, and it arrived through content the trade would not print.
entries.principle: Electronic and small-press publishers built a working erotic romance market from the 1990s, ahead of mainstream trade and outside its heat constraints. They demonstrated demand, established conventions about frequency and explicitness, and trained a readership in buying digitally — all of which the later self-publishing boom inherited rather than invented.
entries.example: Black Lace launched in the United Kingdom in 1993 and Ellora's Cave in the United States in 2000, and the conventions they established for the category persist in the current indie market.
entries.application: Read the digital transition as content-led rather than technology-led. The channel succeeded first where the trade's specifications forbade what readers were asking for, which is a pattern worth recognising when a current constraint looks permanent.

entries.name: Kindle, Self-Publishing and the Reordering of the Market
entries.description: Romance became the genre where independent publishing works, for reasons specific to how romance is read.
entries.principle: Romance readers read in volume, buy by trope and heat rather than by review, and follow series — a behaviour profile that suits algorithmic discovery and subscription reading better than any other genre's. Self-publishing consequently took a larger share of romance than of any comparable category, and the market's structural conventions now follow the channel's incentives: series-first, rapid release, trope-forward description.
entries.example: The subscription page-read model in particular rewards continued reading rather than the purchase decision, which is the direct cause of several current conventions that are frequently discussed as if they were aesthetic developments.
entries.application: Know which of the genre's current norms are channel artefacts. A convention produced by a payment mechanic is one you may decline if you are not publishing into that mechanic.

entries.name: 2019 to 2024: The Crisis and the Collapse
entries.description: The genre's professional body confronted its own record, fractured, and filed for bankruptcy within five years.
entries.principle: The Romance Writers of America acknowledged in 2018 that under half a percent of RITA finalists had been Black authors and that none had won. Kennedy Ryan won in 2019, in the award's final year. A disciplinary action against an author who had raised racism complaints, and its rapid reversal, precipitated mass resignations, sponsor withdrawal and the cancellation of the awards. RWA filed for Chapter 11 in May 2024, the plan was confirmed on 8 July 2024, and the case was terminated by final decree that November, with roughly eighty per cent of membership lost. The body still operates in reduced form.
entries.example: The awards record shows the discontinuity precisely: the RITA ran 1990–2019; the Vivian was announced in 2020 and awarded once, for 2021, with one award rescinded; the Diamond Heart is the body's current published-book award, first cycle 2025–26. Guidance describing the Vivian as ongoing is stale rather than wrong.
entries.application: Do not cite RWA as the genre's governing authority in present-tense terms, and check the date on any award claim from this period. No successor body of comparable scope emerged; the genre's promise is now maintained by readers and retailers.

entries.name: BookTok, Romantasy and the Present Shape
entries.description: A social-media-driven readership arrived in the 2020s, and the data about it is routinely misreported.
entries.principle: The 2020s brought a large new romance readership through social recommendation, with romantasy as its most visible form. The commercial effect was real and the reporting of it is unreliable in one specific way: the standard market figures are print-only point-of-sale data, in the genre most skewed to ebook and subscription. Any market-share claim must name its instrument.
entries.example: In 2022 romance print sales rose sharply — reported at around forty per cent, on the order of nineteen million units — while romance ebook sales fell over the same period, which indicates a genuinely new print readership rather than a format shift. The two figures are only intelligible together.
entries.application: Quote market data with its instrument named, and be sceptical of any romance sales claim that does not. The genre's most commonly cited figures systematically undercount it, and the undercount is largest exactly where the growth is.

entries.name: Attachment Theory and Its Over-Application
entries.description: The most-borrowed psychological framework in current romance craft advice, and the most over-extended.
entries.principle: Attachment theory originates in observational work on infant–caregiver behaviour and was later extended to adult romantic relationships. The adult extension is a live research area rather than a settled one: the categorical style labels are contested, measurement varies substantially between instruments, and stability over time is weaker than popular accounts imply. The framework is genuinely useful as a source of consistent character behaviour and is not a diagnostic system.
entries.example: Popular craft advice routinely assigns characters a fixed attachment style and derives their whole behavioural repertoire from it, which is a stronger claim than the research supports even where the underlying pattern is real.
entries.application: Use attachment as a source of behavioural consistency, not as a character key. Give a character a history that produces a pattern, then let the pattern be inconsistent under pressure, because that is what the observational literature actually shows.

entries.name: Pair Bonding and the Limits of the Animal Model
entries.description: The neurochemical account of bonding is real, partial, and routinely overstated in genre discussion.
entries.principle: There is substantial evidence that particular neuropeptides and reward-system activity are involved in social bonding, much of it derived from non-human animal models. Extending it to human romantic pair bonding is legitimate as a line of inquiry and weak as an explanation of any particular relationship, because human bonding is culturally mediated in ways the animal models cannot capture. The mechanism is not the meaning.
entries.example: The paranormal subgenre's mating-bond conventions frequently invoke a biological inevitability that reads as scientific, and the effect is to make a chosen relationship look involuntary — which is a craft decision with consequences rather than a finding.
entries.application: If your world uses a biological bond, decide what it can and cannot override and write the rule down, because the consent question in your book descends entirely from it. Do not import the vocabulary of neurochemistry to make an authorial decision look inevitable.

entries.name: Security as the Genre's Endpoint
entries.description: What the guarantee describes, in behavioural terms.
entries.principle: The state a romance ending depicts is best described as felt security: confidence that the other person is reliably available and responsive, and that conflict will not end the relationship. This is a more precise account of the genre's promise than happiness, and it explains why an ending can be satisfying without being cheerful — the guarantee is about reliability rather than mood.
entries.example: Endings that depict a couple facing ongoing difficulty without doubting each other satisfy readers reliably, whereas endings that supply contentment without demonstrating reliability draw the specific complaint that the ending felt unearned.
entries.application: Write the ending as evidence of availability and responsiveness rather than as a description of feeling. Show one of them being reachable at the moment it is expensive, which is the behavioural core of what the promise claims.

entries.name: The Anxious–Avoidant Pattern as a Plot
entries.description: A behavioural dynamic that maps unusually well onto romance structure, with a caution attached.
entries.principle: The pattern in which one party's pursuit intensifies the other's withdrawal, and vice versa, is well described in the relationship literature and is a durable engine for a novel because it is self-sustaining and requires deliberate action to interrupt. The caution is that the popular version treats the two positions as fixed personality types; the research describes them as interactional patterns that shift with partner and circumstance.
entries.example: Long-burn romance frequently runs on exactly this dynamic, and the strongest versions show the roles swapping at least once, which is both more accurate and more interesting than a fixed assignment.
entries.application: Build the cycle and then break it deliberately on the page, because a pattern that resolves without anyone changing their behaviour reads as capitulation. Let each party occupy both positions at some point.

entries.name: Repair Is the Mechanism
entries.description: The relationship literature's most transferable finding for this genre, and it is not about conflict avoidance.
entries.principle: Across several research traditions, what distinguishes durable relationships is not the absence of conflict but the presence of repair — the capacity to re-establish connection after rupture. This is directly useful to romance because it identifies what the genre's reckoning scene is actually depicting, and it explains why an ending that skips the repair feels hollow regardless of how the conflict resolved.
entries.example: The genre's grovel convention is a repair sequence in dramatic form, and the versions that work are the ones where the repair is enacted rather than promised — which matches what the literature identifies as effective.
entries.application: Stage the repair rather than reporting it. The specific behaviours the research describes — accurate acknowledgement, accepting influence, resuming contact — are also, conveniently, the components of a scene.

entries.name: What Attachment Language Gets Wrong in Craft Advice
entries.description: A direct correction, because the vocabulary has spread faster than the caveats.
entries.principle: Three errors recur in romance craft discussion: treating attachment styles as fixed and diagnostic; treating "secure" as a personality achievement rather than a relational state; and treating therapeutic vocabulary as available to characters in periods and settings where it did not exist. The third is a historical-accuracy problem as much as a psychological one, and readers of historical romance detect it immediately even when they cannot name it.
entries.example: A Regency heroine who describes her own behaviour in terms of avoidance and self-regulation is using a framework that had not been formulated, which is an anachronism of the same order as a wristwatch.
entries.application: Let characters have the pattern and not the vocabulary. Period characters may be perceptive about themselves in the terms their own culture supplied — moral, religious, humoural, social — and a writer who does the translation gets both the psychology and the period right.

entries.name: Desire and the Uncertainty Effect
entries.description: Uncertainty about another person's regard sustains attention, which is why the genre defers.
entries.principle: There is reasonable evidence that uncertainty about whether another person likes you sustains thinking about them, and the effect is one plausible mechanism behind the genre's slow-burn conventions. The finding should be held loosely — effect sizes in this literature are modest and contexts vary — but it is consistent with what the form has arrived at by trial.
entries.example: Dual-viewpoint romance deliberately forfeits this effect for the reader while preserving it between the characters, which is a structural trade rather than an oversight and explains why the convention pairs so often with a strong external obstacle.
entries.application: Preserve uncertainty between the characters even where you have removed it for the reader. What sustains a reader in dual viewpoint is watching two people fail to know what the reader knows, which is dramatic irony doing the work uncertainty does elsewhere.

entries.name: Novelty, Habituation and the Long Relationship
entries.description: Why the genre ends where it does, and what a continuing couple has to solve.
entries.principle: Responses to a repeated stimulus attenuate, which is well established in general terms and much less well specified for long relationships than popular accounts suggest. What the relationship literature more reliably supports is that shared novel activity and continued curiosity are associated with sustained satisfaction. This has a direct structural consequence: the genre conventionally ends at the point where habituation would begin, and books that continue past it must find a different engine.
entries.example: The continuing-couple model solves it by moving the source of tension outside the relationship entirely, which is why the successful examples are attached to investigation, war or a long external plot.
entries.application: If you write past the ending, give the couple new external material rather than manufactured doubt. Curiosity about each other under new conditions is the honest version of what those books are depicting.

entries.name: Arousal Misattribution
entries.description: A famous finding, heavily cited in craft advice, that should be handled with care.
entries.principle: The proposition that physiological arousal from one source can be misread as attraction is well known from a small number of classic studies, and it is exactly the kind of striking mid-century finding that later replication work has treated cautiously. The underlying idea — that context shapes how bodily states are interpreted — is broadly supported; the specific dramatic version, that danger reliably produces attraction, is a stronger claim than the evidence carries.
entries.example: The convention that shared peril generates romance is old and effective in fiction, and its effectiveness in fiction is not evidence for the mechanism; the romantic-suspense tradition works because proximity and stakes are structurally useful, whatever the physiology.
entries.application: Use shared danger for the structural reasons — enforced proximity, revealed character, compressed time — rather than because you believe it produces attraction. A card that cites the bridge study as settled science is doing the thing this collection exists to avoid.

entries.name: Responsive Versus Spontaneous Desire
entries.description: A distinction from sex research that the genre's conventions frequently contradict.
entries.principle: Contemporary sex research distinguishes desire that arises spontaneously from desire that emerges in response to context and stimulation, and reports the responsive pattern as common, particularly though not exclusively among women. Romance convention overwhelmingly depicts spontaneous desire arriving unbidden, which is a narrative convenience rather than a representation of how desire is commonly reported.
entries.example: Scenes in which the negotiation and the approach are given as much attention as the act depict responsive desire accurately, and readers frequently report those scenes as more convincing without being able to say why.
entries.application: Write the conditions as well as the impulse. A character who becomes interested during rather than before is both more common and more interesting to read, because the scene then has a progression rather than a starting state.

entries.name: What Fantasy Is Not a Prediction Of
entries.description: The correction that has to be made before any discussion of the genre's darker content.
entries.principle: There is no supported basis for treating a reader's enjoyment of a fictional scenario as an indication that they want it to occur. Research on sexual fantasy has consistently found that fantasy content does not straightforwardly map to desired real events, and that this is unremarkable rather than pathological. This is the single most important finding in this collection for anyone writing or defending dark romance.
entries.example: The genre's captivity and coercion registers have been subject to recurring public argument on the assumption that depiction implies endorsement and enjoyment implies desire, and neither inference is supported.
entries.application: Do not build a defence of dark content on the claim that readers are working something out. Build it on the accurate and simpler claim that fiction is not a statement of preference, and then meet the actual craft obligation, which is that the book must take a position on what it depicts.

entries.name: Narrative Transportation
entries.description: The absorbed state readers of this genre are pursuing, and what produces it.
entries.principle: Transportation describes the experience of being absorbed into a narrative world, with reduced awareness of surroundings and reduced counter-arguing. It is one of the better-supported constructs in the reading literature and is associated with vivid mental imagery, coherent narrative structure and emotional engagement. It is also the state romance readers most consistently describe seeking, which explains the genre's premium on smooth structure over stylistic difficulty.
entries.example: The genre's conventions — familiar structure, declared expectations, minimal formal obstruction — are all transportation-friendly, which is a coherent design rather than a failure of ambition.
entries.application: Treat anything that breaks absorption as expensive, and spend that cost deliberately. Formal experiment in this genre is possible and must be paid for with something the reader values at least as much.

entries.name: Identification Is Not Substitution
entries.description: A correction to the oldest condescension about romance readers.
entries.principle: The persistent claim that romance readers insert themselves into the heroine and experience the book as wish-fulfilment substitution is not supported by the ethnographic and empirical work that exists. Readers describe assessing characters, judging decisions, disagreeing with protagonists and reading critically. Identification in the research sense involves sharing a character's perspective, not replacing them.
entries.example: Reader communities routinely and vigorously criticise heroines' decisions, which is behaviour incompatible with the substitution model and observable in any review thread.
entries.application: Write heroines who can be disagreed with. The substitution theory produces bland protagonists designed to be occupied rather than met, and the actual readership is far more interested in someone whose choices they can argue about.

entries.name: The Interiority Advantage
entries.description: Why prose romance retains a specific power that screen adaptation cannot reproduce.
entries.principle: Prose grants direct access to a character's thought, and there is reasonable evidence that engagement with fiction involving rich mental-state description is associated with social-cognitive processing. Whatever the strength of the broader claims made about fiction and empathy — which are contested and have had replication difficulties — the narrower point holds: prose supplies interiority directly, and romance is a genre organised around it.
entries.example: Screen adaptations of romance routinely compensate for lost interiority with voiceover, letters or invented confidant scenes, which is direct evidence of what the medium change costs.
entries.application: Use what the medium gives you. If your novel's most powerful scenes would survive adaptation unchanged, you are probably not using interiority hard enough.

entries.name: Mirroring, Mentalising and the Reader's Model
entries.description: Readers build and continuously revise a model of each character, which is what makes withheld information work.
entries.principle: Reading fiction involves inferring characters' beliefs, intentions and knowledge — mentalising — and tracking who knows what. Romance depends on this more heavily than most genres, because dramatic irony between two viewpoint characters requires the reader to maintain two separate and partly incorrect models simultaneously. This is cognitively demanding and is one reason the form's apparent simplicity is misleading.
entries.example: Dual-viewpoint romance requires a reader to hold each character's mistaken model of the other alongside the true state, which is three models running at once and is routinely performed without effort by readers the genre is patronised for.
entries.application: Keep the models trackable. Every time you switch viewpoint, make clear what that character currently believes, because a reader who loses track of who knows what loses the irony that the structure exists to generate.

entries.name: Why Known Endings Do Not Reduce Engagement
entries.description: The empirical answer to the genre's most common dismissal.
entries.principle: Work on spoilers and on re-reading indicates that foreknowledge of outcome does not reliably reduce enjoyment and can increase it, plausibly because attention shifts from what happens to how and why. The findings are modest and have been debated, but they are consistent with an extremely large natural experiment: an entire genre whose readers know the ending in advance and read in volume.
entries.example: Re-reading behaviour in romance is unusually high, and readers describe returning to books specifically for the passages between known events — which is what the shift-of-attention account predicts.
entries.application: Stop protecting the outcome and start constructing the route. The reader's attention is on cost, process and texture, and a book that withholds those to protect a surprise nobody expected has spent its resources on the wrong thing.

entries.name: Predictability as a Feature
entries.description: The reliability of the ending is what permits the intensity of the middle.
entries.principle: A guaranteed outcome allows a reader to engage with distressing material at a depth they would not risk otherwise, because the resolution is known to be safe. This is the strongest available explanation for why romance can carry grief, abuse, addiction and bereavement more directly than genres without a guarantee — the promise is not a softening but a licence.
entries.example: Romances dealing with severe material routinely go further into it than comparable literary treatments, precisely because the reader has been assured of where the book ends.
entries.application: Use the guarantee to go further, not less far. A romance that treats the promise as a reason to keep everything gentle has taken the constraint and declined the compensation.

entries.name: Emotional Regulation and Re-Reading
entries.description: Why readers return to books whose endings they know exactly.
entries.principle: Readers describe using fiction deliberately to manage mood, and re-reading known books is a common and effective strategy because the emotional trajectory is predictable. This is a reported and observable behaviour rather than a contested theory, and it explains a purchasing and reading pattern that the genre's critics have consistently misread as compulsion.
entries.example: Comfort re-reading is described openly and specifically by romance readers, frequently with reference to particular scenes rather than whole books.
entries.application: Write the re-read scene deliberately. Readers return to the reunion, the declaration and the first acknowledgement far more than to the plot, and knowing which of your scenes is that scene tells you where to spend your best writing.

entries.name: Safety and the Ability to Feel Risk
entries.description: A structural point about how the promise interacts with tension.
entries.principle: A reader who is certain of the outcome can afford to feel the danger fully, which is why the guarantee does not flatten tension in practice. What it does is relocate it: the reader's anxiety attaches to the cost and the process rather than the outcome. Books that misunderstand this try to generate doubt about the ending and produce a reader who is not anxious but suspicious.
entries.example: The reliable failure mode is the romance that appears to threaten its own ending, which readers experience as the author breaking faith rather than as raised stakes.
entries.application: Never threaten the ending. Threaten what it will cost, who will be hurt on the way, and what each of them will have to give up — those are unlimited, and the outcome is not available to spend.

entries.name: Reading Under Stress
entries.description: Romance readership rises in difficult periods, and the explanation is not escapism as usually meant.
entries.principle: The genre's readership expands during periods of general instability, which is frequently explained as escape. The better account is that a guaranteed resolution is a rare commodity when outcomes elsewhere are uncertain, and that reading a book whose ending is assured is a form of regulated engagement rather than avoidance. Escapism implies not looking; romance readers are looking at difficult material with a safety rail.
entries.example: The genre's growth through the early 2020s coincided with a period of general disruption, and reader accounts emphasise reliability of outcome rather than avoidance of subject matter.
entries.application: Do not write down to a supposedly escapist readership. The evidence suggests they are seeking reliability rather than absence of difficulty, and books that supply only the second are the ones described as forgettable.

entries.name: The Comfort Objection, Answered
entries.description: The charge that reassurance is a lesser aim, and what can properly be said against it.
entries.principle: The objection holds that a form guaranteeing consolation cannot tell the truth. The answer is structural rather than defensive: the guarantee constrains the ending only, and constrains it to optimism rather than to ease, so everything before it remains available. A genre that must argue its way to a credible optimistic ending has set itself a harder problem than one permitted to end in collapse, which is the opposite of the charge.
entries.example: Novels in this genre that carry addiction, abuse or bereavement to a credible optimistic resolution have solved a harder structural problem than an equivalent book that ends in loss, and the difficulty is visible in how often the attempt fails.
entries.application: When defending the form, argue from the constraint rather than from the pleasure. The strongest case for romance is that its ending is an obligation to be met, and meeting it honestly is technically demanding.

entries.category: Reading as Practice, and the Critiques
entries.name: Radway and the Ethnographic Turn
entries.description: The first sustained empirical study of romance readers, and what it did and did not establish.
entries.principle: Janice Radway's *Reading the Romance* (1984) studied a community of readers directly and argued that romance reading functioned partly as a claim on time and attention within constrained domestic lives. It was field-defining and has been substantially criticised since — for the size and specificity of its sample, for interpreting readers' accounts through a framework they did not share, and for a compensatory reading that later scholars including Radway herself revisited.
entries.example: The study's most durable contribution is methodological: it treated readers as informants rather than as symptoms, which had not previously been done.
entries.application: Cite Radway for the method and the questions rather than for the conclusions. Reference works that present the 1984 findings as the settled account of why people read romance are four decades out of date.

entries.category: Reading as Practice, and the Critiques
entries.name: Modleski and the Compensation Argument
entries.description: The strongest version of the case that the genre manages a dissatisfaction rather than resolving it.
entries.principle: Tania Modleski's *Loving with a Vengeance* (1982) read mass-market romance as a form that acknowledges women's anger and disappointment and then resolves them in ways that leave the underlying conditions untouched. It is the most serious feminist critique of the genre's structure and deserves engagement rather than dismissal, because it identifies a real mechanism — the reinterpretation of a man's bad behaviour as concealed love.
entries.example: The forced-seduction convention of the same period is the clearest instance of exactly the mechanism Modleski describes, which is one reason the critique landed.
entries.application: Test your own book against the argument. If the hero's early behaviour is redeemed by revealing his feelings rather than by his changing his conduct, you have written the structure Modleski identified, and you should know that you have.

entries.category: Reading as Practice, and the Critiques
entries.name: Regis and the Structural Defence
entries.description: The first sustained argument that romance is a form with a history rather than a product with a market.
entries.principle: Pamela Regis's *A Natural History of the Romance Novel* (2003) defined the genre by the courtship and its ending, identified recurring narrative elements across four centuries, and argued directly against the position that the form is inherently regressive. Her elements are descriptive rather than prescriptive — the 2003 book itself states they can occur in any order, be doubled, or share a scene, and a decade later she wrote that she would likely relabel them "pragmatic" rather than essential — and almost every secondary account converts them into a sequence.
entries.example: The eight elements are routinely presented as a beat sheet in craft guidance, which is a misuse Regis's own text explicitly forecloses.
entries.application: Use Regis to diagnose a finished draft, not to plan one. If you want a prescriptive tool, use a tool that was built to be prescriptive and knows it.

entries.category: Reading as Practice, and the Critiques
entries.name: The Internal Critique
entries.description: The genre's sharpest criticism has consistently come from inside it.
entries.principle: Romance's readers, authors and critics have argued about consent, race, class and representation within the field for decades, and generally in advance of external commentary. The 2019 crisis was the culmination of a long-running internal argument rather than an external intervention, and the reform of the forced-seduction convention was driven by writers and readers rather than by critics.
entries.example: Reader-critic communities and author-led criticism documented the genre's problems with race and consent extensively before either received sustained attention outside the field.
entries.application: Read the internal criticism before the academic literature. It is more current, more specific, and more directly useful about what a book will be held to now.

entries.category: Reading as Practice, and the Critiques
entries.name: What the Research Does Not Support
entries.description: A closing card, because the useful thing a reference can do is mark its own limits.
entries.principle: Several claims circulate in romance craft discussion with more confidence than the evidence carries: that reading romance measurably changes relationship expectations; that fictional preference indicates real-world desire; that attachment styles are fixed and diagnostic; and that any single neurochemical account explains bonding. Each is either contested, weakly supported, or a stronger version of a modest finding. Marking them is more useful than repeating them.
entries.example: The broader literature on fiction and social cognition, frequently invoked to defend the genre, has itself had replication difficulties, and a defence built on it is less secure than one built on the form's structural demands.
entries.application: Defend the genre on craft grounds, which are solid, rather than on psychological ones, which are contested. And when a craft book cites a study, check whether the claim is the study's or the author's — in this field the gap is usually where the advice went wrong.

entries.name: Ann Radcliffe
entries.description: Gave the courtship novel its danger, and gave the dangerous man a rational explanation.
entries.meta: English, 1764–1823. No awards — the category did not exist. Two live misattributions: Radcliffe College honours a different Ann Radcliffe, and several Minerva Press novels were falsely catalogued as hers, including two of 1790. The 1809 novel Manfrone belongs to neither Ann nor Mary Ann Radcliffe.
entries.knownFor: The explained supernatural, and a heroine whose investigation of a man and a house is the plot rather than a subplot.
entries.signature: Extended landscape and architecture used as delay, so that apprehension accumulates across pages in which nothing happens — the technique romantic suspense still runs on.

works.title: The Mysteries of Udolpho
works.note: the novel Austen's Northanger Abbey is written against, and the direct ancestor of the gothic romance paperback boom

works.title: Gaston de Blondeville
works.note: posthumous

entries.name: Samuel Richardson
entries.description: Established that a woman's inner life could carry a novel, and that virtue could be a negotiation.
entries.meta: English, 1689–1761. No awards. A printer by trade who came to fiction through a commissioned book of model letters, which is why the epistolary method is structural rather than stylistic in his work.
entries.knownFor: The sentimental novel, and the first sustained demonstration that sustained access to a woman's consciousness is enough to hold a long narrative.
entries.signature: Letters as evidence — documents with a writer, a recipient and a purpose, which gives interiority a reason to exist on the page and lets the reader hold what the characters cannot.

works.title: Pamela, or Virtue Rewarded
works.note: the heroine's virtue is explicitly an asset under negotiation, and the origin of the marriage-after-coercion plot

works.title: Clarissa
works.note: the counter-case, in which the coercion is not redeemed

works.title: The History of Sir Charles Grandison

entries.name: Jane Austen
entries.description: Supplies the period the genre keeps returning to, and the technique for making manners generate plot.
entries.meta: English, 1775–1817. No awards. **She used no pen name**: the novels appeared anonymously, the first as "By a Lady" and the rest as by the author of the preceding book. Northanger Abbey and Persuasion were published together in December 1817 with an 1818 title page.
entries.knownFor: Free indirect style, and obstacles built entirely from money, information and what may be said in whose hearing.
entries.signature: The evidentiary reversal — hostility founded on a specific matter of fact, so that changing a character's mind requires changing what they know rather than how they feel.

works.title: Pride and Prejudice
works.note: the single most imitated structure in the genre

works.title: Northanger Abbey
works.note: posthumous

works.title: Persuasion
works.note: posthumous, and the genre's founding second-chance novel

entries.name: Charlotte Brontë
entries.description: Wrote the plain heroine who refuses on principle, and the hero who is also the suspect.
entries.meta: English, 1816–1855. No awards. Published as Currer Bell, a pen name of her own choosing shared in form with her sisters' — a deliberate ambiguity of gender rather than a publisher requirement.
entries.knownFor: First-person moral authority in a heroine with no beauty, money or family, and a prior claim that is a living woman rather than a piece of information.
entries.signature: Refusal as the demonstration of worth — the heroine's most defining act is walking away from the thing she wants most, on terms she sets.

works.title: Jane Eyre
works.note: supplies the gothic romance its template and its moral spine, and remains the genre's most influential single novel after Austen

works.title: The Professor
works.note: posthumous

entries.name: Emily Brontë
entries.description: The genre's darkest inheritance, and the argument about whether it belongs here at all.
entries.meta: English, 1818–1848. No awards. Published as Ellis Bell. Her single novel is routinely marketed as a romance and structurally is not one — the genre cites it constantly and cannot deliver its ending.
entries.knownFor: Obsessive attachment pursued past every limit, followed across two generations and never redeemed.
entries.signature: Revenge conducted through courtship, with the improvement of the avenger never permitted to excuse the intention behind it.

works.title: Wuthering Heights
works.note: the founding text for dark romance's central problem, and the clearest demonstration of what the genre's guarantee actually excludes

entries.name: Elizabeth Gaskell
entries.description: Put the courtship inside an argument about industry, wages and class.
entries.meta: English, 1810–1865. No awards. Her Life of Charlotte Brontë was withdrawn after a libel threat and reissued in censored second and third editions — a documented fact, though the identity of the complainant should be treated with care in any account.
entries.knownFor: The industrial courtship, in which the couple cannot proceed until a substantive disagreement about how people should be paid is settled.
entries.signature: Ending on an inversion of the financial relation rather than on a reconciliation of feeling — the heroine becomes the hero's creditor.

works.title: North and South
works.note: the model for every romance in which the obstacle is a position rather than a misunderstanding

works.title: Wives and Daughters
works.note: posthumous and unfinished

entries.name: Mary Elizabeth Braddon
entries.description: The sensation novel's most prolific practitioner, and the genre's first great professional.
entries.meta: English, 1835–1915. No awards. Wrote under at least four names beyond her own, including Babington White and Lady Caroline Lascelles — all personal pen names. A plagiarism accusation over the novel Circe was made by a personal enemy and never litigated, and should be recorded as an accusation rather than a finding.
entries.knownFor: The bigamy plot, the secret past and the respectable woman with a criminal history, produced at industrial speed for a mass readership.
entries.signature: A heroine whose concealment is rational and self-interested rather than tragic, which is closer to modern romantic suspense than anything else in the period.

works.title: Lady Audley's Secret
works.note: the sensation novel's defining text and the ancestor of the woman-with-a-past plot

entries.name: Thomas Hardy
entries.description: The counter-case: courtship written with the social penalties fully enforced.
entries.meta: English, 1840–1928. **He won no Nobel Prize** despite many nominations, and the Order of Merit he received in 1910 is a Crown honour rather than a literary award. Any Nobel claim is false. Note also that the serial text of Tess is bowdlerised, so a citation must say which text it means.
entries.knownFor: Sexual double standards depicted with their consequences intact, and courtships destroyed by exactly the mechanisms romance conventionally overcomes.
entries.signature: The unwanted suitor written as pitiable rather than villainous, which is more unsettling than a straightforward antagonist and much harder to do.

works.title: Far from the Madding Crowd
works.note: three suitors, all of whom damage her, and the genre's best study of what an unwanted claim actually costs

entries.name: Edith Wharton
entries.description: Showed social enforcement operating without anyone needing to state it.
entries.meta: American, 1862–1937. Pulitzer Prize for the Novel, 1921 — awarded after the trustees overrode a jury that had selected another book, which is a documented irregularity worth stating. The New York State Edith Wharton Citation of Merit is named for her and postdates her death: she did not win it. Her fiction contains antisemitic characterisation, notably in The House of Mirth, and its presence is established scholarship even where its function is debated.
entries.knownFor: The renunciation ending, and a precise account of how money and standing enforce a marriage outcome without a threat being made.
entries.signature: Constraint conveyed through what characters decline to say, so that the reader infers the machinery from the silence around it.

works.title: The Age of Innocence
works.note: the definitive account of social enforcement as a romance obstacle

entries.name: E. M. Hull
entries.description: Wrote the abduction romance that made the genre a mass phenomenon and set its worst template.
entries.meta: English, 1880–1947. Full name Edith Maude Hull, published under initials. No awards. Two persistent errors: her sequel is The Sons of the Sheik, plural, and is distinct from the 1926 film with the singular title; and the novel is **not** an interracial romance, because the plot retroactively reveals the abductor to be of European parentage.
entries.knownFor: The desert abduction romance, an international bestseller and film phenomenon that established forced seduction as a commercial template half a century before the paperback boom repeated it.
entries.signature: Coercion laundered by the heroine's eventual consent, and racial anxiety resolved by retracting the premise rather than examining it — the two failures are connected and both were inherited.

works.title: The Sheik
works.note: the origin of the modern genre's discarded convention, and required reading for understanding what the 1970s boom was repeating

entries.name: Elinor Glyn
entries.description: Made romantic fiction scandalous, profitable and cinematic, and coined the vocabulary of sex appeal.
entries.meta: British, 1864–1943. No awards. The tiger-skin doggerel universally attached to her name is **not hers** — its author is unknown and it is first traceable to a mid-century biography. Her association with the word "It" as a term for sexual magnetism is documented and is her most durable contribution to popular vocabulary.
entries.knownFor: Frank sexual content in mainstream commercial fiction decades before the category system permitted it, and an early career as a Hollywood screenwriter and consultant.
entries.signature: Aristocratic settings and a directness about desire that made her books notorious, sold enormously, and demonstrated the market that later publishers spent decades declining to serve.

works.title: Three Weeks
works.note: the succès de scandale that proved the commercial scale of frank romantic fiction

entries.name: Daphne du Maurier
entries.description: Perfected the technique the entire gothic romance boom would imitate for thirty years.
entries.meta: British, 1907–1989. Mystery Writers of America Grand Master, **1978** — frequently misdated. Her 1938 award for Rebecca was the **American Booksellers Association's National Book Award** (a booksellers'-vote award given 1936–1942), a distinct, earlier prize — not the modern National Book Award founded in 1950 — and the two are conflated in current marketing. Dame Commander, 1969 — an honour of state, not a literary award. A plagiarism suit against her failed, and a separate claimed resemblance to a 1934 Brazilian novel was never litigated.
entries.knownFor: The unnamed narrator, the dead first wife, and a suspicion sustained so completely that the reader's uncertainty is the plot.
entries.signature: Withholding through the narrator's genuine ignorance rather than her dishonesty, which is why the revelation survives re-reading — the standard every gothic romance since has failed to meet.

works.title: Rebecca
works.note: the most imitated romantic suspense novel in English and the direct template for the 1960s gothic paperback boom

entries.name: Margaret Mitchell
entries.description: Wrote the century's biggest romance-adjacent bestseller, and one of its most durable propaganda texts.
entries.meta: American, 1900–1949. Pulitzer Prize for the Novel, 1937; her 1936 award was the **American Booksellers Association's National Book Award** (a booksellers'-vote award given 1936–1942), a distinct, earlier prize — not the modern National Book Award founded in 1950. A 1937 plagiarism suit against her failed. The novel's Lost Cause framing and its treatment of enslaved characters are not incidental, and belong on the record alongside her documented and long-concealed funding of medical scholarships for Black students at Morehouse College. State both; neither cancels the other.
entries.knownFor: A heroine who is unlikeable, competent and economically ruthless, and a central relationship the author refuses to resolve.
entries.signature: Economic independence written as the thing that destroys her heroine's marriages, and presented as neither a moral failing nor a problem to be fixed.

works.title: Gone with the Wind
works.note: the genre's most commercially significant near-miss, delivering every romance component except the guarantee

entries.name: Kathleen Winsor
entries.description: Demonstrated in 1944 that the market for explicit historical romance was enormous and unserved.
entries.meta: American, 1919–2003 — her birth year is given variously and should be treated with caution. No awards. Forever Amber was banned in a number of US states and prosecuted in Massachusetts, where the case was dismissed in March 1947; the details of the appellate history circulate in unreliable forms and should be verified before restating.
entries.knownFor: A vast Restoration-era bestseller whose sexual frankness triggered censorship actions and outsold nearly everything else of its decade.
entries.signature: A picaresque heroine who ascends through men and is never punished by the narrative for it, which is closer to the 1970s boom than to anything else in the 1940s.

works.title: Forever Amber
works.note: the proof of concept for the explicit historical, twenty-eight years before the paperback boom acted on it

entries.name: Georgette Heyer
entries.description: Invented the Regency romance as a working literary system, and her conventions now outrank the period.
entries.meta: English, 1902–1974. No awards — she predates them all, and the Historical Novel Prize in Memory of Georgette Heyer, which ran from 1978 to 1989, is named for her and postdates her death. Her novel The Grand Sophy contains an antisemitic caricature that is not incidental and is documented in her private papers as reflecting her own views; a 2023 Sourcebooks edition revised the passage, and claims of an earlier silent revision are unverified.
entries.knownFor: Constructing the Regency idiom — vocabulary, social calendar, class markers, comic register and reusable plot shapes — from period sources, so completely that the subgenre now derives from her rather than from the era.
entries.signature: Erotic charge carried entirely by dialogue and the management of social distance, with no explicit content whatever.

works.title: These Old Shades
works.note: the Georgian register established first

works.title: Devil's Cub
