entries.author: Jude Deveraux
entries.awards: None
entries.description: Pocket Books, July 1989, **hardcover** at 341 pages, with the mass-market edition following in June 1990 — which is where the framing of the boom as…
entries.text: Pocket Books, July 1989, **hardcover** at 341 pages, with the mass-market edition following in June 1990 — which is where the framing of the boom as uniformly mass-market breaks. The novel made time-travel romance a commercial category and built it on the only obstacle that cannot be negotiated: two people who belong to periods that cannot both hold them, so someone must give up a century. **Its ending was not rewritten in the 2002 reissue** — a useful contrast with the McNaught case in this same batch, since the two books are routinely discussed together as examples of authorial revision and only one of them is.

entries.name: Gentle Rogue
entries.author: Johanna Lindsey
entries.awards: None — checked against the 1990 to 1992 RITA winner and finalist lists
entries.description: The seafaring adventure romance at the height of Lindsey's commercial run, and a representative instance of the disguise-at-sea plot that the subgenre…
entries.text: The seafaring adventure romance at the height of Lindsey's commercial run, and a representative instance of the disguise-at-sea plot that the subgenre worked repeatedly. Its inclusion is as a control: an enormously successful book by an enormously successful writer, in a category with an active award, that won nothing and is absent from the finalist lists. The genre's canon assembled from award records would not contain Lindsey at all, which is the practical case for the pack's contested-canon method.

entries.name: Paradise
entries.author: Judith McNaught
entries.awards: None
entries.description: Pocket Books **hardcover**, 1991, 489 pages, with the mass market following in June 1992 — the second hardcover-first title in this batch and…
entries.text: Pocket Books **hardcover**, 1991, 489 pages, with the mass market following in June 1992 — the second hardcover-first title in this batch and confirmation that by the early 1990s the boom's leading authors had moved out of the format the era is named for. The novel is McNaught's contemporary corporate romance rather than a historical, and it marks the point at which the maximalist emotional register migrated from period settings into the present day, which is the route by which the boom's structural habits entered contemporary romance.

entries.name: Outlander
entries.author: Diana Gabaldon
entries.awards: **RITA, Best Romance of 1991** — RWA's top overall category, presented at the 1992 ceremony
entries.description: Published in the United States in 1991 and in the United Kingdom the same year by Century under the title **Cross Stitch**; the pack uses the US title…
entries.text: Published in the United States in 1991 and in the United Kingdom the same year by Century under the title **Cross Stitch**; the pack uses the US title as primary and records both. Its award is the batch's most instructive, and the award's *name* is the trap. RWA's top overall RITA ran from 1990 to 1996 as **"Best Romance of [book year]"**, and it is **omitted entirely from the most-used online award index**, which shows this book only as a losing finalist in two other categories. It is also widely miscited as "Romance of the Year" — a retailer shelf label RWA never used, which collides with an unrelated magazine award of that exact name. A genuine top-category win therefore reads as an error to anyone checking, and citing it under the wrong name makes it unverifiable. The novel itself grounds a time-travel premise in specific Jacobite history rather than generic tartan, and made the Highland setting a global phenomenon.

entries.name: Flowers from the Storm
entries.author: Laura Kinsale
entries.awards: None — a verified negative
entries.description: The genre's strongest demonstration that a physical constraint can carry an entire courtship. Kinsale's hero loses language after a stroke, which…
entries.text: The genre's strongest demonstration that a physical constraint can carry an entire courtship. Kinsale's hero loses language after a stroke, which forces the whole relationship into gesture, touch and inference and makes the constraint the engine rather than an obstacle to be overcome. The heroine forfeits her religious community and her standing within it, permanently and on the page, which is why the ending reads as a decision rather than a reward. It has placed at or near the top of the genre's major reader polls for two decades without ever having won an award, and the poll record and the award record disagree about this book more sharply than about any other.

entries.name: For My Lady's Heart
entries.author: Laura Kinsale
entries.awards: None — a verified negative
entries.description: A medieval romance written partly in Middle English, which is a technical decision almost no commercial romance has attempted before or since and which…
entries.text: A medieval romance written partly in Middle English, which is a technical decision almost no commercial romance has attempted before or since and which the novel sustains without losing its readership. Kinsale sets a vow against a life and gives her heroine no third option, so the black moment is a decision rather than a misfortune. The card sits beside the previous one to make a point about the award record: Kinsale has two RITAs, and neither is for either of the two novels most often cited as her best.

entries.name: Dreaming of You
entries.author: Lisa Kleypas
entries.awards: None — the 1994 Kleypas RITA finalist is a different title
entries.description: One of the most durably popular historical romances of the 1990s, and a demonstration of Kleypas's structural signature: social exposure escalated…
entries.text: One of the most durably popular historical romances of the 1990s, and a demonstration of Kleypas's structural signature: social exposure escalated alongside intimacy so that the two curves cross, and physical distance tracked with enough precision that a half-step is legible as an event. The award note matters because reference sources attach a finalist placing to this book that belongs to another of hers from the same period — the kind of error that survives because the author and the era are right and only the title is wrong.

entries.name: Lord of Scoundrels
entries.author: Loretta Chase
entries.description: Repeatedly voted the best historical romance in the genre by its own readers, and the vote record can be stated precisely: first place in All About…
entries.text: Repeatedly voted the best historical romance in the genre by its own readers, and the vote record can be stated precisely: first place in All About Romance's poll in 2000, 2004, 2007, 2010 and 2013, and first in the RRA-L reader poll every year from 1998 to 2003. Reference sources undercount both. Its 1996 RITA is **omitted from Chase's principal encyclopaedia entry**, which credits her with one win when she has two. What the novel does is keep the antagonism materially transactional to the end — every exchange extracts something, so even the reconciliation is a negotiation rather than a surrender — and it lets the heroine weaponise her own reputation deliberately, turning a constraint imposed on women into an instrument one of them chooses.

entries.name: The Duke and I
entries.author: Julia Quinn
entries.awards: None — a 2001 RITA finalist placing only
entries.description: The opening of the eight-sibling family series that became the genre's most successful screen adaptation and the dominant commercial model for the…
entries.text: The opening of the eight-sibling family series that became the genre's most successful screen adaptation and the dominant commercial model for the historical line. Quinn's Hall of Fame membership rests on three later RITAs and not on this book, which is frequently assumed. The novel uses a public compromise to force a marriage, demonstrating how efficiently the period's rules convert one observed moment into a lifetime arrangement, and it lets the innocent party act decisively and wrongly — which breaks the passivity the trope usually assigns and creates a reckoning the imitators mostly skip. The television adaptation is a separate work and is carded separately.

entries.name: Mr. Impossible
entries.author: Loretta Chase
entries.awards: RITA, 2006
entries.description: Chase's Egypt-set adventure romance, and the clearest instance in the collection of accurate perception reading as intimacy: the heroine identifies…
entries.text: Chase's Egypt-set adventure romance, and the clearest instance in the collection of accurate perception reading as intimacy: the heroine identifies exactly what the hero is bad at and exactly what he is better at than anyone believes, and the correctness of both readings is the courtship. A dating caution — the author's own site heads the book by its award year rather than its publication year, which is how the 2006 date enters catalogues. Chase's award record carries a further trap: an online index labels a 2021 Vivian of hers as a RITA, which would make three; the correct count is two.

entries.name: Devil in Winter
entries.author: Lisa Kleypas
entries.awards: None
entries.description: The Wallflowers novel in which the heroine proposes the arrangement and sets its conditions, which redistributes the power the marriage-of-convenience…
entries.text: The Wallflowers novel in which the heroine proposes the arrangement and sets its conditions, which redistributes the power the marriage-of-convenience trope usually hands to the man by default. Kleypas gives the heroine capital and the hero a title, inverting the usual direction of dependency and making the marriage a genuine transaction between unequal assets rather than a rescue. It is the pack's reference instance for the interconnected-standalone contract, since the series delivers a complete promise per volume while advancing a shared cast whose earlier resolutions are never reopened.

entries.name: The Raven Prince
entries.author: Elizabeth Hoyt
entries.awards: None
entries.description: Published 1 November 2006 — aggregator listings give an August date that the author's own site contradicts. Hoyt's Georgian-set historicals exploit the…
entries.text: Published 1 November 2006 — aggregator listings give an August date that the author's own site contradicts. Hoyt's Georgian-set historicals exploit the period's violence and class range in ways the Regency has to code, and this debut established the register. Its use in the pack is as the model for the grovel enacted rather than spoken: the hero makes a public gesture that forfeits reputation rather than money, which is the currency his character actually values, and the apology is therefore administered in the same venue as the injury.

entries.name: Private Arrangements
entries.author: Sherry Thomas
entries.awards: None
entries.description: A separated couple with directly opposed legal objectives, which is the marriage-in-trouble structure at its most rigorous: every scene is a…
entries.text: A separated couple with directly opposed legal objectives, which is the marriage-in-trouble structure at its most rigorous: every scene is a negotiation with a stated position on each side, and no reconciliation is available through logic. Thomas alternates timelines so that each present-day concession is priced against a withheld past one, and the reader assembles the injury rather than being shown it. The novel is also the debut of a writer working in English as a second language, which she has discussed publicly as a deliberate stylistic advantage rather than an obstacle.

entries.name: Nine Rules to Break When Romancing a Rake
entries.author: Sarah MacLean
entries.awards: None — a 2011 RITA finalist in **Regency** Historical Romance, a separate category from Historical Romance that year
entries.description: The list-driven Regency that placed the crisis where the heroine's project completes rather than at a prescribed percentage of the page count, which is…
entries.text: The list-driven Regency that placed the crisis where the heroine's project completes rather than at a prescribed percentage of the page count, which is the structural argument the pack makes against beat-sheet placement. MacLean's later work made her one of the genre's most visible public advocates, and the card notes the category distinction because 2011 ran two historical categories with different winners, and a finalist placing in one is routinely reported as the other.

entries.name: The Duchess War
entries.author: Courtney Milan
entries.awards: None
entries.description: Self-published in December 2012, at a point when independent publishing in historical romance was still unusual for an author with a traditional track…
entries.text: Self-published in December 2012, at a point when independent publishing in historical romance was still unusual for an author with a traditional track record. Milan's plots run on the period's actual machinery — patent law, medical licensing, inheritance statute — so the obstacle can be defeated only by understanding how it works, and here the heroine has the option of safety and takes the exposed position deliberately with the legal stakes fully specified. Catalogue records for the book carry placeholder dates a year out, which is a standard artefact of self-published metadata and worth knowing when citing indie titles of this period.

entries.name: Bringing Down the Duke
entries.author: Evie Dunmore
entries.awards: None — shortlisted for the Goldsboro Books Historical Romantic Novel Award, 2020
entries.description: The suffragist Regency-successor romance, published in the RITA's final year and therefore at the boundary of the genre's award record. Its credential…
entries.text: The suffragist Regency-successor romance, published in the RITA's final year and therefore at the boundary of the genre's award record. Its credential is frequently overstated on the author's own site as a British romance award; it was a **shortlisting**, and the prize went elsewhere. The novel's craft interest is that its heroine's politics make the conventional ending unavailable, so the book has to construct the specific legal and financial terms on which the guarantee can be paid without her surrendering the campaign — which is the historical line's central negotiation, solved rather than evaded.

entries.name: It Had to Be You
entries.author: Susan Elizabeth Phillips
entries.awards: **RITA, Best Romance of 1994** (presented 1995); *Affaire de Coeur* Romance of the Year, 1994
entries.description: The founding text of the modern American sports romance, and the clearest single instance of the award-name confusion this collection had to resolve.…
entries.text: The founding text of the modern American sports romance, and the clearest single instance of the award-name confusion this collection had to resolve. The book holds two separate honours whose names nearly coincide: RWA's top overall RITA, which the author's own site records under a differently worded label, and a magazine award actually called Romance of the Year. Aggregators collapse them. What the novel established is the Chicago Stars template — a professional football franchise as the series engine, with public status and private humiliation escalated together so the couple's intimacy always carries a reputational cost.

entries.name: Naked in Death
entries.author: J.D. Robb
entries.awards: None
entries.description: The continuing-couple model executed at scale, and the reason it is possible at all. Robb settles the relationship's terms inside the first volume and…
entries.text: The continuing-couple model executed at scale, and the reason it is possible at all. Robb settles the relationship's terms inside the first volume and then runs decades of investigation with the marriage as the reader's fixed point — the threat is always external, and the couple is the stable instrument through which it is faced rather than the thing under threat. That is the entire discipline the model requires: development is available, doubt is not. The pen name was adopted so a separate series could be published at a different pace without saturating the author's own name, which is the commercial half of the same design.

entries.name: Bridget Jones's Diary
entries.author: Helen Fielding
entries.awards: None — a widely cited 1998 audio award belongs to the narrator, not the author
entries.description: Originated as a newspaper column in 1995 before the novel appeared in 1996, and both dates belong on any account of it. Fielding reset the comic…
entries.text: Originated as a newspaper column in 1995 before the novel appeared in 1996, and both dates belong on any account of it. Fielding reset the comic first-person voice for a generation and did it by loosely transposing an Austen plot into a contemporary London that the column had already established as a running joke. The novel's technical achievement is a narrator whose self-deception is transparent to the reader and invisible to herself, sustained across a whole book without becoming cruel — which is much harder than it reads and is why the imitators mostly produced grating protagonists instead of funny ones.

entries.name: Welcome to Temptation
entries.author: Jennifer Crusie
entries.awards: None
entries.description: The pack's model black moment. Crusie turns the town, the family and the law against her heroine simultaneously and requires her to choose between…
entries.text: The pack's model black moment. Crusie turns the town, the family and the law against her heroine simultaneously and requires her to choose between protecting her sister and keeping the man, with both losses fully specified and neither recoverable. It is the model instance because the pressure is external, the choice is genuinely between two goods, and the reader can see exactly what is forfeited at the moment it is forfeited. A note on reception records for this period: star ratings from trade magazines circulate as if they were awards and are review scores.

entries.name: 16 Lighthouse Road
entries.author: Debbie Macomber
entries.awards: None
entries.description: The opening of the Cedar Cove series and the model for the community-engine structure: a town with a functioning local economy and a specific reason…
entries.text: The opening of the Cedar Cove series and the model for the community-engine structure: a town with a functioning local economy and a specific reason people cannot easily leave, which generates couples indefinitely without importing a new external problem each time. Its use in the pack is as the reference case for the interconnected-standalone contract observed correctly — earlier couples return as stable community fixtures who dispense advice and resources rather than as sources of renewed tension. The month and first-edition format could not be established with confidence and are omitted.

entries.name: Bet Me
entries.author: Jennifer Crusie
entries.awards: RITA, 2005, Contemporary Single Title
entries.description: Crusie's second RITA, in a different category from her first — which is why she is not in the RWA Hall of Fame, whose threshold requires three wins in…
entries.text: Crusie's second RITA, in a different category from her first — which is why she is not in the RWA Hall of Fame, whose threshold requires three wins in the same category, and why she is frequently and wrongly said to be. The novel is transparent about its ending from the first chapter and generates its tension entirely from two people's incompatible theories about themselves, which is the strongest available demonstration that the genre's known destination costs it nothing. The heroine overhears a wager about her, giving the antagonism a documentary basis no amount of subsequent charm can simply dissolve.

entries.name: Virgin River
entries.author: Robyn Carr
entries.awards: None — Carr never won a RITA, a 1987 finalist placing only
entries.description: The small-town community engine that the streaming era later made global, and a demonstration that the model's strength is economic rather than…
entries.text: The small-town community engine that the streaming era later made global, and a demonstration that the model's strength is economic rather than atmospheric. Carr gives the town a working medical practice, a bar and a reason for outsiders to arrive, and she uses an abandoned infant to create the proximity the romance requires — so the community generates the plot rather than decorating it. A publisher's promotional list attached to this title circulates as though it were a prize and is not.

entries.name: The Rosie Project
entries.author: Graeme Simsion
entries.awards: Victorian Premier's Literary Award for an unpublished manuscript, 2012
entries.description: Australian, and its bibliographic record is a useful caution: first published by Text Publishing in Australia on 30 January 2013, then by Michael…
entries.text: Australian, and its bibliographic record is a useful caution: first published by Text Publishing in Australia on 30 January 2013, then by Michael Joseph in the United Kingdom and Scribner in the United States that October, with a 2016 Text reissue date circulating in catalogues as though it were the first edition. Reference entries also give the wrong imprint for both the UK and US editions. The novel's craft interest is that its escalation is entirely in the negotiation of how two people will actually live, and its hero designs a compatibility instrument and falls for the one person it disqualifies.

entries.name: The Deal
entries.author: Elle Kennedy
entries.awards: None
entries.description: **Self-published on 24 February 2015**, with a traditional distribution deal following years later on the same ISBN — which is why retailer metadata…
entries.text: **Self-published on 24 February 2015**, with a traditional distribution deal following years later on the same ISBN — which is why retailer metadata now shows a trade publisher on a book that had none. The novel opened the college sports romance at the centre of the new-adult and indie boom, and its structure is a stated arrangement between two people that neither can afford to acknowledge has stopped being one, with the sport's calendar as the plot's clock. Kennedy's RITA is for a different, co-written book and should never be attached to this series.

entries.name: The Hating Game
entries.author: Sally Thorne
entries.awards: None
entries.description: Published 9 August 2016 by William Morrow Paperbacks as a **trade paperback with no hardcover first edition** — a format fact worth recording because…
entries.text: Published 9 August 2016 by William Morrow Paperbacks as a **trade paperback with no hardcover first edition** — a format fact worth recording because it was the commercial template for a decade of imitators. Thorne makes the rivalry structurally real by putting a single promotion between the two leads, so every advance in intimacy is also a strategic concession, and she uses the shared office as a surveillance system that performs their every interaction for an audience of colleagues. The author is Australian and is routinely described otherwise.

entries.name: It Ends with Us
entries.author: Colleen Hoover
entries.awards: None — no juried award of any kind
entries.description: The defining title of the BookTok era and the centre of a live genre-boundary dispute the pack records rather than settles. The dispute is structural:…
entries.text: The defining title of the BookTok era and the centre of a live genre-boundary dispute the pack records rather than settles. The dispute is structural: one position holds that the book is not a romance by the genre's own definition, because its ending resolves the protagonist's life rather than the central relationship; the other holds that the ending is emotionally satisfying and optimistic on the genre's own terms and therefore qualifies. Both are arguable and the pack takes neither. What is not disputed is the award record — every "award-winning" description of this author traces to reader-vote wins rather than to any juried prize.

entries.name: The Kiss Quotient
entries.author: Helen Hoang
entries.awards: None
entries.description: The standard the neurodivergence trope should be held to. Hoang writes an autistic heroine whose difficulty is real, specific and not cured by the…
entries.text: The standard the neurodivergence trope should be held to. Hoang writes an autistic heroine whose difficulty is real, specific and not cured by the relationship, and the novel emerged from the author's own diagnosis in adulthood during the period she was writing it. Its first intimate scene establishes disability, logistics and negotiation together, which sets the terms every later scene works within — and its hero leads through patience and explicit checking-in, generating tension through restraint rather than through resistance.

entries.name: The Wedding Date
entries.author: Jasmine Guillory
entries.awards: None — no juried award has been located for this author
entries.description: The debut that opened the trade contemporary wave, and a low-conflict, high-competence courtship between adults with functioning careers, where the…
entries.text: The debut that opened the trade contemporary wave, and a low-conflict, high-competence courtship between adults with functioning careers, where the obstacle is scheduling and self-protection rather than damage. Its meet traps two strangers in a stopped lift and uses the enforced idleness to establish voice and compatibility before either has a chance to perform. The author left legal practice in January 2019, **after** this book was published rather than in order to write it — a sequence reported backwards almost everywhere.

entries.name: Get a Life, Chloe Brown
entries.author: Talia Hibbert
entries.awards: None
entries.description: Published November 2019, into the gap left by the RITA's retirement — and a correction worth recording, because the inaugural Vivian deliberately…
entries.text: Published November 2019, into the gap left by the RITA's retirement — and a correction worth recording, because the inaugural Vivian deliberately covered both 2019 and 2020 titles to fill the cancelled cycle, so the book **was** eligible and simply did not place. Hibbert inverts the expected trope assignment by giving the prickly role to the disabled heroine and the sunshine role to the man, which defuses the genre's habit of making one party the other's emotional caretaker, and she structures the middle around a list so each scene has a declared external task and a concealed relational one.

entries.name: The Flatshare
entries.author: Beth O'Leary
entries.awards: **American Library Association Reading List, Romance category winner, 2020**
entries.description: A juried librarian award that is absent from the author's principal reference entry entirely — the kind of credential that disappears while reader…
entries.text: A juried librarian award that is absent from the author's principal reference entry entirely — the kind of credential that disappears while reader votes get amplified, which is the archive problem operating in real time. The premise is the craft point: two people share a flat in shifts and are almost never in it together, so intimacy accumulates through notes and objects rather than through presence, and the courtship happens in the spaces the other person leaves behind. It is the clearest instance in the collection of a structural premise doing the work a conflict would otherwise have to.

entries.name: Beach Read
entries.author: Emily Henry
entries.awards: None — its Goodreads Choice placing was **second**, and Goodreads Choice is a reader vote rather than a prize
entries.description: Published 19 May 2020, correcting a date that circulates two weeks early. The breakout that established the literary-register trade contemporary, and a…
entries.text: Published 19 May 2020, correcting a date that circulates two weeks early. The breakout that established the literary-register trade contemporary, and a model for building the obstacle out of two incompatible theories of what writing is for — an aesthetic disagreement as well as a professional one, which cannot be settled by either party succeeding. Henry's narrators convey attraction through the precision of what they observe about the other person, which is the pack's rule about attention stated as a whole career.

entries.name: The Love Hypothesis
entries.author: Ali Hazelwood
entries.awards: None — RITA eligibility is date-impossible
entries.description: The book that established the STEM workplace romance as a category, written by a working neuroscientist. Its fanfiction history requires exact wording:…
entries.text: The book that established the STEM workplace romance as a category, written by a working neuroscientist. Its fanfiction history requires exact wording: a version of the story was posted to a fan archive between October 2018 and July 2019 under a different title, in the Star Wars fandom, and was removed by the author — so **the text as published was never itself posted**, and looser formulations in either direction are inaccurate. The novel sets the relationship inside an academic power structure and lets the structure supply the obstacle, which is more durable than any personal secret.

entries.name: Twisted Love
entries.author: Ana Huang
entries.awards: None
entries.description: **Self-published on 21 April 2021** under the author's own imprint, with a distribution deal following in September 2022 — and retailer metadata now…
entries.text: **Self-published on 21 April 2021** under the author's own imprint, with a distribution deal following in September 2022 — and retailer metadata now shows the distributor on the original ISBN, which makes the book look traditionally published from the start. It opened the series that defined the 2020s dark-romance market. Its craft weakness is instructive and is carded in the Tropes collection: the stated barrier substantially dissolves after consummation, leaving the later conflict to be supplied by an external threat arriving from outside the couple.

entries.name: Things We Never Got Over
entries.author: Lucy Score
entries.awards: None
entries.description: **Self-published on 12 January 2022** under the author's own imprint, with distribution taken over that October — the same metadata-overwrite pattern…
entries.text: **Self-published on 12 January 2022** under the author's own imprint, with distribution taken over that October — the same metadata-overwrite pattern as the two preceding cards, on the same ISBN. Its significance is the delayed-discovery pattern: the book broke out through social recommendation well after release, which is the defining commercial shape of the current market and the reason a backlist title is now a viable asset rather than a dead one. The novel uses an inherited small-town network as the support system the heroine has never had, so staying is the actual romantic decision.

entries.name: Restoree
entries.author: Anne McCaffrey
entries.awards: None — a verified negative
entries.description: A romance structure inside a science-fiction premise, written partly as a corrective to how women were then being depicted in the field, and the…
entries.text: A romance structure inside a science-fiction premise, written partly as a corrective to how women were then being depicted in the field, and the earliest card in this category. McCaffrey's later firsts are frequently misstated — she was the first woman to win a Hugo in a **fiction** category rather than the first woman to win a Hugo, and her Hugo and Nebula were for different novellas that are routinely transposed. This book won nothing and is nonetheless the point at which the two genres' compatibility was demonstrated in commercial publishing.

entries.name: Shards of Honor
entries.author: Lois McMaster Bujold
entries.awards: None — a **finalist** for the Compton Crook Award, which it lost
entries.description: The courtship built out of two officers' incompatible codes of honour, and the model for attraction generated by professional conduct under command…
entries.text: The courtship built out of two officers' incompatible codes of honour, and the model for attraction generated by professional conduct under command pressure. Bujold's major awards are for later books in the same sequence, and this one's frequently cited Compton Crook credential was a losing finalist placing; a Locus first-novel placing attached to it is a **poll ranking** rather than a nomination. The novel matters here because it demonstrates that a courtship can be conducted entirely as an assessment of professional character, with the romance and the military plot resolving as one movement.

entries.name: Dark Prince
entries.author: Christine Feehan
entries.awards: None — a verified negative; the author is widely described as RITA Award-winning and is a finalist only
entries.description: First published by Love Spell, an imprint of Dorchester — **not** Avon, which appears on the author's own site because it published a revised edition…
entries.text: First published by Love Spell, an imprint of Dorchester — **not** Avon, which appears on the author's own site because it published a revised edition in 2011. The book opened the modern paranormal romance boom and established the lifemate bond as the subgenre's central mechanism. Its founding difficulty is carded plainly: the claiming operates over the heroine's stated refusal and the novel does not register the override as a problem, which is the convention later writers spent two decades addressing. Her other honours come from a reader listserv and a trade magazine.

entries.name: Kushiel's Dart
entries.author: Jacqueline Carey
entries.awards: Locus Award, **Best First Novel**, 2002; Gaylactic Spectrum Award — **nomination** only
entries.description: The strongest demonstration in fantasy that an erotic and religious logic can be a worldbuilding principle rather than a decoration. Carey builds a…
entries.text: The strongest demonstration in fantasy that an erotic and religious logic can be a worldbuilding principle rather than a decoration. Carey builds a formal precept governing desire and consent, so submission is a vocation with an explicit ethical framework, every negotiation is conducted in a shared language, and the arrangement is defined and revocable in a way almost no romance manages. The award correction matters: the Locus win was in the first-novel category, and it is routinely upgraded to Best Fantasy Novel, in which it placed eighteenth.

entries.name: Dead Until Dark
entries.author: Charlaine Harris
entries.awards: Anthony Award, 2002 — a **crime-genre** award, not a romance one
entries.description: The series opener that carried paranormal romance into mainstream television. Harris's telepathic narrator is the structural point: the ability partly…
entries.text: The series opener that carried paranormal romance into mainstream television. Harris's telepathic narrator is the structural point: the ability partly equalises a supernatural power gap that would otherwise be absolute, which is a design answer to the subgenre's consent problem rather than an evasion of it. The author has **never won an Agatha**, only nominations, and the phantom win comes from an Agatha nomination and the Anthony landing in the same year for the same book — a coincidence that has propagated for two decades.

entries.name: Night Pleasures
entries.author: Sherrilyn Kenyon
entries.awards: None from RWA nationally — her PRISM and Golden Quill honours are **RWA chapter** awards
entries.description: The Dark-Hunter novel that established the series at scale, and the entry point to one of paranormal romance's largest interlocking mythologies. The…
entries.text: The Dark-Hunter novel that established the series at scale, and the entry point to one of paranormal romance's largest interlocking mythologies. The structural interest is that each volume's couple is constrained by obligations inherited from the series' cosmology rather than from their own circumstances, which is a different engine from the brotherhood model and scales differently. The award note is general: chapter awards are frequently reported as national ones across this whole subgenre, and the distinction is not cosmetic.

entries.name: Dark Lover
entries.author: J.R. Ward
entries.awards: None — it **lost** the 2006 RITA in Paranormal
entries.description: A **mass-market paperback original** from Signet Eclipse, September 2005; two reference sources call it a hardcover and it was not. The series opener…
entries.text: A **mass-market paperback original** from Signet Eclipse, September 2005; two reference sources call it a hardcover and it was not. The series opener that set the warrior-brotherhood template and placed dominance inside a military hierarchy with obligations that outrank the hero, which supplies the limit the alpha archetype usually lacks. Ward's three RITAs are for other books, one of them a contemporary category romance published under her legal name — so attaching a RITA to this title is wrong twice over.

entries.name: Twilight
entries.author: Stephenie Meyer
entries.awards: None for this title; the author's 2009 British Book Award was a **children's** category award for a later book in the series
entries.description: The book that made paranormal romance a mainstream phenomenon and reshaped publishing schedules for a decade. Its protective dynamic is written at…
entries.text: The book that made paranormal romance a mainstream phenomenon and reshaped publishing schedules for a decade. Its protective dynamic is written at maximum intensity, with the surveillance and decision-making it entails presented as devotion — which is why it is simultaneously the subgenre's commercial peak and its most-used teaching example. Two distinct criticisms attach to the series and should not be merged: the depiction of the central relationship's control dynamics, and the use of Quileute identity together with a fabricated origin story, on which a museum has published a documented account noting the Nation has received none of the franchise's revenue.

entries.name: Slave to Sensation
entries.author: Nalini Singh
entries.awards: None — a verified negative; the author has one RITA **nomination**, in 2014, for a different book
entries.description: The subgenre's best correction to the convention *Dark Prince* established. Singh treats the mating bond as a condition the characters must interrogate…
entries.text: The subgenre's best correction to the convention *Dark Prince* established. Singh treats the mating bond as a condition the characters must interrogate and can resist, so the ending is a decision rather than a mechanism completing itself — and she builds the psychic-suppression system with worked-out social, political and biological consequences rather than as atmosphere. Each contact costs more under an established rule set, which is escalation performed by the worldbuilding instead of by the plot.

entries.name: Moon Called
entries.author: Patricia Briggs
entries.awards: None — a verified negative; the author's entire genre-award record is nominations
entries.description: The model for a heroine who is materially weaker than everyone around her and wins anyway. Briggs makes pack hierarchy a genuinely coercive force her…
entries.text: The model for a heroine who is materially weaker than everyone around her and wins anyway. Briggs makes pack hierarchy a genuinely coercive force her protagonist actively resists, so the rule system functions as an antagonist rather than as a romantic convenience — the opposite settlement from the mating-bond books, and a more demanding one to write. The award note is worth keeping because "has won numerous awards" appears on aggregator sites for this author and is unsupported.

entries.name: Magic Bites
entries.author: Ilona Andrews
entries.awards: None — a verified negative
entries.description: The series opener from a husband-and-wife byline, and the pack's reference case for an **honestly signalled** slow burn: the first volume settles…
entries.text: The series opener from a husband-and-wife byline, and the pack's reference case for an **honestly signalled** slow burn: the first volume settles almost nothing romantically, and because the series declares its shape openly, readers read the deferral as design rather than as withholding. Attraction is established during combat and negotiation, registering as an involuntary reading of the other's competence. The series later resolves its romance well before it ends and continues on external stakes, which is the continuing-couple model executed in urban fantasy.

entries.name: Halfway to the Grave
entries.author: Jeaniene Frost
entries.awards: None — the author's sole credential is a trade **magazine** reviewers' award
entries.description: The comic urban-fantasy romance at the subgenre's commercial peak, and a clean instance of first-person restriction doing structural work: the reader…
entries.text: The comic urban-fantasy romance at the subgenre's commercial peak, and a clean instance of first-person restriction doing structural work: the reader learns the other party's state only through what the narrator can observe, which sustains uncertainty that dual viewpoint would have spent. The card also carries a research caution — this author's series are misnamed in her principal encyclopaedia entry, which additionally lists series that do not exist, so her bibliography should not be sourced from it.

entries.name: Ice Planet Barbarians
entries.author: Ruby Dixon
entries.awards: None — a verified negative
entries.description: **Self-published in 2015 and issued by a traditional publisher on 30 November 2021**, and both dates belong on the card because the six-year gap is the…
entries.text: **Self-published in 2015 and issued by a traditional publisher on 30 November 2021**, and both dates belong on the card because the six-year gap is the entire story of how the indie channel now feeds the trade. The novel compresses survival, language barrier, physical dependence and biological difference into a single premise, which is the most efficient proximity engine in the current market. The author has declared the byline a deliberate pseudonym and no legal name is public; the pack follows that choice.

entries.name: A Court of Thorns and Roses
entries.author: Sarah J. Maas
entries.awards: None — and the author has **no juried award win of any kind**
entries.description: Published as young adult in 2015 and later positioned toward an adult readership, so both flat labels are wrong. A specific misattribution to correct:…
entries.text: Published as young adult in 2015 and later positioned toward an adult readership, so both flat labels are wrong. A specific misattribution to correct: the 2015 Goodreads Choice young-adult fantasy award went to a **different Maas title** published the same year, and is routinely transferred to this one — which matters because the transferred credit is itself only a reader vote. The book established the modern romantasy series template and, with it, the convention of carrying one couple across several volumes, which is where the genre's deferred-guarantee problem enters at scale.

entries.name: Uprooted
entries.author: Naomi Novik
entries.awards: **Nebula Award, Best Novel** (2015 award, presented 2016); **Locus Award, Best Fantasy Novel, 2016**; **Mythopoeic Award, Adult Literature, 2016**; **British Fantasy Award, Robert Holdstock Award for Best Fantasy Novel, 2016**. Finalist and loser: Hugo Best Novel 2016 and World Fantasy Best Novel 2016
entries.description: The strongest juried record in this batch by a wide margin, and worth stating in full because the wins and the losses are routinely blended into a…
entries.text: The strongest juried record in this batch by a wide margin, and worth stating in full because the wins and the losses are routinely blended into a single vague claim. Its relevance to this pack is structural rather than decorative: it takes the **single-volume settlement**, paying the genre's guarantee in full on delivery, which is the option most romantasy declines without appearing to consider it. The two magic-workers disagree about method in ways that are technically substantive, so the argument survives every increase in affection.

entries.name: Fourth Wing
entries.author: Rebecca Yarros
entries.awards: **British Book Awards, Pageturner Book of the Year, 2024**; Goodreads Choice, Best Romantasy, 2023 — a reader vote
entries.description: The defining commercial phenomenon of the 2020s romantasy boom, and the pack's principal case study in the deferred guarantee. The British Book Award…
entries.text: The defining commercial phenomenon of the 2020s romantasy boom, and the pack's principal case study in the deferred guarantee. The British Book Award is a genuine win and is frequently downgraded to a shortlisting or reported without its category; the Goodreads placing was in the romantasy category rather than fantasy, which is a different award that year; and the 2024 Dragon Award went to the **sequel**, not to this book. The volume ends on a reversal that suspends the relationship's status, which readers arriving through the romance shelf rather than the fantasy one reported as a broken contract rather than as momentum.

entries.name: Maurice
entries.author: E. M. Forster
entries.awards: None
entries.description: Written in 1913–14 and published posthumously in 1971 by Edward Arnold in the United Kingdom and W. W. Norton in the United States. Forster wrote a…
entries.text: Written in 1913–14 and published posthumously in 1971 by Edward Arnold in the United Kingdom and W. W. Norton in the United States. Forster wrote a deliberately happy ending for two men under a legal regime that criminalised them, and stated in a terminal note dated September 1960 that the happy ending was the entire point and was precisely what made publication impossible in his lifetime. That note circulates in variant transcriptions online and is not quoted here for that reason. It is the clearest demonstration in English that an optimistic ending is an argument rather than an evasion — made half a century before the genre organised itself enough to have the argument, and by a writer who paid for it with sixty years of silence.

entries.name: Tipping the Velvet
entries.author: Sarah Waters
entries.awards: Betty Trask Award, 1999; **shortlisted** for the Ferro-Grumley Award — the 2000 win went to a different Waters novel
entries.description: Waters's debut, and the book that brought the historical sapphic novel to a wide literary readership. Its craft contribution to this pack is the…
entries.text: Waters's debut, and the book that brought the historical sapphic novel to a wide literary readership. Its craft contribution to this pack is the treatment of male dress as a professional instrument, an erotic one and a survival strategy in turn, with the novel refusing to resolve it back into a single explanation. Waters moves her narrator through several positions of dependency and makes each one materially specific about food, wages and rooms — which is the master-and-servant dynamic written with the economics intact rather than as atmosphere.

entries.name: Fingersmith
entries.author: Sarah Waters
entries.awards: **Crime Writers' Association Historical Dagger, 2002**; **shortlisted** for the Booker Prize, 2002
entries.description: Waters has been Booker-shortlisted three times and has never won, a distinction routinely collapsed — and note that the prize foundation's own site…
entries.text: Waters has been Booker-shortlisted three times and has never won, a distinction routinely collapsed — and note that the prize foundation's own site misattributes one of her shortlistings to the wrong novel. The book is the pack's model for honest withholding: two narrators hold incomplete and incompatible information, so the secret is structural rather than concealed and neither party has to behave stupidly to sustain it. It is also a leverage system in which every party believes they are the one applying it, with the actual hierarchy disclosed late.

entries.name: The Magpie Lord
entries.author: KJ Charles
entries.awards: None established — a frequently cited award nomination is single-sourced and is not asserted here
entries.description: The publication direction is backwards in most accounts: this was **traditionally published first**, as an ebook by Samhain in September 2013, and…
entries.text: The publication direction is backwards in most accounts: this was **traditionally published first**, as an ebook by Samhain in September 2013, and **self-published later**, in 2017, after that publisher closed. It matters because the standard indie-to-trade narrative runs the other way, and the reverse case is what happened to a large number of queer romances when the small digital presses that had sustained the category folded. The novel is the pack's model for signalling a continuing-couple structure honestly, so readers know from the first volume what each subsequent one will and will not settle.

entries.name: Him
entries.author: Sarina Bowen and Elle Kennedy
entries.awards: **RITA, Contemporary Romance: Mid-Length, 2016**
entries.description: **Self-published in July 2015 and never traditionally issued**, and it won a RITA the following year — which is the historically significant fact,…
entries.text: **Self-published in July 2015 and never traditionally issued**, and it won a RITA the following year — which is the historically significant fact, because it demonstrates the award was genuinely open to the independent channel at a point when that was still contested. A wording caution: the award was **one prize shared by two co-authors**, not a tie between two books, and "co-won" is routinely misread as the latter. The novel makes the morning after the site of the actual risk, because the acknowledgement is what neither man can take back.

entries.name: Unmasked by the Marquess
entries.author: Cat Sebastian
entries.awards: None — no award, win or nomination, could be established despite frequent "award-winning" descriptions
entries.description: Published as an ebook by Avon Impulse in April 2018, with the mass-market edition following in May — the later date routinely overwrites the first in…
entries.text: Published as an ebook by Avon Impulse in April 2018, with the mass-market edition following in May — the later date routinely overwrites the first in catalogues. The novel is the pack's reference instance for the reckoning correctly assigned: it stages disclosure and consent as the same act in a setting where both are dangerous, and keeps the repair owed by the person who reacted badly rather than by the person who disclosed. That assignment is the thing the genre most often gets backwards, and the card exists partly to mark it.

entries.name: Red, White & Royal Blue
entries.author: Casey McQuiston
entries.awards: **Alex Award (Young Adult Library Services Association), 2020**; Goodreads Choice Best Romance and Best Debut Novel, 2019 — reader votes
entries.description: A Lambda Literary Award is widely attributed to this book and it is **not on the 2020 slate at all**, as winner or finalist; its one juried honour is…
entries.text: A Lambda Literary Award is widely attributed to this book and it is **not on the 2020 slate at all**, as winner or finalist; its one juried honour is the Alex, given by a library association for adult books with teen appeal. The novel grounds its enmity in a public incident with institutional consequences, which prevents the common failure of an antagonism existing only in the two participants' moods, and it forces the disclosure by exposure rather than by choice — shifting the question from whether to come out to who owns the timing.

entries.name: Heated Rivalry
entries.author: Rachel Reid
entries.awards: None
entries.description: The novel has no award. Its television adaptation was **created, written and directed by another writer** and has since accumulated substantial…
entries.text: The novel has no award. Its television adaptation was **created, written and directed by another writer** and has since accumulated substantial industry recognition, none of which belongs to the novelist — a distinction reference sources collapse, and the reason this card states it. The book itself ties the closet to professional survival in a specific industry, so the concealment has a career cost that can be calculated rather than only feared, and public visibility becomes the mechanism of the concealment rather than a consequence of it.

entries.name: Boyfriend Material
entries.author: Alexis Hall
entries.awards: None — a 2020 Goodreads Choice placing was fifth, and Goodreads Choice is a reader vote rather than a prize
entries.description: The breakout that demonstrated first-person single point of view working for comic voice rather than for immediacy. Hall makes the performance a…
entries.text: The breakout that demonstrated first-person single point of view working for comic voice rather than for immediacy. Hall makes the performance a reputational necessity for both men in different registers, so the fake relationship is doing real work in two lives at once — and locates the wound in public humiliation rather than private trauma, which gives it an ongoing external cause the relationship cannot simply outlast. It is the pack's cleanest example of an obstacle that is neither a secret nor a misunderstanding.

entries.name: Written in the Stars
entries.author: Alexandria Bellefleur
entries.awards: **Lambda Literary Award, Lesbian Romance, 2021**; a bookstore award, 2020 — a retailer's honour rather than a juried prize
entries.description: The Lambda win is real and was confirmed independently, because **the relevant ceremony page omits this book and names a different winner** — which is…
entries.text: The Lambda win is real and was confirmed independently, because **the relevant ceremony page omits this book and names a different winner** — which is how a genuine win becomes unverifiable to anyone checking the obvious source. The novel builds its fake arrangement around a family event, so the ceremony exposes the pretence rather than confirming the real relationship, and it is one of the titles that marked sapphic romance's move into mainstream trade distribution.

entries.name: Careless Whispers
entries.author: Rochelle Alers
entries.awards: None
entries.description: Rochelle Alers's debut, published by Doubleday's Starlight line in late 1988 — **not** the title most reference entries give, which garble a series…
entries.text: Rochelle Alers's debut, published by Doubleday's Starlight line in late 1988 — **not** the title most reference entries give, which garble a series name for a book, and **not** 1996, which is the date one widely used genre wiki assigns it. A 1998 reissue's identifier has displaced the first edition in retail metadata. The card is here to fix a bibliographic record and to mark a starting point: Alers published across independent, category and trade houses as the market's infrastructure repeatedly changed under her, and her career is the clearest single map of that instability.

entries.name: Night Song
entries.author: Beverly Jenkins
entries.awards: None — Jenkins's RWA lifetime honour is 2017 and belongs to her rather than to a book
entries.description: The founding text of the researched Black historical romance. Jenkins built it from documented nineteenth-century Black American life — settlement,…
entries.text: The founding text of the researched Black historical romance. Jenkins built it from documented nineteenth-century Black American life — settlement, homesteading, the cavalry, education — using material the mainstream historical had treated as unmarketable, and she carries the research in the texture rather than parading it. Its structural achievement is that the period's actual institutions supply the obstacles, so they are historically specific rather than generically social, which is the standard the whole subgenre has been held to since.

entries.name: Tonight and Forever
entries.author: Brenda Jackson
entries.awards: None
entries.description: Brenda Jackson's debut, and the start of a career that became the most commercially prolific in this category. The publication month is given three…
entries.text: Brenda Jackson's debut, and the start of a career that became the most commercially prolific in this category. The publication month is given three different ways across sources, including on the author's own list. Her later work built the extended family saga as a category-line structure — dozens of interconnected volumes with a shared cast, which is the community-engine model applied to a single family and sustained further than almost anyone else has managed. Claims that she was the first Black author on particular bestseller lists have no dated primary evidence and are not repeated in this pack.

entries.name: Sealed with a Kiss
entries.author: Gwynne Forster
entries.awards: None
entries.description: **The most thinly documented title in the entire pack.** No author site, no encyclopaedia entry, and no contemporaneous review or trade notice could be…
entries.text: **The most thinly documented title in the entire pack.** No author site, no encyclopaedia entry, and no contemporaneous review or trade notice could be located anywhere; the line attribution rests on later reissue branding rather than on the 1995 artefact itself. The gap is closable but not remotely: Bowling Green State University's Browne Popular Culture Library holds the Gwynne Forster papers, **including the manuscript and synopsis of this exact novel**, and the collection is not machine-readable. This card is the pack's clearest single statement of the archive problem — a debut by a United Nations demographer who published fifty romances, thirty years old, whose publishing record survives principally in a box.

entries.name: Hideaway
entries.author: Rochelle Alers
entries.awards: None
entries.description: Published by Pinnacle, an imprint of Kensington — **not** by the company that appears in one widely mirrored library record, which acquired the…
entries.text: Published by Pinnacle, an imprint of Kensington — **not** by the company that appears in one widely mirrored library record, which acquired the relevant line three years later and could not have published it. The first-edition identifier could not be established, because three of the standard bibliographic databases were unreachable. The book opened the family saga that became Alers's longest-running work, and its title has since been reused for both a series name and a later omnibus, which is the origin of most of the confusion in its catalogue record.

entries.name: Indigo
entries.author: Beverly Jenkins
entries.awards: None found — no contemporaneous award record exists for it
entries.description: Jenkins's Underground Railroad romance, and the pack's model for an obstacle with moral authority: the heroine's commitment to the Railroad is a duty…
entries.text: Jenkins's Underground Railroad romance, and the pack's model for an obstacle with moral authority: the heroine's commitment to the Railroad is a duty she is right to place above the relationship, so the barrier cannot be dismissed as fear or stubbornness. That is the hardest version of the "give the obstacle a defender" rule, because the reader must want the couple together and also want her to keep choosing the work. The novel is routinely named by readers as her best and has no award of any kind, which is this category's recurring shape.

entries.name: A Bollywood Affair
entries.author: Sonali Dev
entries.awards: **American Library Association Reading List, Romance category winner, 2015**
entries.description: A juried librarian award, confirmed on two of the association's own pages, and **understated in the author's principal reference entry as merely…
entries.text: A juried librarian award, confirmed on two of the association's own pages, and **understated in the author's principal reference entry as merely appearing on the list** — the same demotion that happened to another title in this pack, which suggests the error is in how that award is described rather than in any one entry. The novel builds its conflict from the specific obligations of Indian and Indian-American family structures, with family claims that are legitimate and incompatible with each other, so there is no single interference for the plot to overcome.

entries.name: An Extraordinary Union
entries.author: Alyssa Cole
entries.awards: **American Library Association Reading List, Romance category winner, 2018**
entries.description: The second consecutive ALA Reading List romance winner in this category, one year after the previous card's — a pattern worth noticing, since that…
entries.text: The second consecutive ALA Reading List romance winner in this category, one year after the previous card's — a pattern worth noticing, since that award has been recognising this material while the genre's own awards were not. Cole has **no RITA and no Vivian**, checked against the complete 2021 Vivian roster, and the RITA absence for this book is documented as a notable omission. The novel runs Union espionage as romance from documented history, resolving the mission to its own conclusion and requiring a separate reckoning between the two agents.

entries.name: Ayesha at Last
entries.author: Uzma Jalaluddin
entries.awards: None
entries.description: Published in Canada in 2018 and in the United States in 2019, and a bare single year in either direction is contradicted by half the available sources…
entries.text: Published in Canada in 2018 and in the United States in 2019, and a bare single year in either direction is contradicted by half the available sources — so both are given. The novel transposes an Austen plot into a Muslim community in Toronto with its own internal politics, and its craft achievement is that the arranged-marriage expectation is treated as a live and internally contested practice within a specific community rather than as an obstacle imported from outside it. The disagreement is between believers, which is a harder and more interesting structure than belief against love.

entries.name: Long Shot
entries.author: Kennedy Ryan
entries.awards: **RITA, Contemporary Romance: Long, 2019**
entries.description: **Self-published**, and the winner of a RITA in the award's final cycle — a trade edition did not appear until 2023, so any trade publisher on the 2018…
entries.text: **Self-published**, and the winner of a RITA in the award's final cycle — a trade edition did not appear until 2023, so any trade publisher on the 2018 edition is wrong. The "first Black woman to win a RITA" framing needs two corrections that the most-consulted reference entry does not make: **M. Malone won Romance Novella the same night**, contemporary reporting named the two of them jointly as the first African American writers to win, and Ryan herself has objected to the sole-first version. The novel writes a controlling relationship and an escape from it with the mechanics fully explicit, and gives the recovery its own arc rather than folding it into the romance's resolution.

entries.name: The Boyfriend Project
entries.author: Farrah Rochon
entries.awards: None — Rochon was a RITA **finalist** twice and never won
entries.description: The trade breakout of a writer who had worked across category and independent publishing for a decade, and a demonstration of the professional-setting…
entries.text: The trade breakout of a writer who had worked across category and independent publishing for a decade, and a demonstration of the professional-setting romance with the working conditions taken seriously. Its author's two finalist placings sit directly against RWA's own 2018 acknowledgement that no Black author had ever won a category RITA — she is one of the writers that admission was about, and the pack cards the finalist record precisely because a blank award field would otherwise read as absence of achievement rather than as evidence of a filter.

entries.name: Before I Let Go
entries.author: Kennedy Ryan
entries.awards: None — published after the RITA ended and outside the single Vivian cohort
entries.description: The pack's reference instance for the marriage-in-trouble structure. Ryan reunites a divorced couple and requires them to address the specific failure…
entries.text: The pack's reference instance for the marriage-in-trouble structure. Ryan reunites a divorced couple and requires them to address the specific failure that ended the marriage rather than to rediscover attraction, making the original failure diagnosable and partly nobody's fault — which is why the repair takes an entire novel and why the ending reads as earned rather than nostalgic. It is also the clearest case in the collection of the genre's guarantee being paid over grief, therapy and a business partnership without any of the three being softened to make room for it.

entries.name: It Happened One Night
entries.author: Frank Capra
entries.awards: Academy Awards for Best Picture, Director, Actor, Actress and Adapted Screenplay — the 7th ceremony, 1935; the **first film to win all five major categories**
entries.description: Screenplay by Robert Riskin, adapted from a magazine story by Samuel Hopkins Adams. The blanket strung between two beds is the single most imitated…
entries.text: Screenplay by Robert Riskin, adapted from a magazine story by Samuel Hopkins Adams. The blanket strung between two beds is the single most imitated staging decision in screen romance, and it works because it makes the negotiation visible as an object rather than as dialogue. Capra sets a cynic against an enthusiast and makes each one's manner a working method rather than a mood, so the conflict is about how to get through the world — which is the grumpy-and-sunshine pairing before it had a name, and a more durable version than most that followed.

entries.name: The Shop Around the Corner
entries.author: Ernst Lubitsch
entries.awards: **None — no Academy Award nominations at all**
entries.description: Screenplay by Samson Raphaelson from a Hungarian play by Miklós László. The zero-nomination record is worth stating for a film now regarded as one of…
entries.text: Screenplay by Samson Raphaelson from a Hungarian play by Miklós László. The zero-nomination record is worth stating for a film now regarded as one of the great screen romances and remade twice. Its structure is the correspondence romance in which **only one party knows**, which converts a symmetrical device into a sustained ethical problem about what he is entitled to do with the knowledge — a problem the two later remakes both soften. The shop supplies an economic dependency that makes the antagonism consequential, since one of them can cost the other a livelihood.

entries.name: The Lady Eve
entries.author: Preston Sturges
entries.awards: One Academy Award nomination, for the **source story** — Sturges himself received no nomination
entries.description: Written and directed by Sturges, from a story by Monckton Hoffe, who holds the film's only nomination. The con-romance at its most rigorous: the con…
entries.text: Written and directed by Sturges, from a story by Monckton Hoffe, who holds the film's only nomination. The con-romance at its most rigorous: the con woman falls for the mark, is caught, and runs a second and crueller con as revenge, which is the only version of the plot that gives the deceived party a reckoning worth watching. The reveal is staged as a performance the deceiver controls, making the scene an act of aggression rather than a confession — and the film is the pack's demonstration that timing rather than content is what makes disclosure devastating.

entries.name: Casablanca
entries.author: Michael Curtiz
entries.awards: Academy Awards for Best Picture, Director and Adapted Screenplay — three wins, at the 16th ceremony, 1944
entries.description: Screenplay by Julius and Philip Epstein and Howard Koch, from an unproduced play. Released in 1942, eligible in 1943, awarded in 1944 — the three-year…
entries.text: Screenplay by Julius and Philip Epstein and Howard Koch, from an unproduced play. Released in 1942, eligible in 1943, awarded in 1944 — the three-year spread is why its dates are reported inconsistently. It is commonly over-credited: it won three Oscars, Ingrid Bergman was not nominated for it, and its famous song was **never nominated** because it dated from 1931 and was ineligible. The film is carded here as a boundary case: it is routinely called the great screen romance and it resolves by separating the couple permanently, which is exactly the outcome the genre's guarantee exists to exclude.

entries.name: Brief Encounter
entries.author: David Lean
entries.awards: Three Academy Award nominations, no wins; Cannes Grand Prix, 1946 — **shared among eleven films** and not the Palme d'Or, which did not yet exist under that name
entries.description: From Noël Coward's one-act play, with a screenplay credit Coward holds — and yet **Coward is not among the Academy's screenplay nominees**, which named…
entries.text: From Noël Coward's one-act play, with a screenplay credit Coward holds — and yet **Coward is not among the Academy's screenplay nominees**, which named the other three credited writers only. The film keeps its couple almost entirely unphysical and puts the whole charge into proximity in public places, so restraint reads as pressure rather than coolness. Its most consequential scene happens off-screen and is reported afterwards in shame, which makes the omission the point rather than a compromise — the closed door as technique, three decades before the genre named it.

entries.name: Notorious
entries.author: Alfred Hitchcock
entries.awards: Two Academy Award nominations, no wins
entries.description: An **original screenplay** by Ben Hecht, which is unusual among the films carded here. Its romance is generated by an institutional betrayal: the man's…
entries.text: An **original screenplay** by Ben Hecht, which is unusual among the films carded here. Its romance is generated by an institutional betrayal: the man's employer requires the woman's sexual access to a third party, which makes the state a participant in the courtship and his failure to intervene the film's real injury. That is coercive leverage exercised by an organisation rather than by a lover, and it is the most uncomfortable version of the device in this collection — the undercover romance where the duty is not merely competing with the relationship but actively degrading it.

entries.name: Roman Holiday
entries.author: William Wyler
entries.awards: Academy Award for Best Actress, 1954; Writing (Motion Picture Story) — **awarded under a fronted credit and restored to Dalton Trumbo decades later**
entries.description: The blacklist case in this collection, and the record is genuinely tangled. Trumbo, blacklisted and unable to take a credit, was fronted by Ian…
entries.text: The blacklist case in this collection, and the record is genuinely tangled. Trumbo, blacklisted and unable to take a credit, was fronted by Ian McLellan Hunter, who accepted the statuette in 1954. The Academy's database now names Trumbo as the winner of the story award, while still listing the screenplay **nomination** under the original credited names — so the restoration is partial in the record rather than clean. A second statuette had to be struck in 1993 for Trumbo's widow. The film's romance is a mutual concealment in which both parties are working, so the disclosure is a professional betrayal on one side and a constitutional impossibility on the other.

entries.name: An Affair to Remember
entries.author: Leo McCarey
entries.awards: Four Academy Award nominations, no wins
entries.description: Screenplay by Delmer Daves and McCarey, from a story by McCarey and Mildred Cram — and a widely repeated credit adding a further writer belongs to the…
entries.text: Screenplay by Delmer Daves and McCarey, from a story by McCarey and Mildred Cram — and a widely repeated credit adding a further writer belongs to the 1939 film McCarey was remaking, whose blacklisted co-writer was **never restored**, unlike the case in the preceding card. The two blacklist outcomes sitting four years apart in this collection are worth reading together. The film's device is a failure to appear caused by an accident neither party can explain, which makes the reunion a matter of interpretation rather than of forgiveness.

entries.name: Some Like It Hot
entries.author: Billy Wilder
entries.awards: **One** Academy Award — Costume Design, black-and-white
entries.description: Screenplay by Wilder and I. A. L. Diamond. The single-Oscar record is worth stating because the film is routinely described as a multiple winner, and…
entries.text: Screenplay by Wilder and I. A. L. Diamond. The single-Oscar record is worth stating because the film is routinely described as a multiple winner, and because Marilyn Monroe was **never Oscar-nominated in her life** — her award for this film was a Golden Globe. Its craft contribution to the pack is the resolution: Wilder settles the central deception with one line that refuses to treat it as an obstacle at all, which is the funniest and most decisive demonstration that letting characters talk does not have to cost a plot anything.

entries.name: The Apartment
entries.author: Billy Wilder
entries.awards: Five Academy Awards including Best Picture, Director and **Original Screenplay**, at the 33rd ceremony, 1961
entries.description: Written by Wilder and Diamond. A tenth nomination widely reported as Best Original Score was in fact **Sound**; the film received no music nomination.…
entries.text: Written by Wilder and Diamond. A tenth nomination widely reported as Best Original Score was in fact **Sound**; the film received no music nomination. Its proximity engine is professional rather than romantic: the shared space is an obligation with a career attached, so leaving costs the protagonist his livelihood — and the power gradient runs through employment rather than through wealth, which the film names explicitly and refuses to resolve in the powerful party's favour. It is the strongest instance in the collection of an engineered proximity that also indicts the thing doing the engineering.

entries.name: Moonstruck
entries.author: Norman Jewison
entries.awards: Three Academy Awards — Actress, Supporting Actress, and **Original Screenplay** for John Patrick Shanley, 1988
entries.description: An original screenplay, and one of the few romantic comedies to win in that category. Its first kiss arrives early and in anger, creating the plot…
entries.text: An original screenplay, and one of the few romantic comedies to win in that category. Its first kiss arrives early and in anger, creating the plot rather than resolving it — the underused version of the device, and the reason the film's middle has somewhere to go. The family functions as an active constituency with its own competing claims rather than as comic background, which is the meddling-family trope done with the participants given real stakes and real grievances of their own.

entries.name: When Harry Met Sally...
entries.author: Rob Reiner
entries.awards: Academy Award **nomination** for Original Screenplay, lost; **BAFTA win** for Original Screenplay, over the same film that beat it at the Oscars
entries.description: An original screenplay by Nora Ephron, whose three career Oscar nominations all produced losses. The split result on this film — losing the Academy…
entries.text: An original screenplay by Nora Ephron, whose three career Oscar nominations all produced losses. The split result on this film — losing the Academy Award and winning the BAFTA against the same competitor — is routinely merged into a single claim in either direction. The screenplay makes the friendship substantial enough to be worth protecting, so the obstacle is generated entirely by the relationship's own value rather than imported: the hardest and most durable version of friends-to-lovers, and the reason the film is still the reference point.

entries.name: Pretty Woman
entries.author: Garry Marshall
entries.awards: **One** Academy Award nomination — Best Actress, lost
entries.description: The award record is the batch's most-corrected: a widely used reference summary implies three nominations, adding Original Song and Original…
entries.text: The award record is the batch's most-corrected: a widely used reference summary implies three nominations, adding Original Song and Original Screenplay, and **both are false** — the screenwriter was never Oscar-nominated. The film is carded as a `weak` instance in the Tropes collection and the reason is structural: its climactic gesture restates the rescue economy the plot claims to be resolving, and the transaction the whole premise was built on is never actually settled. It is the most commercially successful romantic comedy of its decade and the clearest example of an ending that substitutes spectacle for reckoning.

entries.name: Before Sunrise
entries.author: Richard Linklater
entries.awards: Berlin International Film Festival **Silver Bear for Best Director**, awarded to Linklater personally rather than to the film
entries.description: Written by Linklater and Kim Krizan; the two leads are credited as co-writers only on the sequels. A day's shared journey through a city achieves what…
entries.text: Written by Linklater and Kim Krizan; the two leads are credited as co-writers only on the sequels. A day's shared journey through a city achieves what a long journey does, demonstrating that the requirement is displacement rather than distance — neither can be who they are at home. Its ending is a deferred arrangement that the first sequel reveals as unpaid, which is the risk a happy-for-now takes, and the reason the pack cards the sequel separately as the completed version of the same settlement.

entries.name: In the Mood for Love
entries.author: Wong Kar-wai
entries.awards: Cannes Best Actor for Tony Leung, and the Technical Grand Prize to its cinematographers and production designer — **no prize to the film itself**
entries.description: The award note matters because "won at Cannes" is how this film is universally described, and the prizes went to individuals. It was submitted for the…
entries.text: The award note matters because "won at Cannes" is how this film is universally described, and the prizes went to individuals. It was submitted for the Academy's foreign-language award and **was not nominated** — submission is not nomination, a distinction reference sources drop. The film sustains an entire romance on proximity, clothing and the rhythm of a corridor, with nothing consummated and nothing lacking, and it builds every component of a romance while withholding both the consummation and the ending.

entries.name: Portrait of a Lady on Fire
entries.author: Céline Sciamma
entries.awards: Cannes **Best Screenplay** — an official jury prize to Sciamma — and the **Queer Palm**, an independent sidebar prize; **César for Best Cinematography**, 2020
entries.description: Two distinct classes of Cannes award, frequently reported as one, and a César win that a widely used summary records as a nomination. It received no…
